parts.title: Signed integer range asymmetry

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why invert-and-add-one works
destinations.exact_quote: The [[Minimum signed value|minimum signed value]] is asymmetric. At eight bits, −128 exists but +128 does not. The pattern `10000000` complements and increments back to itself. That is valid residue arithmetic; it does **not** mean a signed language operation may return −128 as the mathematical negation of −128. For an `int` at its minimum, same-type negation, `abs`, and division by −1 cannot represent the answer. Narrow values can promote to a larger type first; always identify the actual operation type.

parts.title: Signed-versus-unsigned comparison hazards

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Follow C++'s types through the expression
destinations.exact_quote: For [[Mixed signedness|mixed-sign comparisons]], do not assume the signed operand stays signed. In `-1 < 1u`, −1 converts to `unsigned int` and the comparison is false. A valid index still needs `index >= 0` *and* a value less than the count. Checked comparison helpers such as `std::cmp_less` avoid surprising conversion comparisons; `std::in_range<T>` checks whether conversion to `T` is representable. These tools do not establish that a pointer is live or that an index belongs to a particular container.

destinations.exact_quote: [[Dynamic allocation and heap|An allocator]] divides larger memory regions into blocks for requests with variable lifetimes. **Metadata** is bookkeeping about those blocks. [[Allocator fragmentation|Internal fragmentation]] is unused capacity inside an allocated block: requesting 37 bytes in a 48-byte size class leaves 11 bytes of slack. **External fragmentation** is separated free space that cannot satisfy a particular contiguous request: two free 16-byte holes are not necessarily a usable 24-byte block. destinations.exact_quote: A **quiet NaN** generally propagates through ordinary arithmetic without signaling invalid solely because it is quiet. parts.title: Why decimal fractions such as 0.1 are usually inexact

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: The stored value is exact; its intended meaning may not be
destinations.exact_quote: Decimal base ten contains factors 2 and 5, so $1/10$ terminates in decimal. Binary base two has only factor 2, so a terminating binary denominator must be a power of two. A **dyadic rational** is an integer divided by a power of two. Every finite binary floating value is dyadic; $1/10$ is not.

parts.title: Instruction execution pipeline intuition

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why a five-stage pipeline is an explanation, not a prediction of modern silicon
destinations.exact_quote: Start with the familiar teaching model: an instruction is fetched from instruction memory, decoded into an operation, executed by some functional unit, accesses data memory where necessary, and eventually commits or retires its architectural result. An elementary five-stage processor makes this sequence visible because each stage can be occupied by a different instruction. Suppose five independent instructions each require one stage per cycle. Without overlapping execution, they need roughly twenty-five stage-cycles; with an ideally filled pipeline, the first result still incurs pipeline startup latency, but later results may retire every cycle. This distinction between **latency** (delay from a particular input to its result) and **throughput** (amount of work completed per unit time) will recur throughout graphics computing. Pipeline depth is not automatically a speedup: longer pipelines increase latency and can amplify recovery after a wrong branch prediction.

parts.title: Superscalar execution

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why a five-stage pipeline is an explanation, not a prediction of modern silicon
destinations.exact_quote: Real out-of-order superscalar CPUs do not generally pass every instruction through exactly these five physical boxes. They may decode instructions into micro-operations, rename registers, issue several instructions per cycle to multiple execution units, execute out of order when their data operands are ready, and retire architectural effects in a constrained order. The five-stage drawing is a conceptual scaffold, not a substitute for a processor-specific execution model. If a professor asks why a CPU could complete a later arithmetic instruction before an earlier cache-missing load, the answer is not that source order has stopped mattering: the CPU can make speculative progress on independent operations while preserving the ISA's required architectural behavior and exception/retirement rules.

destinations.exact_quote: Trace a hot asset loop. One instruction loads the record's mass, another loads x, a third multiplies them and a fourth adds the product to an accumulator. The multiplication cannot begin before its required load values are available: this is a **read-after-write (RAW)** true dependency. But loading the next record's x or mass may be independent, enabling overlap. **Write-after-read (WAR)** and **write-after-write (WAW)** name other kinds of apparent register or storage ordering pressure; register renaming can remove *false name dependencies* when the ISA and microarchitecture permit it. Genuine memory aliasing is harder: the compiler and CPU cannot assume arbitrary stores and loads are unrelated without a justified alias and ordering analysis.

parts.title: Branch prediction

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why a five-stage pipeline is an explanation, not a prediction of modern silicon
destinations.exact_quote: Now consider branches. The loop can skip retired assets by checking an active flag. A modern predictor uses history and patterns to guess the next instruction address before the condition is resolved. A correct prediction keeps the pipeline supplied with useful instructions; a misprediction discards work along the wrong control path and restarts at the correct path. A rough branch-cost contribution is **mispredictions × average recovery cost**, but the actual penalty depends on the processor and the surrounding code's ability to overlap other work. A branch that is almost always taken may cost far less than an unpredictable branch on scattered flags, yet replacing every branch with conditional masking is not always faster. Masking may evaluate operations for inactive elements and increase memory traffic or instructions.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why a five-stage pipeline is an explanation, not a prediction of modern silicon
destinations.exact_quote: Speculative execution is the hardware's attempt to execute predicted future work before all earlier control conditions have retired. parts.title: Register files and register pressure

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why a five-stage pipeline is an explanation, not a prediction of modern silicon
destinations.exact_quote: Registers hold immediate operands and intermediates close to execution units. They are finite. If an optimization creates too many simultaneously live values, some may be **spilled** into stack memory, adding loads and stores. This is *register pressure*. Inlining an enormous templated function or unrolling a loop aggressively may increase pressure enough to hurt performance even when instruction count is reduced. We should inspect compiler assembly and profiling counters before pronouncing more unrolling better.

parts.title: CPU cache hierarchy: L1, L2, L3

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: The asset loop reaches into main memory through multiple levels of storage. A core typically has small, comparatively fast L1 caches, larger/slower L2 caches and some form of shared or distributed last-level cache, backed by DRAM. Exact sizes, associativity, inclusivity and latency vary by CPU, platform and topology. A **cache hit** finds the requested data in the addressed level; a miss causes a request to another level. One source-level load may interact with line-fill buffers, prefetchers, store queues and other mechanisms, so counting source loads does not directly count DRAM transactions.

parts.title: Cache lines as transfer units

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: A cache does not normally fetch a single isolated four-byte float. It obtains a **cache line**, commonly 64 bytes on many current general-purpose CPUs but not universally. If we need one float from a large 64-byte record and never touch the rest, the line brings mostly irrelevant data. If we instead traverse a contiguous array of four-byte x values, each 64-byte line can contain sixteen useful floats, subject to alignment, line size and actual cache implementation. The useful fraction of transferred bytes therefore depends on how the algorithm walks storage, not on how many arithmetic operations appear in its source.

parts.title: Spatial locality

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: **Spatial locality** means nearby addresses are likely to be used close together; **temporal locality** means a recently used address will be accessed again soon enough that retaining its line is useful. A sequential scan of densely packed elements often benefits from spatial locality and hardware prefetching. Pointer chasing through an unpredictable linked structure can create a dependency chain in which the next address is unknown until the current node is loaded. Even if a linked list has the same O(n) traversal complexity as a vector, it can have radically different stalls due to line utilization, prefetchability and allocation locality. Big-O does not model those constant factors or data distribution.

parts.title: Cache associativity

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: Caches are not fully associative infinite dictionaries. A conventional set-associative cache maps addresses to sets, and each set has a limited number of ways. After the line offset bits, some address bits participate in set selection; remaining address information forms the tag (with actual indexing and physical-address constraints depending on the cache). If many simultaneously needed lines map to the same set, they may repeatedly evict each other despite free capacity in other sets. This is a **conflict miss**; an initially unseen line can produce a compulsory miss; a working set too large for effective cache capacity can produce capacity misses. We should test layouts that produce set conflicts rather than assume every performance drop is an L3 miss.

parts.title: Hardware prefetching

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: Prefetchers may recognize predictable sequential or strided streams and begin loading future cache lines before an explicit load demands them. A pointer graph with random next links is less predictable. Prefetching can help hide latency but also consumes bandwidth and cache capacity; an ineffective prefetch may evict useful data. It is helpful to separate **latency**—the time for an access dependency to complete—from **bandwidth**—the sustained volume transferred per second. Many independent outstanding loads can saturate bandwidth despite high individual latency. A serialized pointer chase may be latency-bound despite using little total bandwidth.

parts.title: Translation Lookaside Buffer

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: Virtual addresses introduce another layer. The program operates with virtual addresses that hardware and the OS translate to physical memory using page-table structures, with a **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)** caching recent translations. A TLB miss may require walking page tables, sometimes generating extra memory accesses. Traversing many widely separated pages can exert TLB pressure even if each access touches only a few bytes. Larger pages can reduce the number of translations needed for the same contiguous region, but huge-page availability, fragmentation, OS policy, permissions and portability are real constraints. Huge pages are not a universal "speed" flag. The lab does not allocate huge pages, and no improvement is claimed from merely mentioning them.

parts.title: Huge pages concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: Virtual addresses introduce another layer. The program operates with virtual addresses that hardware and the OS translate to physical memory using page-table structures, with a **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)** caching recent translations. A TLB miss may require walking page tables, sometimes generating extra memory accesses. Traversing many widely separated pages can exert TLB pressure even if each access touches only a few bytes. Larger pages can reduce the number of translations needed for the same contiguous region, but huge-page availability, fragmentation, OS policy, permissions and portability are real constraints. Huge pages are not a universal "speed" flag. The lab does not allocate huge pages, and no improvement is claimed from merely mentioning them.

destinations.heading: When memory traffic becomes more expensive than arithmetic
destinations.exact_quote: On multiprocessor systems with non-uniform memory access (NUMA), the cost of DRAM may depend on the physical node holding a page and the node where the executing core is scheduled. parts.title: Data-oriented design from access patterns

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Rewrite the representation around access patterns, not names
destinations.exact_quote: Return to the 4,096 records. A conventional **array of structures (AoS)** stores one complete Particle object after another. It is convenient for editing one object at a time. Our demonstrative AoS contains four hot floats (x, y, z, mass) and twelve cold floats used by editor/debug features: sixty-four bytes of float fields in total before any additional layout effects. A hot pass reading only x and mass may transfer more unused data than necessary if it scans large cold-rich objects. A **structure of arrays (SoA)** instead keeps all x values contiguous, all mass values contiguous, and so on. Two hot streams can be loaded efficiently, and the compiler may more easily vectorize them.

parts.title: Array of Structures of Arrays

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Rewrite the representation around access patterns, not names
destinations.exact_quote: An **array of structures of arrays (AoSoA)** divides records into small blocks, with arrays of each field inside each block. This can combine block-local entity operations with SIMD-friendly lanes. The right block width depends on target vector widths, cache behavior, alignment and the algorithm's actual accesses; it is not universally 4, 8 or 16. Hot/cold splitting is another independent choice: store rarely used metadata elsewhere so a per-frame update does not repeatedly pull it through the cache.

parts.title: Data compaction and dense iteration

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Rewrite the representation around access patterns, not names
destinations.exact_quote: The [[tools/labs/phase4_cpu_systems_lab.cpp|Phase 4 CPU lab]] constructs the same exactly representable values in both layouts, sums their x × mass values, and verifies equality against 30,720. It also compacts active indices into a dense vector. **Compaction** converts a sparse set of survivors into a contiguous traversal-friendly representation, often using filter/scan/scatter on a GPU or a serial conditional append on a CPU. It has an upfront cost, so it is justified when the saved downstream work outweighs that cost. Existing stable logical handles must not be confused with new dense physical positions: a separate index map or generation checked reference maintains identity.

parts.title: False sharing across CPU cores

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Sharing a cache is not the same as safely sharing a value
destinations.exact_quote: Now parallelize scene updates. Suppose two threads increment independent counters in adjacent locations. If both counters occupy a single cache line, each core's writes can force coherence activity even though the values are distinct and the C++ program has no data race. This is **false sharing**. A data race is a language-level failure when conflicting non-atomic accesses lack required happens-before ordering; false sharing is a *performance* cost from coherence operating at a granularity larger than the variables.

parts.title: Cache coherence intuition

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Sharing a cache is not the same as safely sharing a value
destinations.exact_quote: A cache-coherence protocol such as a MESI-style model tracks line states that can be summarized as Modified, Exclusive, Shared and Invalid. Actual protocols include many additional states and variations. A core cannot simply write any shared copy while other cores simultaneously assume it is unchanged; the protocol arranges ownership, invalidation or other legal transitions. A pair of adjacent counters repeatedly written by different cores may cause the line to migrate. Conversely, two counters in separately aligned regions can reduce that particular interference, but padding increases memory footprint and may harm other access patterns.

parts.title: Memory fences at the hardware level

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Sharing a cache is not the same as safely sharing a value
destinations.exact_quote: Hardware memory fences and the C++ memory model must not be conflated. A CPU may reorder or buffer accesses internally subject to its ISA rules; a compiler may also reorder operations subject to C++ observable-behavior rules. A source-level std::atomic operation with release or acquire semantics constrains which operations can be published and observed between threads when the synchronization conditions actually hold. The final CPU instructions implementing those semantics vary by architecture. A fence instruction is neither a magic cache flush nor a universal cure for incorrect ownership and lifetime.

parts.title: SIMD lanes and vector registers

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: SIMD: one instruction, several elements, but only under a valid contract
destinations.exact_quote: A Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) operation performs the same kind of calculation on multiple lanes of a vector register. A simple vector-addition instruction might add four floats or eight floats at once on one ISA, while another ISA uses different vector lengths or instructions. SIMD improves *potential* arithmetic throughput and can reduce instruction overhead, but it still needs data, registers, issue bandwidth and stores. It does not guarantee faster wall-clock time when memory traffic dominates.

parts.title: SIMD load and store alignment

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: SIMD: one instruction, several elements, but only under a valid contract
destinations.exact_quote: Alignment means that an address is a multiple of a required boundary. Some SIMD loads benefit from or require alignment; others accept unaligned addresses with possible architectural or workload-dependent costs. ISO C++ object alignment, allocator guarantees and an ISA's memory-operation requirements are related but distinct. A programmer cannot assume a vector's data pointer is aligned to a particular extended SIMD width merely because the element is a float. If using aligned instructions, establish or check alignment through the correct allocator and type contracts.

parts.title: SIMD tail handling

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: SIMD: one instruction, several elements, but only under a valid contract
destinations.exact_quote: For a loop processing N elements in packets of W lanes, the main body executes roughly floor(N/W) packets, with a **tail** of N mod W elements. A portable implementation can process the tail with a scalar loop; an architecture-specific implementation may use masked loads/stores. Reading or writing beyond the valid buffer merely because the register contains unused lanes is not allowed. Masked instructions also require checking what the ISA promises about inactive-lane address validity and exceptions. A safe tail strategy is part of correctness, not a tuning detail.

parts.title: Auto-vectorization prerequisites

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: SIMD: one instruction, several elements, but only under a valid contract
destinations.exact_quote: Auto-vectorization depends on the compiler proving enough about loop independence, aliasing, trip counts, alignment and target instruction support. Conditional code, indirect indexing, potential exceptions and unclear alias relationships may block profitable transformations. The practical evidence chain is: compile with explicit optimization and target options, request the compiler's vectorization report, inspect the relevant machine code, check numerical correctness, then benchmark a realistic workload. The absence of a vectorization message does not alone prove poor performance; the presence of one does not prove speedup.

parts.title: Heap allocator goals

destinations.heading: Each allocation makes two promises: suitable storage and controlled lifetime
destinations.exact_quote: The general-purpose heap allocator answers requests for dynamically sized storage with a suitable alignment and a lifetime that can extend past the current function. Its goals can include efficient small allocations, acceptable fragmentation, low tail latency, safe multithreaded use and bounded metadata overhead. These goals conflict: a general allocator that handles arbitrary sizes and lifetimes cannot assume every object disappears at the end of a frame.

parts.title: Free-list allocator

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Each allocation makes two promises: suitable storage and controlled lifetime
destinations.exact_quote: Different ownership patterns suggest different allocation strategies. A free-list allocator maintains reusable blocks and can coalesce adjacent free blocks when its representation and policy support it. A stack allocator can roll back only in last-in-first-out order, often with markers rather than individual frees. A linear or arena allocator advances a cursor and releases storage in bulk, making allocation cheap when all objects share a lifetime boundary. A pool allocator serves fixed-size objects from slots; a slab allocator commonly groups objects of one size class into larger backing slabs. A buddy allocator partitions power-of-two blocks and can merge matched buddies when both become free. A size-class allocator chooses bins for ranges of request sizes and trades memory waste for speed and predictable reuse. None is best independent of the size/lifetime distribution.

parts.title: Allocation fragmentation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Each allocation makes two promises: suitable storage and controlled lifetime
destinations.exact_quote: **Internal fragmentation** is allocated space not used by the requested object, such as padding or rounding a 100-byte request up to a 128-byte size class. **External fragmentation** describes free storage split into blocks that cannot satisfy a needed larger contiguous allocation despite sufficient total free bytes. A simple aggregate percentage of wasted bytes cannot identify all causes of allocation latency. Metadata cost, thread-local caches, lock contention, page retention, NUMA placement and over-alignment should also be measured. A pool can reduce allocation cost for repeated small objects but may waste memory when its capacity remains unused or when object lifetimes vary widely.

parts.title: Placement allocation for engine objects

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Each allocation makes two promises: suitable storage and controlled lifetime
destinations.exact_quote: An allocation does **not** construct every desired C++ object by itself. Storage acquisition reserves appropriately sized and aligned bytes; object construction starts a typed lifetime in valid storage. Using **std::construct_at** or placement new on suitably aligned raw storage is a distinct operation from obtaining the bytes. Destruction ends the object's lifetime and may need to run its destructor before storage is returned or reused. This matters for resources holding strings, file descriptors, mutexes or GPU handles: simply resetting a bump pointer does not automatically call all their destructors.

parts.title: Frame allocators

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Each allocation makes two promises: suitable storage and controlled lifetime
destinations.exact_quote: A **frame arena** is appropriate for scratch arrays that unquestionably die together after a well-defined frame or job epoch. Our lab gives a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource a small aligned local byte array and null upstream. A std::pmr::vector stores one hundred integers in that region; an intentionally unreasonable reserve request exhausts it and throws std::bad_alloc rather than invisibly allocating a second backing region. This makes the capacity boundary observable. Destruction of the vector runs its element destructors, but a monotonic resource normally retains its backing blocks until it is itself released or destroyed. Treating a monotonic buffer like an ordinary per-object free list is conceptually wrong.

parts.title: Threads and shared address spaces

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: The editor wants to prepare visibility and mesh reports while the main thread continues handling input. A std::thread starts independent execution within the process address space; objects can therefore be accessed by multiple threads. Creating and destroying threads is not free: it can involve kernel scheduling resources, stack setup, runtime initialization and later joining. A context switch can change the running thread and incur scheduling and cache effects. The actual cost depends on the OS and workload, but repeatedly creating one thread for every tiny mesh task is normally an unexamined overhead risk. Persistent worker pools amortize it.

parts.title: Data races in the C++ memory model

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: Sharing memory is not the same as safely sharing memory. In the C++ memory model, conflicting accesses to the same non-atomic location by different threads without the required happens-before relation can cause a **data race**, whose behavior is undefined. A counter that sometimes "looks correct" in a release test is not proof of a race-free program. A volatile qualifier is not a C++ thread-synchronization primitive.

destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order

parts.title: Compare-and-exchange

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: **Compare-and-exchange (CAS)** attempts to replace an atomic value only if it equals an expected value. It is indispensable in many lock-free algorithms but not sufficient for safe memory reclamation. An **ABA** problem occurs when a location changes from value A to B and back to A between observations; a CAS testing only the current bits may incorrectly conclude that nothing relevant changed. Generational identities, tagged pointers or other versioning can distinguish some ABA cases, but the lifetime of objects behind atomic pointers still needs safe reclamation such as hazard pointers, epochs, reference counting or a carefully designed ownership protocol. A generation-checked MeshHandle does not make a lock-free queue safe by itself.

parts.title: Acquire semantics

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: In the Phase 4 lab, the producer writes an ordinary integer payload and then stores ready=true with **memory_order_release**. The consumer repeatedly loads ready with **memory_order_acquire**. When the acquire load observes the value written by the release store, the release synchronizes with that acquire, establishing the required happens-before relation for the earlier payload write. The consumer may then safely read the payload, provided no other unsynchronized thread concurrently mutates it. Merely having acquire on one atomic and release on an unrelated atomic is not enough.

parts.title: Mutex locking

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: Locks remain useful. A mutex protects an invariant by making critical sections mutually exclusive. Its unlock/lock synchronization also orders accesses to protected state. A reader-writer lock may allow concurrent readers when contention patterns justify it, but writers can starve under some policies; reader-heavy is not synonymous with faster. A spinlock repeatedly tries ownership and can waste CPU under preemption or long critical sections; it is generally unsuitable when sleeping, blocking I/O or expensive work happens inside the protected region. Lock choice must follow measured wait times, critical-section duration, fairness and scheduler behavior.

parts.title: Condition variables

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: A condition variable solves a different problem: a worker needs to sleep until work appears. The queue state remains protected by a mutex, and the wait must use a **predicate**. Spurious wakeups can occur, and a notification does not store an event forever like a queue message. A worker that wakes must recheck the shared condition while holding the lock. The laboratory's worker checks whether stopping is requested or tasks are nonempty before taking a job. It executes the job *outside* the queue lock so other producers and workers can make progress.

parts.title: Counting semaphores

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: Counting semaphores represent available permits and can coordinate bounded queues or resources without the exact same predicate structure as a condition variable. Latches wait for a count of arrivals; barriers coordinate repeated phases and may have completion actions. They are not interchangeable: a worker waiting for queue work has different semantics from a set of threads that must all finish one simulation phase before any begin the next.

parts.title: Deadlock and circular wait

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Threads share a process address space, not a common execution order
destinations.exact_quote: **Deadlock** occurs when a set of waits cannot progress, often through circular acquisition of resources. A lock ordering discipline eliminates a class of cycles: if code always acquires mutex A before mutex B, it cannot also acquire B and then wait for A through a reversed order. std::scoped_lock can acquire multiple mutexes using a deadlock-avoiding mechanism. But blocking on a future while holding a lock needed by the future's producer can still deadlock; so can tasks waiting on tasks from a fixed-size pool with no free worker. **Livelock** is continued activity without useful progress; **starvation** is failure of a participant to receive needed service despite system progress. A lock can be race-free and still cause unacceptable tail latency or starvation under contention.

parts.title: Job systems

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A job system is a scheduling graph, not merely a vector of threads
destinations.exact_quote: The Phase 4 lab constructs a real small worker pool with a shared mutex-protected deque, a condition variable and packaged_task-backed futures. Callers submit jobs; each worker removes a job under the lock and executes it outside the lock. Exceptions thrown by a user job are stored in the packaged task and can be rethrown by future.get() in the caller. Shutdown changes a protected stop flag, wakes the workers, permits queued work to drain and joins all worker threads. These choices are correct for the exercised protocol; they are **not** work stealing or a complete dependency-aware production scheduler.

parts.title: Work stealing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A job system is a scheduling graph, not merely a vector of threads
destinations.exact_quote: **Work stealing** addresses load imbalance by letting idle workers take work from other workers' queues, commonly using per-worker deques with local and stolen ends. The owner and thief must obey carefully designed synchronization and reclamation rules. A work-stealing deque is significantly more difficult than one mutex-protected queue: empty/single-element races, index wraparound, false sharing, memory ordering and capacity growth all become correctness concerns. The current lab deliberately does not claim to implement it. MIT 6.172's parallelism and Cilk runtime material provides a path to deeper implementations and work/span analysis.

destinations.heading: A job system is a scheduling graph, not merely a vector of threads
destinations.exact_quote: A **task dependency graph** makes execution constraints explicit. parts.title: Sampling profilers

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Profile first: one plausible optimization can hide the real bottleneck
destinations.exact_quote: A **sampling profiler** periodically observes execution stacks with relatively low overhead, yielding statistical evidence of where CPU time is spent. An **instrumentation profiler** records explicitly marked events or functions and can produce precise phase durations and counts but alters the workload through instrumentation cost. **Flame graphs** aggregate stack samples: their horizontal extent represents sampled frequency/weight under the collection method, not source execution chronology or necessarily actual wall-clock span. The tool should be chosen according to the question: instruction stalls need hardware-aware profiling; lock contention needs wait analysis; transient GPU latency needs CPU/GPU timeline correlation; memory ownership needs allocation traces.

destinations.heading: Profile first: one plausible optimization can hide the real bottleneck
destinations.exact_quote: A proper microbenchmark includes warm-up and repeated runs, measures enough work to exceed timer quantization, checks that computations were not optimized away, and reports distributions rather than one favorable number. Cache warmth, CPU frequency, thermal state, background processes, address-space layout and data alignment can all influence results. Statistical noise should be quantified through repeated independent runs, medians and appropriate uncertainty estimates. Comparing two implementations only after a code cleanup, different compiler option or different input is confounded.

destinations.heading: Profile first: one plausible optimization can hide the real bottleneck
destinations.exact_quote: A well-grounded optimization report should state: the original frame/workload and measurement setup; a hypothesis tied to one observed bottleneck; a code change that preserves required semantics; the new profile and end-to-end measurement under the same conditions; variance and failure cases; and whether the change improved the actual user-visible workload. parts.title: Abstract data types versus concrete data structures

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: What an abstract data type promises, and what a representation actually pays
destinations.exact_quote: A *set* promises operations such as insert, contains and erase. It does not promise that those operations use a sorted array, hash table, tree or bitmap. A *map* associates keys with values; a *queue* preserves first-in-first-out order; a *priority queue* extracts an element of highest defined priority rather than oldest arrival. These are **abstract data types (ADTs)**, specified by what results and state transitions are observable. A **data structure** is a representation that implements those operations, with a choice of memory layout and algorithms.

parts.title: Time complexity and operation counting

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: What an abstract data type promises, and what a representation actually pays
destinations.exact_quote: Let n denote the number of stored assets. An operation's running time can be analyzed by counting primitive steps under a declared computational model. The asymptotic upper bound T(n)=O(f(n)) means there exist positive constants C and n₀ such that T(n) ≤ C f(n) for every n≥n₀. Omega similarly states a lower bound, T(n)=Ω(f(n)), and Theta means both hold, T(n)=Θ(f(n)). These are relationships between functions as input size grows, not timing measurements in milliseconds. They also do not capture allocation patterns, cache misses, branch behavior or GPU synchronization.

destinations.heading: What an abstract data type promises, and what a representation actually pays
destinations.exact_quote: Space complexity should identify auxiliary storage separately from input and output storage. Merge sort may allocate Θ(n) temporary storage; in-place heapsort can use O(1) extra array space with an unstable order; recursive depth-first search may use O(V) call-stack frames in a long chain, while an explicit stack makes that usage visible and avoids stack overflow from unbounded recursion. In an engine, the difference between transient scratch and persistent storage also affects frame arenas, thread-local resources and GPU memory budgets.

parts.title: Best, average, and worst-case complexity

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: What an abstract data type promises, and what a representation actually pays
destinations.exact_quote: **Best-, average- and worst-case** statements require different assumptions. A linear search for a key at the front may take one comparison; its worst case scans n elements; an average-case result needs a distribution over positions or inputs. Hash lookup is expected O(1) only under a stated hashing, table and load regime; malicious collisions or pathological clustering can create much worse behavior. A balanced search tree offers O(log n) worst-case search but may have less favorable constants and locality. These distinctions do not license omitting a worst-case failure or calling an empirical benchmark "a proof of average complexity."

parts.title: Singly linked lists

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Why a vector can grow cheaply even though reallocation is expensive
destinations.exact_quote: A linked list avoids relocating existing nodes during insertion at a known position, but the nodes commonly require separately allocated memory and pointer chasing. A singly linked list needs a previous node to delete an arbitrary element efficiently; a doubly linked list stores both previous and next pointers to support local bidirectional edits. An **intrusive list** embeds links inside the caller-owned objects, saving a separate wrapper allocation but imposing a strict lifetime and membership contract, as M018 demonstrated. A queue of render commands may benefit from contiguous or ring-buffer storage even when a list offers the same O(1) logical enqueue/dequeue cost.

destinations.heading: A ring queue is the first container where a boundary bug becomes a temporal bug
destinations.exact_quote: Other queue and stack representations differ. A stack returns last-in-first-out (LIFO), making it useful for explicit DFS or nested temporary lifetimes. A deque supports efficient operations at both ends and often uses segmented storage rather than one contiguous vector; iterator and reference stability contracts differ from vector and must be checked. Scheduling queues may use one priority heap, per-worker double-ended work-stealing deques or separate lanes for latency-sensitive tasks. The queue's ADT contract should reflect its intended ordering, not assume every FIFO is suitable for parallel scheduling.

parts.title: Bloom filters and probabilistic membership

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A Bloom filter is a one-sided answer to a different question
destinations.exact_quote: Sometimes the streaming system wants to ask whether a requested asset is *definitely not present* before performing an expensive lookup. A Bloom filter uses a bit array of length m and k hash functions. Adding a key sets k selected bits. Querying a key checks those bits; if any is zero, the key was never added **under the filter's insertion and no-deletion contract**. If every bit is one, the key is only *possibly* present because other inserted keys may have set the same bits. Hence ordinary Bloom filters permit false positives but not false negatives for inserted keys, assuming the bits were not cleared and the hashing representation is consistent.

parts.title: Bitsets as dense boolean sets

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A Bloom filter is a one-sided answer to a different question
destinations.exact_quote: A **bitset** itself is a dense representation of boolean membership over a bounded integer domain. If our engine tracks a known finite set of component flags, contiguous bits can enable efficient set union/intersection via word-wise operations. However, a huge sparse identifier space wastes memory if directly indexed. A Bloom filter trades exact answers for compact approximate membership; a bitset represents exact membership in its declared universe; a hash set represents exact keys in a dynamic universe. These are distinct ADT contracts.

parts.title: Binary trees

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Trees emerge when the question changes from existence to ordered structure
destinations.exact_quote: A hash table is poorly suited to "find all assets whose names are between A and M" or "give me the next key after this one" without additional ordering. A **binary search tree (BST)** maintains the invariant that keys in the left subtree are ordered before the current key and those in the right subtree after it. Search follows comparisons from root to a child until the key is found or an empty child is reached. Its time is O(h), where h is the tree height. A balanced tree keeps h=O(log n), while an ordinary unbalanced BST can degenerate into a chain with h=Θ(n) under sorted insertion.

parts.title: AVL-tree balancing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Trees emerge when the question changes from existence to ordered structure
destinations.exact_quote: **AVL trees** maintain a bound on each node's left/right subtree height difference and rebalance using single or double rotations. A rotation changes local parent-child links while preserving in-order key order. The algorithm must update stored heights and parent pointers correctly after a structural change; forgetting one can turn an apparently valid tree into an incorrect future insertion or deletion. **Red-black trees** enforce coloring constraints, a black root and NIL leaves, no red-red parent/child relation and equal black-height along root-to-leaf paths. These invariants constrain the longest path relative to the shortest and yield logarithmic height, although their exact balancing and update costs differ from AVL trees. Choosing AVL vs red-black is a tradeoff across lookup frequency, mutation frequency, memory and implementation invariants, not a matter of one being universally "faster."

parts.title: B-trees

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Trees emerge when the question changes from existence to ordered structure
destinations.exact_quote: A **B-tree** generalizes a node to hold multiple sorted keys and child pointers, reducing tree height by increasing branching factor. **B+ trees** commonly store all actual records or payload references in leaves, with internal nodes guiding searches and linked leaves supporting range iteration. Their strength appears when a node maps naturally to a page or cache block; asymptotic logarithms in the number of keys are less informative than the number of blocks touched. Disk-oriented indexes, memory-mapped scene metadata and on-disk package catalogs motivate this model. A single binary node per allocation can be a poor fit when an expensive storage access retrieves an entire page anyway.

parts.title: Binary heaps

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A heap is an ordering promise weaker than a sorted array
destinations.exact_quote: When the navigation or task system needs the next smallest tentative distance, a **priority queue** is the relevant ADT. A binary heap implements it with an array representing a nearly complete binary tree. With zero-based indexing, a node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 when those indices are in bounds; a non-root node's parent is floor((i−1)/2). The min-heap invariant requires each parent key to be no greater than its children. It says nothing about the relative order of siblings or unrelated branches, so simply iterating the array does not produce sorted output.

destinations.exact_quote: When the navigation or task system needs the next smallest tentative distance, a **priority queue** is the relevant ADT. A binary heap implements it with an array representing a nearly complete binary tree. With zero-based indexing, a node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 when those indices are in bounds; a non-root node's parent is floor((i−1)/2). The min-heap invariant requires each parent key to be no greater than its children. It says nothing about the relative order of siblings or unrelated branches, so simply iterating the array does not produce sorted output.

parts.title: Tries and prefix trees

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Trees emerge when the question changes from existence to ordered structure
destinations.exact_quote: A **trie** indexes keys by successive symbols or bits, with branching along the key prefix. A radix tree compresses chains of single-child nodes into labeled edges or larger steps, reducing pointer overhead when paths share long prefixes. The cost depends on key length and representation, not just the number of keys. Tries can support prefix queries and routing; their pointer-heavy variants may waste memory for sparse alphabets. Packed radix nodes or compressed tries can improve locality with different mutation complexity.

parts.title: Disjoint-set union data structure

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Disjoint sets explain connectivity that repeatedly changes
destinations.exact_quote: The broadphase may group colliders into contact islands, a graph algorithm may build a minimum spanning tree, and a simulation may merge connected components. We often need to maintain a partition of elements into disjoint sets under **find** ("which group contains this element?") and **union** ("merge these two groups"). A disjoint-set union (DSU) structure stores a parent forest. Each root represents one set. **Union by size or rank** attaches the smaller/shallower tree under the larger/greater-ranked root. **Path compression** shortens a find path by redirecting visited nodes toward the root.

The same graph data structure cannot make all those meanings interchangeable.

parts.title: Breadth-first search

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A queue discovers reachability one edge at a time
destinations.exact_quote: Suppose a unit moves through a grid in which every allowed step costs one. **Breadth-first search (BFS)** is appropriate. It begins at the source, marks its distance zero and places it in a FIFO queue. When a vertex at distance d is removed, all previously unseen neighbors are assigned distance d+1 and enqueued. Because all edges have equal unit cost and vertices are discovered in nondecreasing depth, the first discovery of each vertex yields its minimum hop count. The proof depends on queue order and equal edge costs; replacing the queue with an arbitrary stack breaks that property.

parts.title: Depth-first search

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A queue discovers reachability one edge at a time
destinations.exact_quote: **Depth-first search (DFS)** instead explores one branch as far as possible before returning. It can be written recursively, using call frames as the implicit stack, or iteratively with an explicit stack. A recursive implementation can overflow the program stack for a very long graph chain; an explicit stack lets the algorithm account for memory, order and limits. Both commonly run O(V+E) time for adjacency-list graphs when vertices/edges are processed in bounded ways.

parts.title: Topological sorting

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A render graph is an ordering proof, not simply a list of passes
destinations.exact_quote: A render graph often needs a **topological order**: every declared dependency A→B must place A before B. A directed graph has a topological ordering if and only if it is acyclic. One way to find that order is **Kahn's algorithm**. Count incoming edges for every vertex, enqueue vertices with indegree zero, remove a ready vertex, append it to the order, decrement its outgoing neighbors' indegrees, and enqueue any that become zero. If fewer than V vertices are emitted, a directed cycle remains.

parts.title: Strongly connected components concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: A render graph is an ordering proof, not simply a list of passes
destinations.exact_quote: A **strongly connected component (SCC)** is a maximal vertex set in which every vertex can reach every other through directed paths. Condensing each SCC into one supervertex produces an acyclic component graph. Algorithms such as Kosaraju or Tarjan find SCCs in O(V+E) time for adjacency-list graphs under standard assumptions. SCCs are useful for diagnosing cyclic modules, scene dependencies or feedback groups. They do not automatically make cyclic tasks executable: cycles may require a fixed-point solver, explicit delays, previous-frame state or a contract that rejects them. A topological sorter is allowed to reject cycles even when an application could intentionally solve a feedback system through a different algorithm.

parts.title: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Shortest paths: the edge assumptions determine the proof
destinations.exact_quote: **Dijkstra's algorithm** keeps the smallest discovered tentative distance to each vertex, repeatedly extracts the currently smallest tentative distance, and relaxes outgoing edges. If edge weight w(u,v) is nonnegative, then once a reachable vertex is extracted with the smallest unsettled distance, no detour through a not-yet-extracted vertex can later produce a shorter path to it. This is the critical invariant behind Dijkstra's correctness. Negative weights invalidate that argument.

parts.title: Bellman-Ford shortest paths

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Shortest paths: the edge assumptions determine the proof
destinations.exact_quote: **Bellman–Ford** relaxes all edges repeatedly. After at most V−1 rounds, every shortest *simple* path in a graph without reachable negative cycles has been considered, because such a path contains no more than V−1 edges. One more improving relaxation indicates a reachable negative cycle under the usual finite-distance interpretation. This algorithm allows negative edge weights, unlike Dijkstra, but costs O(VE) in a straightforward implementation. The lab checks one negative-edge graph and detects an intentionally created reachable negative cycle.

destinations.exact_quote: An **admissible heuristic** never overestimates the true remaining optimal cost h*(n), so h(n) ≤ h*(n). A **consistent heuristic** satisfies h(u) ≤ w(u,v)+h(v) for each edge and h(goal)=0, under the conventional nonnegative route-cost model. Consistency is a triangle inequality on heuristic potential and implies that f values behave nondecreasingly along improvements in a way that permits particularly simple closed-set handling. Admissibility and consistency are related but not synonymous.

parts.title: Kruskal's algorithm

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Minimum spanning trees solve a different global problem
destinations.exact_quote: Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges by increasing weight and adds each edge only when it connects two distinct current components. A disjoint-set union detects whether adding an edge would close a cycle. The **cut property** justifies the greedy choice: under the standard MST conditions, a minimum-weight edge crossing a cut respecting the current partial forest is safe to add (with tie caveats concerning uniqueness). The Phase 5 lab computes a known four-vertex MST cost 1+2+3=6 and rejects a disconnected input rather than silently claiming a tree of all vertices.

parts.title: Prim's algorithm

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Minimum spanning trees solve a different global problem
destinations.exact_quote: Prim's algorithm grows a tree outward from the current connected set, repeatedly choosing the smallest edge crossing from the current tree into an unvisited vertex. It can use a priority queue and runs under different complexity bounds depending on adjacency representation and heap choice. Both find an MST for suitable connected undirected weighted graphs; neither is equivalent to Dijkstra or Bellman–Ford. A physics-island graph can use DSU connectivity without ever needing an MST, while an offline network-connection problem may require the MST objective. The abstract question determines the algorithm.

parts.title: Linear search

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Searching and sorting: the order of keys is itself a contract
destinations.exact_quote: Return to the editor's asset records. Finding one key in an unsorted vector requires **linear search**, O(n) comparisons in the worst case. Once a sequence is sorted according to a consistent comparator, **binary search** can discard half the remaining search interval per comparison, taking O(log n) comparisons for random-access iterators. But sorting the input costs work, and insertion or deletion may require moving data to maintain sorted order. parts.title: Selection sort

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Searching and sorting: the order of keys is itself a contract
destinations.exact_quote: Sorting algorithms have different contracts. **Selection sort** repeatedly selects the minimum of the remaining suffix, doing Θ(n²) comparisons even on favorable input in its straightforward form; it can minimize swaps in some contexts but is not a general high-performance choice. **Insertion sort** shifts elements into a sorted prefix, running O(n²) worst case but efficiently handling very small or nearly sorted arrays. **Bubble sort** repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; it also has quadratic worst-case behavior and offers little benefit in a production engine beyond illustrating local inversions and stability conditions.

parts.title: Merge sort

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Searching and sorting: the order of keys is itself a contract
destinations.exact_quote: **Merge sort** divides the input, sorts each half and merges them, giving Θ(n log n) comparisons under the standard implementation with O(n) auxiliary array storage; it can be stable by choosing the earlier equivalent element first. **Quicksort** partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the partitions. Its average performance is typically good under appropriate pivot and input assumptions, but poor pivots can produce Θ(n²) time; its partition scheme and duplicate-key handling are part of correctness. **Heapsort** offers O(n log n) worst-case time with a typical in-place array implementation but does not preserve equal-key order.

parts.title: Stable sorting

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Searching and sorting: the order of keys is itself a contract
destinations.exact_quote: A **stable sort** preserves the relative order of elements considered equal by its comparator. This matters when a renderer sorts by depth but wants earlier submission order among equal keys, or when multiple stable sorts establish a compound ordering. Stable does not mean deterministic across arbitrary parallel implementations with ambiguous floating-point keys: the comparator must satisfy a strict weak ordering and the execution must define any remaining tie policy. NaNs can violate the expected ordering model if floating comparisons are used without a consistent total-order policy.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Morton keys turn 2D proximity into a sortable integer—within limits
destinations.exact_quote: Spatial grids often classify objects into cells with integer coordinates. **Morton ordering**, also called Z-order, interleaves coordinate bits so that points sharing high-order spatial bits tend to share prefixes of the key. For 16-bit x and y, put x bit i at key bit 2i and y bit i at bit 2i+1. The Phase 5 lab explicitly expands those bits and verifies Morton(1,2)=9. Sorting by these keys can improve locality of cells and serve spatial partitioning or LBVH construction.

parts.title: Prefix sums or scans

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Prefix scans turn counts into a proof of nonoverlapping output
destinations.exact_quote: One of the most important bridges from CPU algorithms to GPU execution is the **prefix sum**, or scan. Suppose a GPU or CPU culling pass identifies per-cell counts c=[3,0,4,2]. An **exclusive scan** produces output offsets o=[0,3,3,7] with total 9. Cell i owns the half-open interval [o_i,o_i+c_i), yielding [0,3), [3,3), [3,7), [7,9). Every range is disjoint, and together they fill [0,9). This is more than a speed trick: it is an allocation and indexing correctness proof.

parts.title: Parallel scan concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Prefix scans turn counts into a proof of nonoverlapping output
destinations.exact_quote: A serial scan takes O(n) work and O(n) output space. A parallel scan can use an up-sweep/down-sweep tree, work-efficient block-local methods or hierarchical block aggregation, balancing total **work** against **span** and synchronization. A naive parallel algorithm may perform extra work or require a global barrier not available within one GPU workgroup. On GPUs, multi-dispatch scans and decoupled-lookback approaches involve device-specific synchronization and forward-progress assumptions; a portable CPU vector loop does not prove their correctness. This is exactly where Phase 4's task-dependency and memory-order reasoning becomes necessary.

parts.title: Two-pointer algorithms

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Windows, recursion, dynamic programming and greedy proofs are algorithmic choices
destinations.exact_quote: Many common engine operations are not named data structures at all; they are patterns for arranging computation. A **two-pointer algorithm** maintains two indexes with an invariant, such as advancing from both ends of a sorted collision-pair list until a target relationship is found. A **sliding window** maintains a contiguous active interval while extending its right boundary and removing expired left elements. If each pointer only moves forward O(n) times, the total work can be linear, despite a loop nested inside another loop. The proof depends on monotonic motion and the exact window predicate; arbitrary negative weights or nonlinear update rules can invalidate an easy window argument.

parts.title: Dynamic programming state formulation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Windows, recursion, dynamic programming and greedy proofs are algorithmic choices
destinations.exact_quote: **Dynamic programming (DP)** applies when subproblems overlap and the result can be composed from smaller optimal subproblem results. A DP state must contain enough information to make the recurrence valid. **Memoization** evaluates states on demand and caches their answers, often via recursion; **tabulation** fills a table in an order satisfying dependencies. They can compute the same recurrence but differ in reachability, recursion overhead, storage and traversal order. The Phase 5 lab finds the minimum number of coins to make total six from denominations {1,3,4}: two coins of value three. A naive greedy choice 4+1+1 uses three coins, showing that a locally largest denomination is not always globally optimal.

parts.title: Reservoir sampling

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Randomization needs a probability proof as well as a seeded test
destinations.exact_quote: **Reservoir sampling** can select one uniformly from a stream of unknown length without retaining all elements. Initially keep the first. At the i-th observed item (one-based), replace the reservoir with probability 1/i. By induction, an earlier element remains chosen after step i with probability (1/(i−1))×((i−1)/i)=1/i, while the newest element is selected with probability 1/i. Every item thus has equal probability when the stream ends. The proof assumes the random choice really implements the intended distribution.

parts.title: LRU cache data structure

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: An LRU cache and a sparse set reconnect algorithms to engine ownership
destinations.exact_quote: The streaming system may keep only K active mesh descriptions in a memory cache. A **Least Recently Used (LRU)** cache evicts the entry that has not been accessed for the longest time under the cache's declared observation model. An ordered linked list can record recency, and a hash table can map keys to list iterators. On a hit, splice the existing node to the front; on insertion when full, remove the tail and erase its index entry. With appropriate hashing and container guarantees, lookup and recency adjustment are expected O(1). The laboratory exercises capacity two: access key one before inserting key three, then verify key two is evicted.

parts.title: Sparse-set data structure

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: An LRU cache and a sparse set reconnect algorithms to engine ownership
destinations.exact_quote: A **sparse set** is valuable for entity IDs drawn from a sparse universe when most active components should be iterated densely. A sparse array maps an entity index to a dense position, while a dense array stores the active entity IDs and component values. Lookup checks bounds and verifies that the dense entry at the candidate position really belongs to the queried ID; otherwise an old sparse position can falsely report membership after swap-remove. Removing one entity often swaps the final dense element into the hole and updates its sparse index. This keeps iteration dense but invalidates positional references, explaining the need for logical handles.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Immediate footing — covector and dual space
destinations.exact_quote:
### Immediate footing — covector and dual space

A covector is a linear measurement that takes a vector to a scalar; in coordinates it can be written as a row $n^T$ acting on displacement $t$ by $n^Tt$. The dual space contains all such linear measurements. A normal to a surface can be defined as a covector that returns zero on every tangent displacement: $n^Tt=0$. Under a basis change, vector and covector coordinates transform differently so their pairing stays the same. In an orthonormal Euclidean frame a covector is often identified with a normal column vector, but that identification depends on the metric.

parts.title: Why surface normals transform differently from positions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: First-use completion — how coordinate measurements become normals, gradients, and reliable code
destinations.exact_quote:
#### First-use completion — how coordinate measurements become normals, gradients, and reliable code

We can now derive rather than memorize the inverse-transpose rule. Write the physical displacement as $v=Bc$, with the two columns of $B$ holding the basis directions and $c$ holding their coefficients. A coordinate measurement is a *row* $\ell$ acting on $v$. If we want the number it reports to remain unchanged, then
$$
\ell(v)=\ell(Bc)=(\ell B)c.
$$
Thus the same measurement is represented by the row $\ell B$ in the new coordinate system; conversely, a row specified on $c$ becomes $\ell_c B^{-1}$ when we express it in the world coordinates $v$. This is not a special normal-vector trick: it follows from demanding that measuring the same displacement gives the same scalar. A vector's coordinates and the coordinates of a linear measurement cannot generally obey the same conversion rule.

destinations.heading: Immediate footing — matrix
destinations.exact_quote:
### Immediate footing — matrix

A matrix is a rectangular table that defines an input-output rule formed from weighted sums after input and output coordinates are chosen. With column vectors, its columns are the images of the input coordinate directions. For example, $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$ maps $\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$ to $\begin{bmatrix}4\\7\end{bmatrix}$ because $A\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2+2\\1+6\end{bmatrix}$. The matrix shape determines which inputs it accepts. Row-major and column-major describe memory layout, not a different mathematical map.

The **identity** $I_n$ has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It sends every basis direction to itself, so $I_n\mathbf x=\mathbf x$. For an $m\times n$ matrix, use $I_mA=A$ and $AI_n=A$. destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: The origin exposes the limit of an ordinary linear map
destinations.exact_quote:
## The origin exposes the limit of an ordinary linear map

Our robot can now rotate, stretch and shear a displacement. But it still cannot place the panel somewhere else in the workcell using a three-by-three linear map alone. The reason is already inside the definition of linearity. A linear map $L$ obeys $L(a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v)=aL(\mathbf u)+bL(\mathbf v)$. Set both coefficients to zero and we obtain $L(\mathbf0)=\mathbf0$. The origin is fixed. A translation by a nonzero vector $\mathbf t$ sends zero to $\mathbf t$, so translation is not linear in ordinary three-dimensional coordinates.

parts.title: Dynamic matrix storage and strides

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: Dynamic matrix storage makes factorization dimensions and lifetimes explicit
destinations.exact_quote:
## Dynamic matrix storage makes factorization dimensions and lifetimes explicit

Decomposition input sizes are runtime values, so fixed `Mat3` types are not enough. An owning dense matrix should keep dimensions and one contiguous allocation. For row-major storage, element $(i,j)$ is at offset $i\cdot s+j$, where $s$ is the row stride and equals the number of columns for tightly packed storage. A non-owning view needs a pointer, row count, column count, row stride, and extent/capacity information sufficient to verify that the last referenced element is within the allocation. `std::vector<std::vector<double>>` is usually a poor dense numerical layout: rows may have separate allocations, rows are not guaranteed adjacent, and pointer chasing impedes cache use and library interoperability.

parts.title: SIMD matrix multiplication

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs.md
destinations.heading: SIMD and loop order change the execution schedule, not the matrix question
destinations.exact_quote:
## SIMD and loop order change the execution schedule, not the matrix question

SIMD means **single instruction, multiple data**. A four-lane operation may multiply four corresponding scalar pairs at once. For a row dot vector, lane products still need to be added into one result. That addition is a **horizontal reduction**, because several lanes contribute to one scalar. A lane-wise result and a reduction have different data movement and rounding behavior.

### The sign changes the stored value without changing the orientation

The inverse of $-q$ is $-q^{-1}$, so $(-q)p(-q)^{-1}=qpq^{-1}$. Thus $q$ and $-q$ are different algebraic values with the same three-dimensional rotation action. destinations.heading: Norm repair and sign selection solve different problems
destinations.exact_quote:
### Norm repair and sign selection solve different problems

Floating-point composition perturbs the unit constraint. Explicit Euler integration also leaves the unit sphere even in exact arithmetic because it follows a tangent-line approximation to curved motion. A renormalization policy can normalize after each update or when the measured squared-norm error exceeds a justified threshold. Use finite/range-safe normalization; a NaN can evade an ordinary `if (n2 <= 0)` test, and squaring extreme finite coefficients can overflow.

destinations.heading: Norm repair and sign selection solve different problems
destinations.exact_quote:
### Norm repair and sign selection solve different problems

Floating-point composition perturbs the unit constraint. Explicit Euler integration also leaves the unit sphere even in exact arithmetic because it follows a tangent-line approximation to curved motion. A renormalization policy can normalize after each update or when the measured squared-norm error exceeds a justified threshold. Use finite/range-safe normalization; a NaN can evade an ordinary `if (n2 <= 0)` test, and squaring extreme finite coefficients can overflow.

The ideal pinhole image is not necessarily where a real lens sends a ray. A distortion model maps ideal normalized coordinates $(x,y)$ to measured coordinates $(x_d,y_d)$. Coefficients are tied to the declared model and coordinate units; they are not universal lens facts.

parts.title: Asset hot reloading

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds.md
destinations.heading: Asset hot reloading
destinations.exact_quote:
Hot reload is not:

```text
file changed
destroy old object
load new object.
```

```text
source change detected
        ↓
derive new artifact
        ↓
validate artifact
        ↓
create replacement runtime resource
        ↓
replacement fully ready?
      /    \
    no      yes
    |        |
keep old    publish new
             |
             v
         retire old safely
```

parts.title: CMake target model

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds.md
destinations.heading: Dependencies, composition, and the build graph
destinations.exact_quote: CMake expresses build relationships through targets. `PRIVATE` requirements are for the target's own compilation/link; `INTERFACE` requirements are for consumers; `PUBLIC` does both. These are usage requirements, not merely visibility adjectives. A public header that includes a dependency's header may require that dependency to be transitive; an implementation-only dependency should remain private. Overusing PUBLIC spreads compiler flags and dependencies into unrelated targets. Underusing it creates downstream missing-include or link errors.

destinations.heading: Dependencies, composition, and the build graph
destinations.exact_quote: A build tool schedules a DAG of actions. Ninja or another generator can run independent edges in parallel, but only if generated inputs and dependencies are declared. C++ modules make dependencies more explicit because a consumer needs a compiled module interface artifact before its own compilation; a module cycle remains an architectural cycle. A module or header organization cannot repair unclear ownership.
