parts.title: Why rasterization converts primitives into covered samples

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**What rasterization is actually solving**

Suppose a triangle exists mathematically in continuous 3D space.

Its vertices might be

$$
P_0=(-1,-1,-5),\qquad
P_1=(1,-1,-5),\qquad
P_2=(0,1,-5).
$$

Your display, however, is not continuous. It might be a grid such as

$$
1920\times1080
$$

containing discrete pixel locations, and potentially several **samples per pixel** if multisampling is enabled.

There is therefore a fundamental conversion:

$$
\boxed{\text{continuous geometric primitive}
\longrightarrow
\text{discrete covered samples}}
$$

That conversion is rasterization.

A rasterizer does **not** fundamentally answer:

> “What color is this triangle?”

That is shading.

It answers something closer to:

> “For this projected triangle, which sample locations lie inside it, and what interpolated primitive data should each generated fragment receive?”

The logical pipeline we are constructing is:

$$
\text{vertex/index memory}
\rightarrow
\text{primitive assembly}
\rightarrow
\text{vertex processing}
\rightarrow
\text{clip coordinates}
\rightarrow
\text{clipping}
\rightarrow
\text{perspective divide}
\rightarrow
\text{NDC}
\rightarrow
\text{viewport}
\rightarrow
\text{triangle setup}
\rightarrow
\text{coverage}
\rightarrow
\text{interpolation}
\rightarrow
\text{fragment invocation}
\rightarrow
\text{depth test}.
$$

Keep four words separate throughout this phase:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Pixel** | A discrete image location/storage location. |
| **Sample** | A point where coverage/depth may be evaluated. One pixel can have multiple samples. |
| **Fragment** | Candidate rasterized work generated from a primitive for one pixel/sample region. |
| **Framebuffer value** | The value eventually stored after tests/blending/etc. |

A fragment is therefore not automatically a final pixel.

parts.title: Vertices as attribute records

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Parts 1802–1814 — what enters the graphics pipeline**

A vertex should be mentally understood as an **attribute record**, not as “a position.”

A useful CPU representation is:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;   // Geometry, object/local space.
    Vec3 normal;     // Surface direction.
    Vec2 uv;         // Texture parameterization.
    Vec3 color;      // Optional authored data.
};
```

A GPU vertex fetch operation conceptually receives an index $i$ and reads fields such as

$$
\text{position}[i],\quad
\text{normal}[i],\quad
\text{uv}[i].
$$

The position is only one member of a vertex record.

This distinction becomes extremely important when vertices share a geometric location but require different attributes. A cube has eight geometric corner positions, but a hard-edged textured cube commonly needs more than eight rendering vertices because one corner can require several different normals or UV coordinates.

So:

$$
\text{geometric point} \neq \text{rendering vertex}.
$$

---

parts.title: Vertex reuse and post-transform caches

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
This provides two different savings.

The obvious saving is **memory/bandwidth**: shared vertices do not need duplicate attribute records.

The subtler saving is **vertex shader work**.

Modern hardware normally contains a small cache of transformed vertices. If index $2$ was recently processed and appears again, the previous vertex shader result may be reused instead of invoking the vertex shader again.

Conceptually:

```text
index stream
0 1 2 0 2 3
    │   │
    └───┴─ recently transformed vertices may be reused
```

This is the **post-transform cache** idea from Part 1804.

It is important not to form the wrong abstraction:

> Indexed rendering does not promise “the vertex shader executes exactly once per unique index for the entire draw.”

Cache capacity is finite. Reuse depends on locality and implementation.

The practical mesh-optimization goal is therefore often to reorder triangles so recently used vertices are referenced again soon.

---

parts.title: Vertex-buffer layouts

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Vertex buffer layouts**

There are two major memory organizations.

An interleaved or Array-of-Structures representation is:

```text
Vertex 0: position normal uv color
Vertex 1: position normal uv color
Vertex 2: position normal uv color
...
```

or in C++:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;
    Vec3 normal;
    Vec2 uv;
    Vec3 color;
};

std::vector<Vertex> vertices;
```

A separate-stream / Structure-of-Arrays style representation is:

```text
positions: P0 P1 P2 P3 ...
normals:   N0 N1 N2 N3 ...
uvs:       U0 U1 U2 U3 ...
colors:    C0 C1 C2 C3 ...
```

Neither is universally superior.

If every shader consumes every attribute, interleaving gives convenient spatial locality.

If one pass needs only positions—for example a shadow/depth pass—separate streams can avoid dragging normals, UVs and colors through memory.

Modern engines therefore often use several streams:

```text
stream 0: position
stream 1: normal + tangent + UV
stream 2: skin weights/joints
```

rather than dogmatically choosing pure AoS or pure SoA.

Your Kairo mesh path currently uses an interleaved base vertex stream.

The actual current Vulkan declaration is:

```cpp
meshBinding.binding   = 0;
meshBinding.stride    = sizeof(MeshVertex);
meshBinding.inputRate = VK_VERTEX_INPUT_RATE_VERTEX;
```

with locations:

```text
0 -> R32G32B32 position
1 -> R32G32B32 color
2 -> R32G32B32 normal
3 -> R32G32    UV
```

in `VulkanTriangle.cppm` lines approximately **447–458**.

There is a second vertex stream when skinning data exists.

That is a good real example of a hybrid layout.

---

**Vertex input formats are interpretation contracts**

parts.title: Interleaved versus separate vertex streams

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Vertex buffer layouts**

There are two major memory organizations.

An interleaved or Array-of-Structures representation is:

```text
Vertex 0: position normal uv color
Vertex 1: position normal uv color
Vertex 2: position normal uv color
...
```

or in C++:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;
    Vec3 normal;
    Vec2 uv;
    Vec3 color;
};

std::vector<Vertex> vertices;
```

A separate-stream / Structure-of-Arrays style representation is:

```text
positions: P0 P1 P2 P3 ...
normals:   N0 N1 N2 N3 ...
uvs:       U0 U1 U2 U3 ...
colors:    C0 C1 C2 C3 ...
```

Neither is universally superior.

If every shader consumes every attribute, interleaving gives convenient spatial locality.

If one pass needs only positions—for example a shadow/depth pass—separate streams can avoid dragging normals, UVs and colors through memory.

Modern engines therefore often use several streams:

```text
stream 0: position
stream 1: normal + tangent + UV
stream 2: skin weights/joints
```

rather than dogmatically choosing pure AoS or pure SoA.

parts.title: Vertex input formats

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Vertex input formats are interpretation contracts**

A GPU buffer is fundamentally bytes.

Suppose memory contains:

```text
00 00 80 3F ...
```

Those bytes do not intrinsically mean “1.0.”

The pipeline vertex format tells hardware how to interpret them.

For example:

```cpp
VK_FORMAT_R32G32B32_SFLOAT
```

means:

```text
three consecutive 32-bit IEEE float components
```

whereas a packed normalized 8-bit format could mean:

```text
four 8-bit integers
mapped into [0,1]
```

before being exposed to the shader.

Therefore vertex input consists of at least:

$$
\boxed{\text{buffer}+\text{stride}+\text{offset}+\text{format}+\text{location}}
$$

A classic corruption bug occurs when these contracts disagree.

For example:

```cpp
struct Vertex
{
    Vec3 position;   // offset 0
    Vec3 normal;     // offset 12
    Vec2 uv;         // offset 24
};
```

but Vulkan is told

```text
normal offset = 16
```

Then the GPU faithfully reads incorrect bytes.

There is no semantic notion of “normal” at this stage. Hardware sees offsets and formats.

---

parts.title: Index-buffer formats

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Index formats**

Typical index widths are:

$$
16\text{-bit} \quad \text{or} \quad 32\text{-bit}.
$$

A 16-bit unsigned index can address

$$
2^{16}=65536
$$

possible vertex indices.

Its major advantage is bandwidth.

For $3\,000\,000$ indices:

$$
3\,000\,000\times2 = 6\text{ MB}
$$

versus

$$
3\,000\,000\times4 = 12\text{ MB}.
$$

The index stream is consumed heavily during rendering, so this is not necessarily trivial.

The downside is obviously the maximum vertex range per indexed region.

Your current Kairo implementation chooses the straightforward 32-bit path.

`KairoRenderer/Mesh.cppm`, current main:

```text
23–29   MeshVertex contains Position, Color, Normal, TexCoord
39–46   Mesh owns vector<MeshVertex> and vector<uint32_t>
61      IndexBytes = indexCount * sizeof(uint32_t)
```

and `VulkanTriangle.cppm` currently binds:

```cpp
vkCmdBindIndexBuffer(..., VK_INDEX_TYPE_UINT32);
vkCmdDrawIndexed(...);
```

at approximately lines **716–718** of the current file.

So this is a concrete instance of:

$$
\boxed{\text{theory: indexed geometry}
\rightarrow
\text{Kairo: uint32 index buffer}
\rightarrow
\text{Vulkan indexed draw}}
$$

---

This is **clip space**.

parts.title: Homogeneous clipping

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Why clipping must happen before perspective division**

This is one of the most important conceptual points in M109.

Consider a triangle crossing the camera/near plane.

One vertex may have a valid positive homogeneous $w$; another may approach

$$
w\rightarrow0.
$$

If you divide first,

$$
x/w
$$

can explode toward infinity.

A triangle that is geometrically ordinary in projective space turns into absurd screen coordinates.

Therefore the logical order is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{clip-space primitive}
\rightarrow
\text{homogeneous clipping}
\rightarrow
\text{perspective divide}
}
$$

not:

$$
\text{divide}
\rightarrow
\text{try to clip giant screen triangle}.
$$

The current Vulkan specification defines the usual clip volume as

$$
-w_c\le x_c\le w_c,
$$

$$
-w_c\le y_c\le w_c,
$$

$$
0\le z_c\le w_c
$$

unless the optional negative-one-to-one depth convention is enabled. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest-ratified/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Notice that every inequality is expressed in terms of the homogeneous coordinate $w_c$.

That is why the stage is called **homogeneous clipping**.

---

**Clip planes as signed functions**

Each clipping boundary can be written as

$$
d(\mathbf v)\ge0.
$$

For example, the left plane

$$
x_c\ge-w_c
$$

becomes

$$
x_c+w_c\ge0.
$$

Define

$$
d_L(\mathbf v)=x_c+w_c.
$$

Similarly:

$$
d_R=w_c-x_c,
$$

$$
d_B=y_c+w_c,
$$

$$
d_T=w_c-y_c,
$$

parts.title: Perspective divide during rasterization

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Perspective divide**

Once a primitive has survived clipping, its clip-space positions undergo:

$$
\boxed{
x_d=\frac{x_c}{w_c},\qquad
y_d=\frac{y_c}{w_c},\qquad
z_d=\frac{z_c}{w_c}
}
$$

where the subscript $d$ denotes normalized device coordinates.

This is the perspective divide defined by Vulkan's coordinate transformation stage. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest-ratified/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Typical Vulkan NDC is

$$
x_d,y_d\in[-1,1]
$$

and

$$
z_d\in[0,1].
$$

Do not confuse that with traditional OpenGL's historical

$$
z\in[-1,1].
$$

This distinction becomes particularly important when building projection matrices.

---

parts.title: Viewport transformation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
The viewport transformation maps NDC into actual framebuffer coordinates.

For viewport width $W$, height $H$, origin $(x_0,y_0)$:

$$
x_f=x_0+\frac{W}{2}(x_d+1),
$$

$$
y_f=y_0+\frac{H}{2}(y_d+1)
$$

for a positive-height Vulkan viewport.

The formal Vulkan form is

$$
x_f=\frac{p_x}{2}x_d+o_x,
$$

$$
y_f=\frac{p_y}{2}y_d+o_y,
$$

$$
z_f=p_z z_d+o_z.
$$ :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}


---

**The Vulkan Y problem and what Kairo actually does**

Framebuffer $y$ normally grows downward.

Mathematical camera coordinates normally treat positive $y$ as upward.

There are several ways to reconcile that.

One is a negative Vulkan viewport height.

Another is modifying the projection matrix.

Your current `Camera.cppm` chooses the second strategy.

Current lines roughly 115–140:

```cpp
Mat4f projection = Perspective(...);

// Vulkan positive-height viewport.
// Flip clip-space Y once.
projection(1u, 1u) *= -1.0f;
```

That is a good example of why coordinate-space conventions must be traced rather than guessed.

Your pipeline is effectively:

```text
world Y-up
    ↓
view
    ↓
projection
    ↓
explicit clip-space Y flip
    ↓
positive-height Vulkan viewport
    ↓
framebuffer coordinates
```

If you later introduced a negative-height viewport without removing this projection flip, you would flip twice.

That is a classic “everything is upside down” bug.

---

parts.title: Edge functions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Edge functions**

For directed edge $a\rightarrow b$, define

$$
\boxed{
E_{ab}(p)
=
(b_x-a_x)(p_y-a_y)
-
(b_y-a_y)(p_x-a_x)
}
$$

This is a 2D cross product.

Geometrically,

$$
E_{ab}(p)
$$

is proportional to the signed area of the parallelogram formed by

$$
b-a
$$

and

$$
p-a.
$$

Its sign says which side of the directed line $p$ lies on.

It can be expanded into

$$
E(x,y)=Ax+By+C.
$$

Specifically,

$$
A=-(b_y-a_y),
$$

$$
B=b_x-a_x,
$$

$$
C=(b_y-a_y)a_x-(b_x-a_x)a_y.
$$

Now something wonderful happens.

Moving one pixel in $x$:

$$
E(x+1,y)=E(x,y)+A.
$$

Moving one pixel in $y$:

$$
E(x,y+1)=E(x,y)+B.
$$

So once an edge equation has been evaluated at one location, nearby samples can be evaluated through additions instead of recomputing everything.

This is why edge equations map beautifully to hardware rasterizers.

---

parts.title: Inside-triangle tests from edge functions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Inside-triangle tests**

Assume the triangle orientation has been normalized consistently.

A sample $p$ is inside when it lies on the interior side of all three edges.

Conceptually:

$$
E_{01}(p)\ge0,
$$

$$
E_{12}(p)\ge0,
$$

$$
E_{20}(p)\ge0.
$$

That gives a complete triangle point test.

The rasterizer therefore computes a bounding rectangle:

$$
x_{\min}=
\lfloor\min(x_0,x_1,x_2)\rfloor,
$$

etc.,

then only visits samples inside that box.

This converts a theoretical scan over the entire framebuffer into work approximately proportional to the triangle's screen footprint.

---

parts.title: Top-left rasterization rule

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Why `>= 0` is not sufficient**

Imagine two adjacent triangles sharing exactly one edge.

Triangle A says the shared edge belongs to it.

Triangle B also says the shared edge belongs to it.

Then shared-edge pixels can be shaded twice.

If instead both use a strict test,

$$
E>0,
$$

neither triangle owns the exact boundary.

Then cracks can appear.

Hardware therefore needs a deterministic ownership convention.

The common convention is the **top-left rule**.

Samples exactly on particular top/left boundary edges count as covered; samples exactly on the complementary bottom/right edges do not.

The crucial invariant is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{a shared edge is owned by exactly one adjacent triangle}
}
$$

rather than the wording “top” or “left” itself.

Hardware typically evaluates this using fixed-point/subpixel edge equations so neighboring primitives agree bit-for-bit about the shared edge.

This is one reason naive CPU rasterizers using arbitrary floating-point epsilons can disagree with GPU output at triangle boundaries.

---

parts.title: Pixel centers and coverage

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Pixel centers**

A pixel is an area.

Rasterization uses one or more **sample positions** within that area.

Under conventional single-sample rasterization, a logical pixel at integer coordinate

$$
(i,j)
$$

is normally tested at something equivalent to its center,

$$
(i+0.5,j+0.5).
$$

So asking whether pixel $(7,10)$ is covered does not usually mean evaluating the edge equations at

$$
(7,10).
$$

It means evaluating at the specified sample location inside that pixel.

That half-pixel detail is enough to generate visibly shifted rasterization when implemented incorrectly.

---

destinations.exact_quote:
With 4× MSAA, a pixel conceptually contains four coverage samples:

```text
+----------------+
|    •       •   |
|                |
|       pixel    |
|                |
| •          •   |
+----------------+
```

Their precise locations are implementation-defined or queryable depending on the graphics API/features.

Rasterization now produces a **coverage mask** such as

```text
sample 0 = covered
sample 1 = covered
sample 2 = not covered
sample 3 = covered
```

or binary

```text
1011
```

rather than a single yes/no pixel decision.

This is why MSAA improves geometric edge quality: coverage is measured more finely even if the fragment shader is not necessarily executed independently for every sample.

We will go much deeper into this in M111.

parts.title: Barycentric coordinates from edge functions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Barycentric coordinates emerge directly from the same edge equations**

For triangle

$$
v_0,v_1,v_2
$$

and point $p$, define

$$
A=E_{12}(v_0).
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_0=
\frac{E_{12}(p)}{A}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_1=
\frac{E_{20}(p)}{A}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_2=
\frac{E_{01}(p)}{A}
}
$$

with

$$
\lambda_0+\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1.
$$

The geometry is beautiful.

Each numerator is the area of a subtriangle opposite one vertex.

Therefore at $v_0$:

$$
\lambda_0=1,\quad
\lambda_1=0,\quad
\lambda_2=0.
$$

At the centroid:

$$
\lambda_0=
\lambda_1=
\lambda_2=
\frac13.
$$

The same rasterization state has therefore simultaneously answered:

> Is this point inside?

and:

> Where inside the triangle is it?

---

destinations.exact_quote:
**Affine attribute interpolation**

Suppose vertex colors are

$$
C_0=(1,0,0),
$$

$$
C_1=(0,1,0),
$$

$$
C_2=(0,0,1).
$$

For affine interpolation:

$$
\boxed{
C(p)=
\lambda_0C_0+
\lambda_1C_1+
\lambda_2C_2
}
$$

At the centroid:

$$
C=
\frac13(1,0,0)
+
\frac13(0,1,0)
+
\frac13(0,0,1)
$$

giving

$$
C=
\left(
\frac13,\frac13,\frac13
\right).
$$

That works perfectly when the quantity truly varies affinely in screen space.

But ordinary perspective-projected attributes do not.

parts.title: Perspective-correct interpolation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Deriving perspective-correct interpolation**

Let the original primitive-space barycentric weights be

$$
\alpha_i.
$$

A pre-projection varying $a$ satisfies

$$
a=
\sum_i\alpha_i a_i.
$$

After perspective division, the screen-space barycentrics become different values

$$
\lambda_i.
$$

The relationship is

$$
\alpha_i
=
\frac{\lambda_i/w_i}
{\sum_j\lambda_j/w_j}.
$$

Substitute that into the attribute equation:

$$
a=
\sum_i
a_i
\frac{\lambda_i/w_i}
{\sum_j\lambda_j/w_j}.
$$

The denominator is shared:

$$
\boxed{
a(p)
=
\frac{
\displaystyle
\sum_i\lambda_i\frac{a_i}{w_i}
}{
\displaystyle
\sum_i\lambda_i\frac1{w_i}
}
}
$$

This is the perspective-correct interpolation equation.

The implementation interpretation is even more important than memorizing it.

parts.title: Why naive screen-space interpolation is wrong for perspective

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
This creates one of rasterization's most important traps.

---

**Why naive screen-space interpolation is wrong**

Imagine an edge in 3D with endpoints

$$
A,\qquad B
$$

at different depths.

A texture coordinate varies linearly along the actual 3D edge.

After perspective projection, however, equal intervals in world/view space do **not** become equal intervals on screen.

Perspective performs approximately

$$
x'=\frac{x}{z}.
$$

That division is nonlinear.

Therefore if you calculate screen barycentrics and directly perform

$$
u=
\lambda_0u_0+
\lambda_1u_1+
\lambda_2u_2,
$$

the result is generally not the texture coordinate corresponding to the original projected 3D point.

This causes the classic affine-texture “swimming” or warping seen in early software renderers and some older consoles.

---

parts.title: Interpolating reciprocal w

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
At every vertex, think of storing:

$$
\frac{a_i}{w_i}
$$

and

$$
\frac1{w_i}.
$$

Rasterization linearly interpolates those screen-space quantities.

Then reconstruct:

$$
a=
\frac{a/w}{1/w}.
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{
\text{interpolate reciprocal }w
}
$$

is not some random graphics trick.

It is what mathematically undoes the projective distortion introduced by dividing coordinates by $w$.

---

**A numerical example**

Suppose two endpoints have

$$
u_0=0,\qquad w_0=1
$$

and

$$
u_1=1,\qquad w_1=4.
$$

At the screen midpoint,

$$
\lambda_0=\lambda_1=0.5.
$$

Naive interpolation gives

$$
u_{\text{naive}}
=
0.5(0)+0.5(1)=0.5.
$$

Perspective-correct interpolation instead computes

$$
\frac{u_0}{w_0}=0,
$$

$$
\frac{u_1}{w_1}=0.25,
$$

and

$$
\frac1{w_0}=1,\qquad
\frac1{w_1}=0.25.
$$

Therefore

$$
u=
\frac{
0.5(0)+0.5(0.25)
}{
0.5(1)+0.5(0.25)
}
$$

$$
=
\frac{0.125}{0.625}
$$

$$
=
0.2.
$$

Not

$$
0.5.
$$

That is a massive difference.

The nearer endpoint occupies more of the apparent screen-space perspective relationship.

---

**Canonical interpolation code**

```cpp
template<typename T>
T PerspectiveInterpolate(
    const T& a0,
    const T& a1,
    const T& a2,
    float w0,
    float w1,
    float w2,
    float lambda0,
    float lambda1,
    float lambda2)
{
    // Interpolate reciprocal homogeneous W.
    const float reciprocalW =
        lambda0 / w0 +
        lambda1 / w1 +
        lambda2 / w2;

    // Interpolate attribute/W in screen space.
    const T numerator =
        a0 * (lambda0 / w0) +
        a1 * (lambda1 / w1) +
        a2 * (lambda2 / w2);

    // Recover the original varying.
    return numerator / reciprocalW;
}
```

That one function connects Parts 1832–1835.

---

parts.title: Derivatives dFdx and dFdy concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Screen-space derivatives**

Now consider:

```glsl
dFdx(value)
dFdy(value)
```

These are not symbolic calculus operations performed by a compiler.

The GPU executes fragment work in small neighboring groups—traditionally reasoned about as $2\times2$ quads.

Suppose a varying $f$ has values approximately

```text
f00    f10

f01    f11
```

Then a horizontal derivative can be approximated through neighboring invocation differences such as

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
\approx
f_{10}-f_{00},
$$

and vertically,

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}
\approx
f_{01}-f_{00}.
$$

Vulkan/SPIR-V formally defines fine/coarse derivative behavior over derivative groups/quads; ordinary derivative instructions may use an implementation-selected fine or coarse form. Implicit-LOD texture sampling itself relies on coordinate derivatives. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This is why fragments outside the actual primitive can sometimes exist as **helper invocations**: a neighboring live fragment may need their values to calculate derivatives.

They participate in computation but must not produce ordinary framebuffer side effects.

---

**What your Kairo fragment shader actually uses derivatives for**

This is one of the strongest repository mappings in this pass.

Current `triangle.frag`, lines approximately **121–136**:

```glsl
const vec3 geometricNormal = normalize(inNormal);

const vec3 dpdx = dFdx(inWorldPosition);
const vec3 dpdy = dFdy(inWorldPosition);

const vec2 duvdx = dFdx(inTexCoord);
const vec2 duvdy = dFdy(inTexCoord);

const float determinant =
    duvdx.x * duvdy.y -
    duvdx.y * duvdy.x;
```

Then it reconstructs a tangent:

```glsl
tangent =
    (dpdx * duvdy.y -
     dpdy * duvdx.y) /
    determinant;
```

This is solving the local differential system

$$
dP
=
T\,du+B\,dv.
$$

Across screen $x$:

$$
P_x
=
T\,u_x+B\,v_x
$$

and across screen $y$:

$$
P_y
=
T\,u_y+B\,v_y.
$$

Write this as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
P_x & P_y
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
T & B
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
u_x & u_y\\
v_x & v_y
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The UV Jacobian determinant is

$$
D=u_xv_y-u_yv_x.
$$

Solving gives

$$
\boxed{
T=
\frac{
P_xv_y-P_yv_x
}{D}
}
$$

which is exactly what your shader implements.

It checks

$$
|D|>10^{-8}
$$

before dividing.

So the code is not merely “using dFdx for normal maps.”

It is solving a local $2\times2$ coordinate transformation between screen-space variation and texture-space variation.

That is the math-to-code bridge your curriculum is asking for.

---

**Derivative failure cases**

If UVs collapse locally,

$$
D\approx0,
$$

the tangent basis becomes singular.

Examples include degenerate UV triangles, duplicated UV coordinates and extremely compressed texture parameterization.

Then

$$
1/D
$$

becomes enormous and the tangent can explode numerically.

Your shader handles this by leaving the geometric normal in place when

$$
|D|\le10^{-8}.
$$

There is another important failure mode: derivatives inside highly divergent control flow.

If neighboring invocations do not execute compatible paths, derivative availability and meaning become tricky. Shader languages and APIs impose specific derivative-group rules; this is why derivative-based operations should not be casually hidden behind arbitrary per-fragment branches.

---

parts.title: Early depth testing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Early versus late depth testing**

The conceptual pipeline might be drawn:

```text
rasterize
  ↓
fragment shader
  ↓
depth test
```

but that can waste enormous work.

Suppose an expensive fragment shader executes 200 instructions and the resulting fragment is completely hidden behind existing geometry.

If the GPU already knows its depth will fail, it would prefer:

```text
rasterize
  ↓
depth test
  ↓
if visible → execute shader
```

That is **early depth testing**.

parts.title: Late depth testing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
Vulkan explicitly models early-fragment-test and late-fragment-test pipeline stages: early tests occur before fragment shading, late tests after it. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/VulkanSC/specs/1.0-extensions/man/html/VkPipelineStageFlagBits2KHR.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

But whether an implementation can perform the optimization depends on shader behavior.

Things such as writing fragment depth, certain side effects, sample-mask manipulation or discard behavior can constrain what may safely happen early.

Your current Kairo fragment shader performs:

```glsl
if (alphaMask && alpha < cutoff)
    discard;
```

so you should not imagine the implementation as a simplistic immutable stage diagram.

Real GPUs often separate:

```text
early rejection
fragment execution
late/commit tests
```

and use hierarchical visibility optimizations around them.

destinations.exact_quote:
**Depth buffer representation**

Your current Kairo implementation uses

```cpp
VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT
```

in `VulkanDepth.cppm`.

So each depth sample has a 32-bit floating-point depth component.

The image is created with

```cpp
VK_IMAGE_USAGE_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_BIT
```

and resides in device-local memory.

Current `VulkanTriangle` rendering clears depth to:

```cpp
depthClear.depthStencil = { 1.0f, 0u };
```

and uses viewport:

```cpp
minDepth = 0.0f;
maxDepth = 1.0f;
```

The pipeline currently performs:

```cpp
depth.depthTestEnable  = VK_TRUE;
depth.depthWriteEnable = VK_TRUE;
depth.depthCompareOp   = VK_COMPARE_OP_LESS;
```

around current lines **541–545**.

Therefore Kairo currently means:

```text
nearer → smaller depth
farther → larger depth

clear = 1
accept incoming if incoming < stored
```

That is conventional depth, not reversed-Z.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Depth comparison functions**

Common comparisons conceptually include

```text
NEVER
LESS
EQUAL
LESS_OR_EQUAL
GREATER
NOT_EQUAL
GREATER_OR_EQUAL
ALWAYS
```

The choice is not cosmetic.

For conventional Z:

$$
\text{clear}=1,\qquad
\text{compare}=LESS
$$

is typical.

For reversed-Z:

$$
\text{clear}=0,\qquad
\text{compare}=GREATER
$$

or `GREATER_OR_EQUAL` is typical.

If you reverse the projection but forget the comparison function, almost everything disappears.

If you reverse the compare function but forget to change the clear value, nearly everything also disappears.

These parameters form one invariant.

destinations.exact_quote:
**Depth write control**

Depth **testing** and depth **writing** are separate.

Opaque rendering normally uses:

```text
depth test  = enabled
depth write = enabled
```

because the nearest opaque surface should occlude later geometry.

Transparent rendering commonly uses:

```text
depth test  = enabled
depth write = disabled
```

because transparent fragments should generally be tested against opaque geometry without making the first transparent surface permanently hide every transparent layer behind it.

Your Kairo pipeline already reflects this distinction.

Its opaque pipeline is created with depth writes enabled, while the transparent path requests depth writes disabled.

That becomes important in Pass 2 when we cover transparency ordering.

---

parts.title: Depth precision

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Why perspective depth is nonlinear**

This is the foundation of Parts 1844–1845.

Let positive camera distance be

$$
d=-z_v>0.
$$

For a finite near plane $n$ and far plane $f$, conventional Vulkan-style normalized depth can be expressed as

$$
\boxed{
z(d)
=
\frac{f}{f-n}
-
\frac{fn}{(f-n)d}
}
$$

Check the near plane:

$$
d=n.
$$

Then

$$
z(n)=
\frac{f}{f-n}
-
\frac{f}{f-n}
=0.
$$

Check the far plane:

$$
d=f.
$$

Then

$$
z(f)=
\frac{f}{f-n}
-
\frac{n}{f-n}
=1.
$$

So:

$$
n\rightarrow0,
\qquad
f\rightarrow1.
$$

But note the $1/d$ term.

Depth is not linear with world-space distance.

---

**Why most conventional depth precision sits near the camera**

Differentiate:

$$
z(d)=A-\frac{B}{d}
$$

where

$$
B=\frac{fn}{f-n}.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\frac{dz}{dd}
=
\frac{B}{d^2}
}
$$

The change in depth value per metre therefore falls roughly as

$$
\frac1{d^2}.
$$

Far away, huge changes in world distance produce tiny depth-buffer differences.

That is where Z-fighting comes from.

Two surfaces can have different actual distances but quantize to effectively the same depth value.

---

**Your camera settings show why this matters**

Current `CameraPose` defaults include approximately:

$$
n=0.1
$$

and

$$
f=5000.
$$

The ratio is

$$
\frac fn=50000.
$$

For those values, conventional depth gives approximately:

| Distance $d$ | Conventional depth |
|---:|---:|
| $0.1$ | $0$ |
| $1$ | $0.900018$ |
| $10$ | $0.9900198$ |
| $100$ | $0.99901998$ |
| $1000$ | $0.999919998$ |
| $5000$ | $1$ |

Look at what happened.

The first 10 metres consumed nearly the entire numerical interval.

Everything from hundreds to thousands of metres is crushed extremely close to 1.

This is why casually reducing the near plane from

$$
0.1
$$

to

$$
0.001
$$

can destroy depth precision.

The near plane is not only a clipping parameter.

It is a precision-control parameter.

---

parts.title: Reversed-Z testing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Decide which samples a triangle owns
destinations.exact_quote:
**Reversed-Z**

Reversed-Z swaps the mapping:

$$
\boxed{
\text{near}\rightarrow1
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{far}\rightarrow0
}
$$

For finite far plane, one suitable depth mapping is

$$
\boxed{
z_R(d)
=
-\frac{n}{f-n}
+
\frac{fn}{(f-n)d}
}
$$

Check:

$$
z_R(n)=1,
$$

$$
z_R(f)=0.
$$

Notice also:

$$
z_R(d)=1-z_{\text{conventional}}(d).
$$

For your $0.1$ to $5000$ camera:

| Distance | Reversed depth |
|---:|---:|
| $0.1$ | $1$ |
| $1$ | $0.099982$ |
| $10$ | $0.0099802$ |
| $100$ | $0.0009800$ |
| $1000$ | $0.0000800$ |
| $5000$ | $0$ |

With an infinite far plane,

$$
f\rightarrow\infty,
$$

this simplifies beautifully:

$$
\boxed{
z_R(d)=\frac nd
}
$$

which yields

$$
d=n\rightarrow1
$$

and

$$
d\rightarrow\infty\rightarrow0.
$$

---

**Why reversed-Z helps floating-point depth so much**

A common incomplete explanation is:

> “Reversed-Z has more precision.”

That is not enough.

If the depth buffer were uniformly spaced fixed-point values, merely replacing $z$ with $1-z$ would not magically create more representable levels.

The important interaction is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{projective }1/d\text{ depth distribution}
+
\text{floating-point relative precision}
}
$$

IEEE floating point has dense representable numbers near zero.

Conventional depth sends distant geometry toward

$$
1,
$$

where floating-point values are relatively coarse in absolute spacing.

Reversed-Z sends distant geometry toward

$$
0,
$$

where floating-point representation provides progressively smaller absolute spacing.

Those two nonlinearities partially counteract each other.

This is why:

$$
\boxed{\text{reversed-Z + floating-point depth}}
$$

is particularly powerful.

Your existing `D32_SFLOAT` format is therefore already a good format for adopting reversed-Z.

---

**Converting Kairo to reversed-Z**

At a conceptual level you would need one coherent change set.

Current state:

```cpp
clearDepth = 1.0f;
compare    = VK_COMPARE_OP_LESS;
projection = conventional depth;
```

Reversed state:

```cpp
clearDepth = 0.0f;
compare    = VK_COMPARE_OP_GREATER;
projection = reversed-Z depth mapping;
```

If using an infinite reversed projection, the far-plane term can often disappear from the perspective projection entirely.

But do not blindly patch only those two Vulkan values.

You must audit every place that assumes:

```text
smaller depth = closer
```

including shadow maps, depth reconstruction, linear-depth debug views, SSAO/SSR later, occlusion systems, Hi-Z reduction direction and any manual depth comparison shader.

For example, your current shadow shader performs:

```glsl
projected.z - receiverBias > storedDepth
```

for shadow-map comparison.

That shadow pipeline currently has its own conventional depth semantics.

Changing camera depth and changing shadow depth are separable decisions.

That is exactly the sort of cross-system assumption that breaks when reversed-Z is treated as a one-line optimization.

---

parts.title: Stencil buffers

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Depth alone is not enough: the stencil buffer**

A depth buffer stores a geometric ordering quantity.

A stencil buffer stores something fundamentally different:

$$
\boxed{\text{small integer state associated with framebuffer samples}}
$$

Usually the stencil value is 8 bits:

$$
s\in[0,255].
$$

Stencil is not intrinsically:

- an object ID,
- a mask,
- a shadow flag,
- an outline marker,
- a portal number.

It is simply integer state that the raster pipeline can compare and modify according to rules.

You assign the semantics.

Conceptually, each sample may contain:

```text
color     = RGBA
depth     = z
stencil   = uint8
```

For packed depth-stencil formats, depth and stencil may physically share one image format, such as `D24_UNORM_S8_UINT` or `D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT`.

Your current Kairo viewport does **not** have stencil.

It uses:

```cpp
VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT
```

for its depth attachment.

That contains depth only.

So M111 stencil theory is currently **canonical theory rather than implemented Kairo behavior**.

---

parts.title: Stencil operations

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**The stencil test**

For an incoming fragment, define:

$$
s_a = \text{stored stencil value},
$$

$$
s_r = \text{stencil reference}.
$$

The pipeline can compare them using operations analogous to depth:

$$
s_r \stackrel{?}{<,>,=,\neq,\dots} s_a.
$$

But stencil also has masks.

A more accurate conceptual comparison is

$$
(s_r \land M_c)
\quad\text{compare}\quad
(s_a \land M_c),
$$

where $M_c$ is the compare mask.

The Vulkan stencil test is explicitly per sample, and Vulkan maintains separate front-face and back-face stencil state. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/fragops.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

That last fact matters enormously.

Stencil configuration is not necessarily:

```text
one operation for the whole triangle
```

but potentially:

```text
front-facing polygons → one policy
back-facing polygons  → another policy
```

which enables techniques such as stencil shadow volumes.

---

**Stencil has three different update paths**

Suppose a fragment arrives.

Three major events can occur:

```text
stencil test fails
depth test fails
depth test passes
```

Stencil lets you specify an operation for each.

Conceptually:

```cpp
if (!StencilTest())
{
    stencil = StencilFailOp(stencil);
}
else if (!DepthTest())
{
    stencil = DepthFailOp(stencil);
}
else
{
    stencil = PassOp(stencil);
}
```

Typical operations include:

```text
KEEP
ZERO
REPLACE
INCREMENT
DECREMENT
INVERT
INCREMENT_AND_WRAP
DECREMENT_AND_WRAP
```

This gives stencil its power.

It is not merely a boolean mask.

It is a tiny state machine attached to every sample.

---

**Example: drawing an outline using stencil**

Imagine drawing an object with an outline.

First pass:

```text
draw object normally
depth test enabled
stencil reference = 1
on successful fragment:
    stencil = 1
```

The object's visible pixels now have:

$$
s=1.
$$

Second pass:

Render a slightly enlarged version of the object, but only where

$$
s\neq1.
$$

That means the enlarged geometry appears only outside the original object's stencil footprint.

Result:

```text
enlarged colored silhouette
minus
original object area
=
outline
```

The important point is not memorizing the trick.

The important point is understanding the stencil machine:

$$
\text{geometry generates samples}
\rightarrow
\text{stencil classifies existing sample state}
\rightarrow
\text{pipeline conditionally permits/modifies fragments}.
$$

---

**Stencil write masks**

Suppose the stored stencil byte is

```text
10101100
```

and you only want to modify its lower four bits.

Use a write mask:

```text
00001111
```

Conceptually:

$$
s_{\text{new}}
=
(s_{\text{old}}\land\neg M_w)
\;|\;
(s_{\text{op}}\land M_w).
$$

That lets different subsystems share stencil bits.

For example:

```text
bits 0–2 : portal region
bit 3    : selection mask
bits 4–7 : lighting classification
```

Whether sharing stencil like this is wise depends heavily on engine complexity, but mathematically the facility exists.

---

destinations.exact_quote:
**Backface culling**

A closed opaque surface normally has one side facing outward.

For many meshes, triangles facing away from the camera cannot contribute visible pixels.

Rasterizing them wastes:

- triangle setup,
- coverage testing,
- potential fragment work,
- bandwidth.

So we classify each triangle by projected orientation.

From Pass 1, projected signed area is:

$$
A_2 =
(x_1-x_0)(y_2-y_0)
-
(y_1-y_0)(x_2-x_0).
$$

Its sign determines winding under a particular coordinate convention.

For example:

$$
A_2>0
$$

may mean counter-clockwise.

Then the pipeline can declare:

```text
front face = CCW
cull mode  = back
```

and discard triangles classified as back-facing before fragment rasterization.

---

**Winding is a convention, not physical truth**

parts.title: Front-face winding

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Winding is a convention, not physical truth**

The triangle

$$
(v_0,v_1,v_2)
$$

and triangle

$$
(v_0,v_2,v_1)
$$

contain the same geometric points.

But their orientation is reversed.

So the renderer needs a convention:

```text
counter-clockwise projected ordering = front-facing
```

or

```text
clockwise projected ordering = front-facing.
```

Vulkan exposes this with `frontFace`.

Your Kairo pipeline currently sets:

```cpp
rasterizer.frontFace = VK_FRONT_FACE_COUNTER_CLOCKWISE;
```

but also:

```cpp
rasterizer.cullMode = VK_CULL_MODE_NONE;
```

Therefore the declared front-face convention currently does **not eliminate either side** in your main mesh path.

Both sides rasterize.

That is effectively two-sided rasterization.

---

**Why negative-scale transforms can reverse winding**

Suppose a model matrix has scale

$$
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Its determinant is

$$
\det S=-1.
$$

That means it reverses orientation.

A triangle that was CCW in object space can become CW after transformation.

This is why mirrored transforms can unexpectedly interact with face culling.

The deeper invariant is:

$$
\boxed{
\det(M_{3\times3})<0
\Rightarrow
\text{orientation reversal}
}
$$

although projection and viewport conventions also participate in final screen winding.

So a broken culling bug cannot always be solved by flipping `frontFace`. You must understand the entire transform chain.

---

destinations.exact_quote:
**Two-sided rendering**

Some surfaces genuinely require both sides:

```text
leaves
cloth
paper
thin sheets
some particles
debug geometry
```

Then backface culling can be disabled.

But two-sided rendering introduces another question:

> What should the surface normal mean on the back side?

Suppose the front normal is

$$
N.
$$

For a back-facing fragment, you may want

$$
N'=-N.
$$

Shader languages provide mechanisms such as `gl_FrontFacing` that let the fragment shader distinguish orientation.

A typical two-sided shading policy is:

```glsl
vec3 N = normalize(inNormal);

if (!gl_FrontFacing)
    N = -N;
```

This is not universally correct—for physically thin materials you may want a specialized BSDF—but it demonstrates that “disable culling” is only the first half of two-sided rendering.

---

destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Scissor testing**

A viewport and scissor are commonly confused.

The **viewport** transforms normalized device coordinates into framebuffer coordinates.

The **scissor** rejects fragments outside a rectangular framebuffer region.

So:

$$
\boxed{\text{viewport = coordinate transformation}}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{\text{scissor = rectangular coverage restriction}}.
$$

If your viewport is

```text
0,0 → 1920×1080
```

parts.title: Viewports

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
A viewport and scissor are commonly confused.

The **viewport** transforms normalized device coordinates into framebuffer coordinates.

The **scissor** rejects fragments outside a rectangular framebuffer region.

So:

$$
\boxed{\text{viewport = coordinate transformation}}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{\text{scissor = rectangular coverage restriction}}.
$$

If your viewport is

```text
0,0 → 1920×1080
```

but your scissor is

```text
400,200 → 800×600,
```

geometry still transforms relative to the viewport but fragments outside the 800×600 rectangle are discarded.

Scissors are extremely useful for:

```text
UI clipping
split-screen regions
editor panes
partial clears
shadow atlas regions
damage regions
```

without writing custom shader clipping code.

---

**Kairo viewport and scissor**

Your current `VulkanTriangle::Record` dynamically configures:

```cpp
viewport.width    = viewportExtent.width;
viewport.height   = viewportExtent.height;
viewport.minDepth = 0.0f;
viewport.maxDepth = 1.0f;

scissor.extent = viewportExtent;

vkCmdSetViewport(...);
vkCmdSetScissor(...);
```

So today:

$$
\text{viewport rectangle}
=
\text{scissor rectangle}.
$$

That means the scissor is not currently performing an interesting crop.

But because viewport/scissor are dynamic pipeline state, you can change them without rebuilding the graphics pipeline.

---

parts.title: Color attachments

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Attachments: persistent destinations of rasterization**

A render pass may write several outputs.

A fragment shader might emit:

```glsl
layout(location = 0) out vec4 color;
layout(location = 1) out uint objectID;
```

These map to color attachments.

Meanwhile fixed-function depth testing updates a depth attachment.

So conceptually a framebuffer might be:

```text
Attachment 0:
RGBA16F HDR color

Attachment 1:
R32_UINT object ID

Attachment 2:
D32_FLOAT depth
```

That is almost exactly your current editor viewport.

Kairo's `VulkanViewportTarget` currently creates:

$$
\text{color} = \texttt{R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT},
$$

$$
\text{objectID} = \texttt{R32_UINT},
$$

$$
\text{depth} = \texttt{D32_SFLOAT}.
$$

This is a very good example of why “the framebuffer” is not synonymous with “the final color image.”

A framebuffer is a set of images participating together in rendering.

---

parts.title: Load operations

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Load operations**

When a render pass begins, what should an attachment's existing contents mean?

Vulkan gives operations conceptually equivalent to:

```text
LOAD
CLEAR
DONT_CARE
```

`LOAD` means:

> Preserve the previous contents because this pass needs them.

`CLEAR` means:

> Initialize the attachment to a known value.

`DONT_CARE` means:

> Previous contents do not matter.

This is not only semantic.

On tile-based architectures especially, avoiding unnecessary attachment preservation can save memory traffic.

---

parts.title: Store operations

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Store operations**

At the end of the pass, you similarly decide:

```text
STORE
DONT_CARE
```

`STORE` means later work needs the generated contents.

`DONT_CARE` means the attachment can be discarded after its current purpose has been fulfilled.

This is one of the simplest places where knowing future resource lifetime directly turns into GPU bandwidth optimization.

---

**Kairo's load/store decisions tell us its dataflow**

Current viewport attachments:

```text
HDR color:
load  = CLEAR
store = STORE

Object ID:
load  = CLEAR
store = STORE

Depth:
load  = CLEAR
store = DONT_CARE
```

Why?

Color must survive because the editor samples/presents it later.

Object ID must survive because picking can copy a pixel to a readback buffer later.

Depth only needs to participate during rasterization in that pass.

The viewport does not currently sample it later.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{depth persistence after this pass has no value}
}
$$

and `DONT_CARE` is appropriate.

That is exactly the sort of resource-lifetime reasoning a render graph will automate later.

---

parts.title: MSAA coverage samples

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**MSAA changes the framebuffer from one sample to many**

At 1×:

```text
one pixel
└── one coverage/depth/color sample
```

At 4× MSAA:

```text
one pixel
├── sample 0
├── sample 1
├── sample 2
└── sample 3
```

Each sample has an exact sample location.

Rasterization tests primitive coverage against those sample positions, producing a coverage mask. Vulkan describes multisampling precisely this way: each framebuffer pixel has `rasterizationSamples` exact sample points, each attachment holds per-sample color/depth/stencil state, and the resulting multisampled color can later be resolved to a single-sample image. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/primsrast.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

So MSAA is not:

> “Render the image bigger and shrink it.”

That is supersampling.

---

**A 4× MSAA edge example**

Suppose a pixel contains four samples:

```text
•      •

   / triangle boundary

•      •
```

and the triangle covers three.

Coverage mask:

```text
1110
```

Three depth samples may now pass.

If fragment shading is performed once at pixel frequency, the result can conceptually be replicated to covered color samples.

On resolve, suppose three samples contain red:

$$
(1,0,0)
$$

and one contains background black:

$$
(0,0,0).
$$

A simple box resolve gives

$$
C=
\frac{3(1,0,0)+(0,0,0)}4
=
(0.75,0,0).
$$

The edge therefore appears partially covered rather than as a binary staircase.

---

parts.title: Supersampling versus multisampling

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Stencil, culling, scissor/viewports, attachments, load/store, MSAA
destinations.exact_quote:
**Supersampling versus multisampling**

Suppose final target resolution is

$$
1920\times1080.
$$

For 4× supersampling, you could render approximately

$$
3840\times2160
$$

and downsample.

Everything runs at the higher resolution:

```text
coverage
depth
fragment shader
texture sampling
post-process intermediates
```

This produces excellent quality but is expensive.

4× MSAA instead stores multiple coverage/depth/color samples per pixel while often avoiding 4× full fragment shading.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{SSAA attacks general high-frequency shading + geometry aliasing}
}
$$

whereas

$$
\boxed{
\text{MSAA primarily attacks polygon-edge coverage aliasing}
}
$$

and is much cheaper when fragment shading is expensive.

It does not magically fix shader aliasing inside a triangle.

A high-frequency normal map can still shimmer under MSAA.

That is the domain of mipmapping, anisotropic filtering, TAA, supersampling and other sampling strategies later.

---

parts.title: Alpha blending

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Blending is a framebuffer recurrence**

Suppose a new fragment produces source color

$$
C_s
$$

and the framebuffer currently stores destination color

$$
C_d.
$$

A general blend operation can be written

$$
\boxed{
C_{\text{out}}
=
\operatorname{Op}
\left(
F_s C_s,
F_d C_d
\right)
}
$$

where $F_s$ and $F_d$ are configurable factors.

For ADD:

$$
C_{\text{out}}
=
F_sC_s+F_dC_d.
$$

Vulkan exposes exactly this model: source/destination RGB and alpha factors plus separate blend operations per color attachment. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/framebuffer.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This means blending is not fundamentally a “transparency feature.”

It is a programmable recurrence on framebuffer state.

Transparency is one important use.

---

parts.title: Standard source-over blending

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Standard straight-alpha source-over**

Let

$$
\alpha_s
$$

be source opacity.

For straight/unassociated RGB, the standard color equation is

$$
\boxed{
C_{\text{out}}
=
\alpha_s C_s
+
(1-\alpha_s)C_d
}
$$

The corresponding output alpha is

$$
\boxed{
\alpha_{\text{out}}
=
\alpha_s+
(1-\alpha_s)\alpha_d
}
$$

which expands to

$$
\alpha_s+\alpha_d-\alpha_s\alpha_d.
$$

This is the Porter-Duff source-over operator.

The Vulkan configuration is:

```cpp
srcColor = SRC_ALPHA;
dstColor = ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA;
colorOp  = ADD;

srcAlpha = ONE;
dstAlpha = ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA;
alphaOp  = ADD;
```

And that is precisely what the current Kairo transparent pipeline uses.

So your current renderer is a concrete straight-alpha source-over implementation.

---

**A numerical blend trace**

Suppose the framebuffer currently stores blue:

$$
C_d=(0,0,1)
$$

and a 25% opaque red fragment arrives:

$$
C_s=(1,0,0),\qquad \alpha_s=0.25.
$$

Then

$$
C_{\text{out}}
=
0.25(1,0,0)
+
0.75(0,0,1)
$$

so

$$
\boxed{
C_{\text{out}}
=
(0.25,0,0.75)
}
$$

The important conceptual point:

The source RGB $(1,0,0)$ does **not** mean the final contribution is full red.

Alpha scales its contribution during blending.

---

Instead of storing

Then source-over becomes

C'_{\text{out}}
=
C'_s+(1-\alpha_s)C'_d
}
$$

which uses

```text
source factor      = ONE
destination factor = ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA
```

rather than multiplying source RGB by alpha during the blend.

parts.title: Why premultiplied alpha improves composition behavior

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Why premultiplied alpha is more than an optimization**

Consider a transparent texel.

Straight-alpha representation could contain

$$
C=(1,0,0),\qquad \alpha=0.
$$

That texel is “fully transparent red.”

Another could contain

$$
C=(0,1,0),\qquad \alpha=0.
$$

They are visually identical in isolation.

But interpolate those RGB values during texture filtering and hidden color can leak into partially transparent edge texels.

In premultiplied representation:

$$
\alpha=0
\Rightarrow
\alpha C=(0,0,0).
$$

Transparent texels have a canonical zero contribution.

That makes interpolation and filtering behave much more naturally.

This is one of the deepest reasons production compositing systems often prefer premultiplied alpha.

However, every layer must agree.

If the texture/shader already outputs premultiplied RGB but the blend state still uses `SRC_ALPHA`, you multiply by alpha twice:

$$
C_{\text{contribution}}
=
\alpha(\alpha C)
=
\alpha^2C.
$$

The result becomes too dark.

Your current Kairo pipeline is **straight alpha**, so do not start premultiplying shader output unless you change the blending state too.

---

parts.title: Additive blending

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Additive blending**

Set

$$
F_s=1,\qquad F_d=1.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
C_{\text{out}}=C_s+C_d
}
$$

This is useful for phenomena where contributions accumulate:

```text
glows
energy effects
light-like particles
some bloom accumulation
```

On HDR floating-point targets this can exceed 1:

$$
(2.1,0.7,4.4)
$$

which is perfectly reasonable before tone mapping.

Additive blending is mathematically commutative:

$$
A+B=B+A,
$$

so pure additive transparent particles are much less sensitive to ordering than source-over transparency.

---

parts.title: Multiplicative blending

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Multiplicative blending**

Suppose:

$$
C_{\text{out}}=C_sC_d
$$

component-wise.

Then a source value of 1 leaves the destination unchanged:

$$
1\cdot C_d=C_d,
$$

while zero blacks it out.

This has historically been useful for modulation, darkening and certain decal/effect models.

One blend-state representation can be:

```text
source factor      = DST_COLOR
destination factor = ZERO
```

giving

$$
C_sC_d.
$$

Again, “blending” is much broader than transparency.

---

parts.title: Transparency order dependence

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Why ordinary transparency is order dependent**

Take black background and two 50%-opaque layers:

Red:

$$
R=(1,0,0),\quad \alpha=0.5.
$$

Blue:

$$
B=(0,0,1),\quad \alpha=0.5.
$$

Red over background:

$$
C_1=(0.5,0,0).
$$

Then blue over that:

$$
C_2
=
0.5(0,0,1)+0.5(0.5,0,0)
$$

$$
=
(0.25,0,0.5).
$$

Reverse the order.

Blue first:

$$
C'_1=(0,0,0.5).
$$

Then red:

$$
C'_2
=
0.5(1,0,0)+0.5(0,0,0.5)
$$

$$
=
(0.5,0,0.25).
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{
R\operatorname{over}B
\neq
B\operatorname{over}R
}
$$

and ordinary alpha transparency requires approximate back-to-front ordering.

---

**Why transparent geometry usually does not write depth**

Imagine:

```text
front transparent pane
rear transparent pane
```

If the front pane writes depth, the rear pane can fail the depth test entirely.

But physically we need both contributions.

So a common configuration is:

```text
depth test  = ON
depth write = OFF
```

This allows transparent geometry to respect opaque occluders while not preventing later transparent layers from contributing.

Your Kairo transparent pipeline does exactly this:

```cpp
m_TransparentPipeline =
    CreatePipeline(...,
                   depthWrite = VK_FALSE,
                   alphaBlend = true);
```

The opaque path uses depth writes.

---

**Kairo's current transparency sorting**

Current Kairo collects blended draws and stable-sorts them using approximate camera distance:

$$
d^2=\|T_{\text{model}}-P_{\text{camera}}\|^2.
$$

Larger distance is drawn first.

That is a reasonable object-level approximation.

But imagine two long transparent objects that intersect.

Object A's origin may be farther from the camera even though half of A is in front of B and half is behind it.

There exists no single object ordering that solves the geometry.

That is why order-independent transparency is a research/advanced-rendering topic, rather than something sorting can completely solve.

---

parts.title: Alpha testing or cutouts

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Alpha testing / cutouts**

Some materials are not really translucent.

A leaf texture might represent:

```text
leaf     → fully opaque
outside  → fully empty
```

Instead of blending partial opacity, use a threshold:

$$
\text{if }\alpha < \alpha_c
\Rightarrow
\text{discard}.
$$

For example:

$$
\alpha_c=0.5.
$$

Then pixels become binary:

$$
\text{opaque or absent}.
$$

Advantages include:

```text
depth writes remain useful
sorting becomes much easier
hidden geometry can be rejected
```

The cost is aliasing around thin edges.

Your current `triangle.frag` implements exactly this for its mask mode:

```glsl
if (maskMode && baseColorAlpha.a < cutoff)
    discard;
```

So Kairo already has all three broad alpha semantics:

```text
opaque
masked/cutout
blended
```

---

parts.title: Alpha-to-coverage

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Alpha-to-coverage**

Suppose 4× MSAA gives four coverage bits.

Instead of converting alpha into framebuffer blending, alpha-to-coverage converts alpha approximately into a sample mask.

For example:

$$
\alpha\approx0.5
$$

might produce coverage of roughly two of four samples.

Conceptually:

```text
alpha 0.0 → 0000
alpha 0.25 → perhaps 1000
alpha 0.5 → perhaps 1010
alpha 0.75 → perhaps 1110
alpha 1.0 → 1111
```

Actual patterns are implementation-dependent and may use dithering.

The key benefit for foliage is that covered samples can still participate normally in depth.

So alpha-to-coverage can provide antialiased cutout edges without conventional translucent depth-write problems.

But it needs multisampling.

Your present 1× Kairo viewport cannot benefit meaningfully from alpha-to-coverage.

---

parts.title: Overdraw

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Overdraw**

Suppose one final pixel is shaded by six opaque triangles before the nearest visible result survives.

The display shows one color.

The GPU may have performed six fragment shader executions.

Define an intuitive overdraw factor:

$$
O=
\frac{\text{fragment/sample work generated}}
{\text{visible output work}}.
$$

Large $O$ means enormous wasted work.

Common causes include:

```text
dense foliage
particles
large overlapping UI
poor draw ordering
very high geometric density
full-screen effects
```

Overdraw is particularly painful when fragment shaders are expensive.

---

parts.title: Fill-rate limitations

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Fill rate and bandwidth are not the same thing**

“Fill rate” informally describes the ability to process/write large numbers of fragments or samples.

But the bottleneck might actually be:

$$
\text{shader ALU},
$$

$$
\text{texture bandwidth},
$$

$$
\text{attachment bandwidth},
$$

$$
\text{ROP/blending throughput},
$$

or some combination.

Consider Kairo's viewport.

Approximate attachment sizes:

$$
RGBA16F = 8\text{ bytes},
$$

$$
R32UI = 4\text{ bytes},
$$

$$
D32F = 4\text{ bytes}.
$$

That is roughly

$$
16\text{ bytes/sample}
$$

of attachment state before considering reads, compression, caches or tiling.

At 3840×2160:

$$
8\,294\,400\text{ pixels}.
$$

At 60 fps:

$$
8.2944\times10^6
\times16
\times60
\approx7.96\times10^9
$$

or almost

$$
\boxed{8\text{ GB/s}}
$$

of raw per-frame attachment traffic for a single write of each value.

With 4× samples, naive raw traffic would approach:

$$
\approx32\text{ GB/s}.
$$

Real architectures use compression and tiles to avoid much of this, but the estimate explains why unnecessary overdraw and multisampling can be expensive.

---

parts.title: Early-Z optimization through front-to-back drawing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Early-Z and front-to-back opaque ordering**

Suppose a nearby wall covers almost the entire screen.

If you draw 100 objects behind the wall first, their fragments may shade and later become hidden.

If you draw the wall first, subsequent fragments can often fail depth early.

Thus for opaque geometry:

$$
\boxed{
\text{front-to-back sorting}
\rightarrow
\text{better opportunity for early depth rejection}
}
$$

This competes with state sorting.

If switching material pipelines is expensive, you may choose:

```text
perfect depth sorting but many pipeline switches
```

or

```text
material batching but more overdraw.
```

Production renderers solve a multi-objective optimization rather than using one universal sort.

---

**Early-Z is not an absolute promise**

We discussed early versus late depth in Pass 1.

parts.title: Occlusion queries concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Occlusion queries**

An occlusion query asks approximately:

> How many samples survived visibility testing for this draw?

A common use is:

```text
draw cheap bounding proxy
→ query visible sample count
→ skip expensive object next frame if zero
```

The danger is synchronization.

If the CPU does:

```text
issue query
wait immediately
decide what to draw
```

you can force CPU/GPU serialization.

The GPU may have to finish enormous amounts of queued work before the CPU receives the result.

Production use therefore often accepts latency:

```text
frame N query
frame N+1 or N+2 result
```

and uses conservative logic so temporary stale visibility does not cause popping.

---

parts.title: Hierarchical Z concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Blending, transparency, alpha testing, overdraw, early-Z, queries, Hi-Z
destinations.exact_quote:
**Hierarchical Z**

Testing every incoming sample against full-resolution depth is already useful, but many pixels can often be rejected in blocks.

Imagine an 8×8 block.

If every stored depth within that block is closer than an incoming primitive, the entire block can be discarded.

A Hi-Z structure stores coarse conservative summaries.

For conventional Z:

```text
near = 0
far  = 1
depth test = LESS
```

one useful conservative level stores the maximum depth of a region:

$$
H=\max(z_1,\dots,z_n).
$$

Suppose an incoming object's nearest possible depth over the block is

$$
z_{\text{near,obj}}.
$$

If

$$
z_{\text{near,obj}}\ge H,
$$

then since every existing sample satisfies

$$
z_i\le H\le z_{\text{near,obj}},
$$

the object is behind every stored depth value.

Reject the whole block.

---

**Reversed-Z reverses the Hi-Z reduction direction**

Under reversed-Z:

```text
near = 1
far  = 0
depth test = GREATER
```

the conservative bound flips.

A useful hierarchy stores

$$
H_R=\min(z_1,\dots,z_n).
$$

If the candidate object's nearest/highest depth satisfies

$$
z_{\text{near,obj}}\le H_R,
$$

then every existing sample is at least as near as the candidate, so it cannot pass `GREATER`.

This illustrates an important lesson from Pass 1:

> Reversed-Z is not merely a projection matrix change.

Any subsystem interpreting depth ordering must be audited.

Hi-Z is one of them.

---

parts.title: Instanced rendering

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Instanced rendering**

If many objects use the same mesh and pipeline, issue one draw:

$$
\boxed{
\text{one mesh}
+
N\text{ instance records}
}
$$

instead of $N$ independent draws.

A conceptual instance record:

```cpp
struct InstanceData
{
    Mat4 model;
    Vec4 color;
};
```

Then the vertex shader receives an instance index:

$$
i=\text{InstanceIndex}.
$$

It fetches

$$
M_i
$$

and computes

$$
p_w=M_i p_o.
$$

One indexed draw can now request:

```text
indexCount   = mesh indices
instanceCount = 50,000
```

and the vertex workload becomes logically

$$
\text{each mesh vertex}
\times
\text{each instance}.
$$

---

parts.title: Instance buffers

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Instance buffers**

One way to supply per-instance data is another vertex-input stream whose rate is:

```cpp
VK_VERTEX_INPUT_RATE_INSTANCE
```

Rather than incrementing once per vertex, the record advances once per instance.

Conceptually:

```text
binding 0:
Vertex 0
Vertex 1
Vertex 2
...

binding 1:
Instance 0 transform
Instance 1 transform
Instance 2 transform
...
```

The vertex invocation sees:

```text
mesh attributes from binding 0
+
instance attributes from binding 1
```

Large modern engines often instead store instance data in structured/storage buffers because those scale better and allow GPU-side indexing, culling and compaction.

---

parts.title: Batching

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Batching is broader than instancing**

Instancing requires meaningful commonality.

Usually:

```text
same mesh
same pipeline
often same material family
```

Batching is the broader strategy of reorganizing work so fewer submissions/state switches are needed.

You may batch by:

```text
pipeline
material
mesh
render pass
texture set
depth bucket
```

But batching has costs.

Suppose two objects are spatially far apart.

Combining them into one monolithic batch may destroy culling granularity.

One invisible object can no longer be removed independently.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{submission efficiency}
\leftrightarrow
\text{culling granularity}
}
$$

is a real design trade-off.

---

parts.title: Multi-draw indirect concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Multi-draw indirect**

Suppose the indirect buffer contains:

```text
command 0
command 1
command 2
...
command 9999
```

With multi-draw indirect, one recorded API command can execute many of these records.

This further reduces CPU submission work.

Vulkan's `multiDrawIndirect` feature controls whether a single indirect command may execute more than one draw record; otherwise the indirect draw count is restricted to zero or one. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/features.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The GPU-driven pipeline then becomes approximately:

```text
compute:
    generate 7,842 visible draw records

graphics:
    execute those 7,842 records from one indirect buffer
```

Khronos' current GPU-driven material describes MDI precisely as the bridge from compute-generated visibility to GPU-side graphics submission. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/samples/latest/samples/performance/multi_draw_indirect/README.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

**GPU-driven rendering**

Now imagine this pipeline:

```text
scene instances
      ↓
compute shader
      ↓
frustum/occlusion/LOD culling
      ↓
visible instance list
      ↓
indirect command buffer
      ↓
graphics draw consumes buffer
```

No CPU readback is required.

The GPU decides:

$$
\text{what survives}
$$

and directly emits the work description consumed by rendering.

That is the core idea of GPU-driven rendering.

The CPU submits a broad workload once.

The GPU specializes it every frame.

parts.title: Mesh shaders concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Mesh shaders change the pre-rasterization model**

The classic path is:

```text
vertex/index buffer
      ↓
fixed-function vertex fetch
      ↓
primitive assembly
      ↓
vertex shader
      ↓
optional tessellation/geometry stages
      ↓
rasterizer
```

Mesh shaders replace much of this front end with workgroup-programmable geometry generation.

Conceptually:

```text
workgroup
  reads meshlet data
  performs culling
  generates vertices
  generates primitive indices
        ↓
rasterizer
```

Khronos describes `VK_EXT_mesh_shader` as a compute-like programmable mechanism that can replace the traditional pre-rasterization vertex/primitive pipeline, with mesh shaders producing vertices and primitives directly for rasterization. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/features/latest/features/proposals/VK_EXT_mesh_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

**Meshlets**

Mesh shaders become much easier to understand if you first understand meshlets.

Instead of one giant indexed mesh:

```text
500,000 triangles
```

partition it into small clusters, for example:

```text
meshlet:
≤ 64 vertices
≤ 126 triangles
bounding sphere
normal cone
material
```

Now each cluster becomes a convenient unit for:

```text
frustum culling
cone/backface culling
LOD
parallel processing
```

A mesh shader workgroup can process one meshlet.

It loads its compact local vertex/index data, rejects the entire cluster if invisible, and otherwise emits the required vertices and primitives.

This creates much finer control over geometry processing than the traditional “feed vertices one by one through fixed assembly” model.

---

parts.title: Task shaders concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Task shaders**

Task shaders are an optional stage before mesh shaders.

Their mental model is:

```text
task workgroup
    ↓
coarse analysis / culling / LOD
    ↓
decide how many mesh workgroups exist
    ↓
emit payload
    ↓
mesh shader workgroups
```

A task shader might inspect a collection of meshlets and decide:

```text
meshlets 0–11 invisible → launch nothing
meshlet 12 visible       → launch one mesh group
meshlet 13 high detail   → launch several groups
```

Current Khronos documentation emphasizes exactly this role: task shaders can perform coarse culling and dynamically emit mesh shader groups via a workgroup-level payload. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/features/latest/features/proposals/VK_EXT_mesh_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Important: mesh shaders are **not automatically faster**.

The extension documentation itself warns that their flexibility can incur platform-dependent cost and that optimized traditional pipelines may remain faster for some workloads. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/features/latest/features/proposals/VK_EXT_mesh_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

That is the right engineering attitude.

---
