parts.title: Raster-order dependencies

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Raster-order dependencies**

The GPU wants to execute fragments aggressively in parallel.

But some operations fundamentally care about ordering.

Suppose fragment B reads the color produced by fragment A at the same pixel and then writes another value.

If the two overlap, ordinary independent fragment execution has a data hazard:

$$
A\rightarrow B
$$

must be enforced.

Typical examples include:

```text
framebuffer feedback
certain order-dependent compositing algorithms
per-pixel linked structures
some programmable blending algorithms
```

You cannot assume:

> “Triangle A was submitted before triangle B, therefore every fragment of A finishes first.”

Graphics APIs expose explicit mechanisms for ordering/synchronization where required. Vulkan's current specification includes rasterization-order attachment access and fragment interlock mechanisms for cases where same-pixel ordering must be constrained. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/latest/pdf/vkspec.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The performance lesson is important:

$$
\boxed{
\text{ordering constraints reduce freedom for parallel execution}
}
$$

so use them only when the algorithm genuinely requires them.

---

**Shader divergence**

parts.title: Shader divergence

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
GPUs execute nearby shader invocations in groups.

Suppose 32 lanes execute:

```glsl
if (materialType == METAL)
    DoMetal();
else
    DoGlass();
```

If every lane takes `METAL`, the group runs efficiently.

If half take each branch, hardware may need to execute:

```text
DoMetal()
with glass lanes masked

then

DoGlass()
with metal lanes masked
```

Useful lane utilization falls.

This is branch divergence.

The important distinction from CPU branch prediction is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{GPU divergence is primarily about lanes disagreeing}
}
$$

rather than predicting one control path incorrectly.

A branch can be perfectly predictable and still divergent.

---

**Divergence is not “branches are bad”**

Consider:

```glsl
if (distance > maxRange)
    return;
```

If nearly the entire wave takes the same path, this branch may be cheap and save huge work.

Conversely, replacing the branch with both computations and selecting afterward could be worse.

The correct question is:

$$
\text{How coherent is this branch across executing lanes?}
$$

not:

$$
\text{Can I remove every `if`?}
$$

This becomes particularly important with material megashaders.

---

parts.title: Shader register pressure

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Register pressure**

Every active shader invocation needs temporary storage.

Suppose a shader uses many live values:

```text
positions
normals
several BRDF intermediates
many texture coordinates
large temporary arrays
```

The compiler may require more registers per invocation.

An SM/CU contains a finite register file.

If each invocation consumes $R$ registers and there are $R_{\text{total}}$ registers available, the rough upper bound on concurrently resident invocations is constrained by

$$
N
\le
\frac{R_{\text{total}}}{R}.
$$

So increasing registers per thread can reduce occupancy.

If pressure becomes severe, values may spill into slower memory.

Therefore a shader optimization that reduces instruction count while doubling register pressure can actually become slower.

This is why GPU performance cannot be reasoned from source-code operation count alone.

---

parts.title: Push or root constants concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Push constants**

Push/root constants target very small, frequently changing data.

Instead of updating a buffer allocation or descriptor for every draw, small bytes can be embedded into command state.

Your current Kairo renderer uses exactly this.

Its `MeshPushConstants` is:

```cpp
struct MeshPushConstants
{
    std::array<float, 32> Values{};
};
```

That is:

$$
32\times4=128\text{ bytes}.
$$

It carries approximately:

```text
model matrix
normal matrix columns
shadow-receive flag / tint/object ID fields
```

and is sent with:

```cpp
vkCmdPushConstants(...)
```

for each draw.

This is a textbook example of dividing data by update frequency:

```text
camera/lights → uniform buffer
object transform → push constants
textures/material → descriptor set
mesh geometry → vertex/index buffers
```

**Render-state objects**

A modern graphics pipeline contains a large amount of state:

```text
shader stages
vertex input
topology
rasterization
culling
front-face
depth test
stencil
multisampling
blending
attachment formats
pipeline layout
```

Older APIs historically allowed much of this to be changed individually as mutable global state.

Modern explicit APIs push toward immutable or semi-immutable pipeline objects.

Why?

Because the driver can compile a coherent hardware configuration ahead of draw time.

The cost is pipeline creation complexity and potentially huge numbers of state combinations.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md

destinations.exact_quote:
**Pipeline state caching**

Suppose pipeline creation involves:

```text
shader translation
hardware code generation
state validation
linking
internal representation construction
```

Doing that during a frame can cause a visible hitch.

Vulkan therefore has pipeline caches that let pipeline-construction results be reused between related pipelines and, when serialized appropriately, between application runs. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/pipelines.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

An important current Kairo detail:

```cpp
vkCreateGraphicsPipelines(
    m_Device,
    VK_NULL_HANDLE,
    ...
);
```

Kairo currently passes:

$$
\boxed{\texttt{VK_NULL_HANDLE}}
$$

as the application pipeline cache.

So **application-provided Vulkan pipeline caching is presently disabled in this path**.

That is not incorrect for a small renderer.

It becomes increasingly relevant as permutation count and pipeline complexity grow.

---

destinations.heading: Instancing, batching, indirect drawing, GPU culling, mesh shaders, execution cost, data binding, PSOs and permutations
destinations.exact_quote:
**Shader compilation**

Your `.vert` and `.frag` source is not what Vulkan GPU hardware executes directly.

Your Kairo path loads precompiled:

```text
*.spv
```

files.

At runtime:

```cpp
ReadSpirv(...)
→ vkCreateShaderModule(...)
→ vkCreateGraphicsPipelines(...)
```

So there are multiple compilation levels:

```text
GLSL source
    ↓ compiler outside/around runtime
SPIR-V
    ↓ Vulkan driver
device-specific machine representation
```

The driver-level stage can still be expensive even though GLSL has already become SPIR-V.

That is why pipeline creation can hitch.

---

double sided?
```

Eight binary switches imply up to:

$$
2^8=256
$$

possible variants.

Twenty switches imply:

$$
2^{20}=1\,048\,576.
$$

This is permutation explosion.

Obviously many combinations are invalid or unnecessary, but the combinatorial growth is real.

The engineering problem becomes deciding what should be:

```text
compile-time shader variant
pipeline state
runtime uniform branch
specialization constant
separate pass/material family
```

There is no single correct answer.

---

**Kairo already has a tiny permutation system**

Current `VulkanTriangle` creates separate pipelines for approximately:

```text
static opaque
static transparent
skinned opaque
skinned transparent
static shadow
skinned shadow
debug lines
```

This is already a small permutation matrix.

For the mesh path:

$$
2\text{ skin states}
\times
2\text{ alpha states}
=
4\text{ primary mesh pipelines}.
$$

As you later add:

```text
two-sided
MSAA mode
depth prepass
wireframe
deferred/forward
clearcoat
transmission
```

you will have to decide carefully which dimensions deserve real PSO variants.

This is where engine rendering architecture begins becoming a combinatorial-management problem rather than only a graphics-math problem.

---

parts.title: Debugging a black frame systematically

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Black-frame debugging, vertex tracing, complete CPU rasterization, GPU mapping
destinations.exact_quote:
**A black frame is not one bug**

Suppose the application window appears and nothing renders.

“Graphics are broken” is too vague to be useful.

The frame is a dependency chain:

$$
\text{scene}
\rightarrow
\text{resource upload}
\rightarrow
\text{command recording}
\rightarrow
\text{submission}
\rightarrow
\text{vertex stage}
\rightarrow
\text{clipping}
\rightarrow
\text{rasterization}
\rightarrow
\text{fragment stage}
\rightarrow
\text{depth/stencil}
\rightarrow
\text{attachment}
\rightarrow
\text{presentation}.
$$

A systematic debugger asks:

$$
\boxed{
\text{What is the last stage that can be proven correct?}
}
$$

Do not randomly edit shaders.

Bisect the rendering machine.

---

**The black-frame attack tree**

Use this exact order because each stage removes huge classes of hypotheses.

1. **Prove the frame exists at all.** Clear the target to violent magenta. If magenta never reaches the screen, geometry and shaders are irrelevant; inspect acquire/record/submit/present and render-target routing. In Kairo, that means following `VulkanRendererRuntime::DrawFrame`: wait/retire → acquire → record → submit → present.

2. **Prove the correct render target is being written.** Kairo renders the 3D scene into `VulkanViewportTarget`, then later presents UI to the swapchain. A valid swapchain does not prove the offscreen viewport pass is correct.

3. **Remove geometry complexity.** Draw one hard-coded triangle with no index buffer, no material, no textures, no lighting, no skinning.

4. **Remove depth and culling.** Disable depth and face culling. If the triangle appears, reintroduce those independently.

5. **Replace the fragment shader with constant output.** `outColor = vec4(1,0,1,1);`. If it now appears, rasterization works and the failure is downstream of interpolation/material shading.

6. **Trace one vertex numerically.** Record object, world, view, clip and NDC coordinates. Verify finite $w$, clip inequalities and expected screen position.

7. **Check vertex layout contracts.** Buffer stride, offsets, formats and shader locations must describe the same bytes.

8. **Check draw ranges.** Index count, index type, bound offsets, vertex offsets and actual buffer sizes.

9. **Check attachment compatibility and writes.** Pipeline render-pass compatibility, color write masks, blend state, depth state and final image layouts.

10. **Only then inspect sophisticated systems.** Descriptor contents, material textures, normal maps, shadow passes, HDR exposure and render-graph synchronization.

That is our one deliberate list for the pass because it is meant to become an actual debugging procedure.

---

**Mapping that procedure onto current Kairo**

Your frame begins in:

```text
VulkanRendererRuntime::DrawFrame()
```

Current flow is:

```text
Retire
  ↓
vkWaitForFences

Acquire
  ↓
vkAcquireNextImageKHR

Record
  ↓
RecordFrameCommands()
  ↓
VulkanTriangle::Record()

Submit
  ↓
vkQueueSubmit

Present
  ↓
vkQueuePresentKHR
```

This already gives you a powerful first divide.

If `vkQueuePresentKHR` succeeds but you see only UI background, the swapchain path can be alive while scene rendering into `VulkanViewportTarget` is wrong.

Within `VulkanTriangle::Record()` the scene path is approximately:

```text
rebuild descriptors
update camera uniforms
upload debug vertices
begin command buffer

optional directional shadow pass

begin viewport render pass
set viewport/scissor
DrawMeshes()
DrawDebugLines()
end viewport render pass

optional picking/capture copy

begin presentation pass
draw editor overlay
end pass

end command buffer
```

So a black viewport while UI remains visible strongly narrows the bug.

---

parts.title: Debugging a broken transform by tracing one vertex

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Black-frame debugging, vertex tracing, complete CPU rasterization, GPU mapping
destinations.exact_quote:
**Broken transform debugging: trace one vertex**

Do not inspect an entire model.

Choose one vertex.

Suppose

$$
p_o=
(1,0,-5,1).
$$

Use identity model and identity view:

$$
M=I,\qquad V=I.
$$

Therefore

$$
p_w=p_o
$$

and

$$
p_v=p_w.
$$

Choose a simple 90° vertical FOV, aspect 1, near 1, far 10.

For a conventional right-handed Vulkan projection, the important relationships are approximately:

$$
x_c=x_v,
$$

$$
y_c=y_v,
$$

$$
w_c=-z_v.
$$

Thus

$$
w_c=5.
$$

A valid Vulkan projection maps the point's depth to about

$$
z_c=\frac{40}{9}\approx4.444.
$$

Therefore:

$$
p_c\approx
(1,0,4.444,5).
$$

Now perspective divide:

$$
x_n=\frac15=0.2,
$$

$$
y_n=0,
$$

$$
z_n=\frac{4.444}{5}\approx0.8889.
$$

All are valid:

$$
-1\le0.2\le1,
$$

$$
-1\le0\le1,
$$

$$
0\le0.8889\le1.
$$

For an 800×600 viewport:

$$
x_f=
\frac{0.2+1}{2}\times800
=
480.
$$

$$
y_f=
\frac{0+1}{2}\times600
=
300
$$

under the simple bottom-left mathematical mapping.

So the vertex should appear around:

$$
\boxed{(480,300)}.
$$

If instead your program gets:

```text
clip w = -5
```

you likely have a sign/convention problem.

If:

```text
w ≈ 0
```

you are near the projection singularity.

If:

```text
z_NDC = -3
```

you have a depth/projection mismatch.

If:

```text
x_NDC = 400
```

you likely have bad matrix data or a missing homogeneous divide.

Tracing one vertex turns “camera broken” into a mathematical diagnosis.

---

**Why this is especially relevant to Kairo**

Current Kairo vertex shader literally gives us the trace:

```glsl
const vec4 worldPosition =
    draw.model * vec4(inPosition, 1.0);

gl_Position =
    camera.projection *
    camera.view *
    worldPosition;
```

So instrumenting one vertex conceptually means extracting:

$$
p_o,
$$

$$
M p_o,
$$

$$
V M p_o,
$$

$$
PVMp_o.
$$

Remember also that Kairo modifies projection Y:

```cpp
projection(1,1) *= -1.0f;
```

because it uses a positive-height Vulkan viewport.

So an apparent Y inversion must be diagnosed with that fact included.

Never debug it as though the projection were a generic textbook matrix.

---

parts.title: Mapping the CPU rasterizer stages one-for-one to a modern GPU graphics pipeline

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Black-frame debugging, vertex tracing, complete CPU rasterization, GPU mapping
destinations.exact_quote:
**One-for-one mapping: CPU rasterizer → GPU pipeline**

Now we can map every significant CPU operation to GPU machinery.

| CPU reconstruction | Modern GPU/Vulkan equivalent |
|---|---|
| `VertexOut` input | vertex/index buffers + vertex fetch |
| object/world/view/projection math | vertex shader |
| clip-space polygon clipping | fixed-function clipping |
| divide by `w` | perspective divide |
| NDC → screen | viewport transform |
| area determinant | triangle setup/orientation |
| reject backface | culling stage |
| edge equations | rasterizer setup |
| pixel-center test | sample coverage |
| top-left tie | API rasterization convention |
| barycentrics | interpolator |
| `a/w` and `1/w` | perspective-correct varying interpolation |
| fragment function | fragment shader |
| depth compare | depth test |
| stencil state machine | stencil test |
| source/destination recurrence | blend unit |
| write color | color attachment |
| depth array | depth attachment |
| framebuffer arrays | Vulkan framebuffer/image attachments |
| outer triangle loop | draw commands |
| repeated object loop | instancing/batching |
| GPU-generated loop | indirect/GPU-driven drawing |

This is Part 1900.

And it is the point of the entire phase.

The GPU pipeline is no longer a diagram you memorize.

It is a hardware-parallel implementation of mechanisms you could reconstruct yourself.

---

**CPU → Kairo → Vulkan → hardware trace**

For one current Kairo mesh:

```text
Mesh
    contains
    MeshVertex[]
    uint32 indices[]
        ↓
CreateMesh()
        ↓
VulkanHostBuffer vertex buffer
VulkanHostBuffer index buffer
        ↓
RenderScene MeshDraw
        ↓
VulkanTriangle::DrawMeshes
        ↓
select pipeline
        ↓
BindMaterial descriptor set
        ↓
MeshPushConstants:
model / normal data / ID
        ↓
vkCmdBindVertexBuffers
vkCmdBindIndexBuffer
        ↓
vkCmdDrawIndexed
        ↓
vertex fetch
        ↓
triangle.vert
        ↓
worldPosition = M p
        ↓
gl_Position = P V worldPosition
        ↓
clipping
        ↓
perspective divide
        ↓
viewport
        ↓
triangle setup / coverage
        ↓
fragment interpolation
        ↓
triangle.frag
        ↓
PBR + texture evaluation
        ↓
mask discard if necessary
        ↓
depth test
        ↓
optional source-over blend
        ↓
HDR color attachment
+
object-ID attachment
        ↓
viewport color becomes shader-readable
        ↓
editor/presentation path
```

That is the actual machine you are working with now.

parts.title: Light as electromagnetic energy versus RGB approximation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Make every color number carry a meaning
destinations.exact_quote:
**Light is not RGB**

Real light is electromagnetic radiation.

At a point, light can be described spectrally by wavelength:

$$
\lambda
$$

and a spectral power distribution such as

$$
L(\lambda).
$$

Visible wavelengths occupy only part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

A physically complete renderer would therefore reason about something like

$$
L(\lambda)
$$

at many wavelengths.

Most real-time renderers do not.

They approximate spectral light with three numbers:

$$
(R,G,B).
$$

This is a drastic compression.

It works because human color vision itself approximately reduces spectral information through three cone-response families.

But:

$$
\boxed{\text{RGB is not light itself}}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{\text{different spectra can produce the same RGB/perceived color}}.
$$

That phenomenon is **metamerism**.

This becomes important whenever spectral effects matter:

- dispersion,
- fluorescence,
- wavelength-dependent IOR,
- thin-film interference,
- unusual illuminants.

Our renderer is fundamentally **tristimulus**, not spectral.

---

**Irradiance**

Suppose flux lands on a surface.

Irradiance is incident flux per unit surface area:

$$
\boxed{
E=\frac{d\Phi}{dA}

$$

with units

$$

$$

$$
100\,\mathrm W
$$

lands uniformly on

$$
10\,\mathrm{m^2},
$$

then

$$
E=10\,\mathrm{W/m^2}.
$$

Irradiance answers:

> How much incoming power reaches this patch?

This quantity integrates incoming light from many directions.

parts.title: Radiance

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Radiometry: the hierarchy
destinations.exact_quote:
**Radiance — the central rendering quantity**

Radiance describes power with both **spatial and directional density**.

Formally:

$$
\boxed{
L=
\frac{d^2\Phi}
{dA_\perp\,d\omega}
}
$$

where

$$
dA_\perp
=
dA\cos\theta.
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
L=
\frac{d^2\Phi}
{\cos\theta\,dA\,d\omega}
}
$$

with units

$$
\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}.
$$

Interpretation:

> How much radiant power travels through an infinitesimal projected surface area inside an infinitesimal direction range?

This is the quantity most directly associated with a ray.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Radiometry: the hierarchy
destinations.exact_quote:
**Solid angle**

Before radiance makes sense, we need angular measure.

In 2D, angle in radians is

$$
\theta=\frac{s}{r}.
$$

In 3D, solid angle is

$$
\boxed{
\Omega=\frac{A_{\text{sphere}}}{r^2}
}
$$

where $A_{\text{sphere}}$ is the area cut out on a sphere of radius $r$.

Unit:

$$
\mathrm{sr}
$$

or steradians.

A complete sphere subtends

$$
4\pi
$$

steradians.

A hemisphere subtends

$$
2\pi.
$$

For differential solid angle:

$$
d\omega
=
\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi.
$$

This is why hemisphere integrals later contain

$$
\sin\theta.
$$

---

parts.title: Radiance invariance along a vacuum ray

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Radiance invariance along a vacuum ray
destinations.exact_quote:
**Radiance invariance along a vacuum ray**

One of the most powerful properties in rendering is:

$$
\boxed{
L(\mathbf x,\omega)
=
L(\mathbf x+t\omega,\omega)
}
$$

for unobstructed propagation through vacuum.

Radiance does **not** fall with inverse square along a ray.

This initially sounds wrong because we know light intensity falls with distance.

The distinction is crucial.

A point emitter spreads its total flux across a growing sphere:

$$
A=4\pi r^2.
$$

Therefore irradiance on a receiving surface decreases approximately as:

$$
E\propto\frac1{r^2}.
$$

But radiance measures directional density.

As distance grows:

- apparent angular size shrinks,
- geometric projected area relationship changes,

in exactly the way required for radiance to remain unchanged along free propagation.

This is why a distant surface does not become visually dimmer merely because it is farther away, assuming no atmosphere and equal projected appearance.

It occupies fewer pixels, but its radiance per corresponding viewing ray remains the same.

---

**The rendering ray interpretation**

parts.title: Human color perception overview

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Human color perception
destinations.exact_quote:
**Human color perception**

The retina contains several photoreceptor classes.

For photopic color vision, three cone types dominate:

$$
L,\quad M,\quad S
$$

with different spectral response curves.

A spectral stimulus

$$
S(\lambda)
$$

generates cone responses roughly like:

$$
R_L=
\int S(\lambda)\bar l(\lambda)\,d\lambda,
$$

$$
R_M=
\int S(\lambda)\bar m(\lambda)\,d\lambda,
$$

$$
R_S=
\int S(\lambda)\bar s(\lambda)\,d\lambda.
$$

This maps an effectively enormous-dimensional spectral function to three response values.

Therefore many different spectra map to the same three responses.

Hence metamers.

Rendering with RGB exploits this dimensional reduction.

---

parts.title: Tristimulus color representation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Tristimulus representation
destinations.exact_quote:
**Tristimulus representation**

A tristimulus system chooses three basis responses.

Common examples include:

$$
XYZ
$$

and

$$
RGB.
$$

CIE XYZ is especially important because it provides a standardized colorimetric space.

RGB spaces choose actual or conceptual red, green and blue primaries.

A color becomes coordinates relative to those basis primaries.

For example:

$$
\mathbf c=
\begin{bmatrix}
R\\G\\B
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

But these numbers are meaningless without knowing:

- primaries,
- white point,
- transfer function.

Thus:

$$
(1,0,0)
$$

in sRGB does not represent the same physical chromaticity as

$$
(1,0,0)
$$

in Display P3.

---

parts.title: Linear RGB

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Linear RGB
destinations.exact_quote:
**Linear RGB**

A linear RGB space is one in which arithmetic corresponds linearly to light.

If:

$$
C_2=2C_1,
$$

then conceptually it represents twice the channel contribution.

That means operations such as:

$$
C=C_1+C_2
$$

and

$$
C=kC_1
$$

have sensible physical meaning.

This is what lighting needs.

Your own `KairoRenderer::PBRMaterial` explicitly documents:

```text
BaseColor = non-negative linear RGB
Emissive  = non-negative linear RGB
```

and `KairoRayTracer::Color3f` similarly establishes:

```text
internal color = linear RGB
values may exceed [0,1]
```

That is the correct internal convention.

---

parts.title: sRGB transfer function

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: sRGB is not linear RGB
destinations.exact_quote:
**sRGB is not linear RGB**

sRGB uses the same primaries and D65 white point for both encoded and linear-light forms, but applies a nonlinear transfer function for stored/display-oriented values. Current W3C color specifications describe linear-sRGB as the same primaries/white point with a unity transfer function and sRGB as the encoded form. [W3C](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

For encoded component $C_s$, decoding to linear light gives:

$$
\boxed{
C_l=
\begin{cases}
\frac{C_s}{12.92},
&
C_s\le0.04045
\\[6pt]
\left(
\frac{C_s+0.055}{1.055}
\right)^{2.4},
&
C_s>0.04045
\end{cases}
}
$$

The inverse conversion is:

$$
\boxed{
C_s=
\begin{cases}
12.92C_l,
&
C_l\le0.0031308
\\[6pt]
1.055C_l^{1/2.4}-0.055,
&
C_l>0.0031308.
\end{cases}
}
$$

These are the exact piecewise transfer functions used by KairoAssets.

---

parts.title: Gamma encoding versus linear light

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: “Gamma 2.2” versus actual sRGB
destinations.exact_quote:
**“Gamma 2.2” versus actual sRGB**

You often see:

$$
C_l\approx C_s^{2.2}.
$$

That is an approximation.

sRGB is not exactly a pure $2.2$ power function.

The lower segment is linear, and the upper exponent is 2.4 with offsets.

Interestingly, your repositories currently show both approaches.

`KairoAssets/TextureArtifact.cppm` uses the proper piecewise conversion:

```cpp
value <= 0.04045
    ? value / 12.92
    : pow((value + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
```

while `KairoRayTracer/Color.cppm` currently encodes PPM output using:

```cpp
pow(linear, 1.0f / 2.2f);
```

So the asset pipeline is proper sRGB, while the simple ray-tracer PPM output uses a gamma-2.2 approximation.

That distinction is useful rather than merely academic.

---

**Why lighting in sRGB is wrong**

parts.title: Why lighting calculations must use linear values

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Why lighting in sRGB is wrong
destinations.exact_quote:
Suppose two lights independently contribute linear intensity

$$
0.25
$$

each.

Correct linear addition:

$$
0.25+0.25=0.5.
$$

Encode afterward.

But if 0.25 were first converted to an sRGB-like encoded value, roughly:

$$
sRGB(0.25)\approx0.537.
$$

Adding the encoded values gives:

$$
0.537+0.537=1.074.
$$

Clamping produces:

$$
1.
$$

That implies white instead of the correct encoded representation of linear 0.5:

$$
sRGB(0.5)\approx0.735.
$$

Massive error.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{decode}
\rightarrow
\text{lighting in linear space}
\rightarrow
\text{tone map}
\rightarrow
\text{display encode}
}
$$

is the correct broad pipeline.

---

**The classic midpoint error**

Imagine averaging black and white texels.

Encoded values:

$$
0,\quad1.
$$

Naive encoded-space average:

$$
0.5.
$$

But decoding sRGB 0.5 gives approximately:

$$
0.214.
$$

So the “average” contains only about 21% linear light.

Correct procedure:

$$
0\rightarrow0_{\text{linear}}
$$

$$
1\rightarrow1_{\text{linear}}
$$

then:

$$
\frac{0+1}{2}=0.5_{\text{linear}}.
$$

Encoding linear 0.5 gives approximately:

$$
\boxed{0.735_{\text{sRGB}}}.
$$

That is a huge practical difference.

This applies to:

- texture filtering,
- mipmap generation,
- image resizing,
- compositing.

---

**Kairo gets this mipmap case right**

parts.title: Color spaces and primaries

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Primaries
destinations.exact_quote:
**Primaries**

An RGB color space is defined partly by three chromaticity primaries.

For sRGB they are approximately:

$$
R=(0.640,0.330),
$$

$$
G=(0.300,0.600),
$$

$$
B=(0.150,0.060).
$$

A Display-P3 red primary is different.

Therefore even if both values are linear:

```text
linear-sRGB   (1,0,0)
linear-P3     (1,0,0)
```

they represent different chromaticities.

A transfer function alone does not define a color space.

---

destinations.heading: White points
destinations.exact_quote:
**White points**

The white point specifies which chromaticity should appear neutral.

sRGB uses D65.

Conceptually, white point defines the reference:

$$
R=G=B
$$

that should appear achromatic under the target viewing/colorimetric model.

When converting between spaces with different white points, chromatic adaptation may be required.

This matters in production pipelines involving:

```text
sRGB
Display P3
ACEScg
Rec.2020
XYZ
```

not merely in photo-editing software.

destinations.heading: HDR numbers
destinations.exact_quote:
**HDR numbers**

Suppose a shader produces:

$$
C=(5.4,1.2,0.3).
$$

This is not “invalid RGB.”

In scene-linear HDR rendering:

$$
C>1
$$

is perfectly ordinary.

The value 1 is not the maximum amount of light in nature.

The constraint:

$$
0\le C\le1
$$

is typically associated with limited output encoding/storage, not with the lighting calculation itself.

This is why floating-point framebuffer formats are useful.

parts.title: Tone mapping motivation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: HDR rendering is not the same as HDR display
destinations.exact_quote:
**HDR rendering is not the same as HDR display**

These are different concepts.

**Scene-linear HDR rendering**

The renderer allows values like:

$$
0.001,\quad0.5,\quad2,\quad100,\quad10000.
$$

**HDR intermediate buffer**

The framebuffer preserves a useful wide numerical range, usually using floating point.

**HDR display output**

The final output targets HDR transfer functions/gamuts such as PQ/HLG and actual HDR-capable displays.

You can have:

```text
HDR scene-linear rendering
→ tone map
→ normal SDR sRGB monitor
```

and that is still an HDR rendering pipeline internally.

---

\quad \text{as }x\rightarrow\infty.
$$

So highlights compress smoothly rather than clipping.

**Filmic tone mapping**

Real film/camera response inspired curves tend to have:

- **toe** near black,
- reasonably linear midtone region,
- **shoulder** compressing highlights.

Conceptually:

```text
output
1 |                   ______
  |                __/
  |             __/
  |          __/
  |       __/
  |    __/
0 |___/
  +-------------------------- input
```

The point is not “make it cinematic.”

The objective is often to preserve:

- midtone contrast,
- highlight rolloff,
- shadow detail,
- acceptable colors.

Common production operators include ACES-inspired fits, Hable/Uncharted-style curves and custom display transforms.

parts.title: Exposure in rendering

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Exposure
destinations.exact_quote:
**Exposure**

Camera exposure is fundamentally a scale applied before display mapping.

A convenient rendering model is:

$$
\boxed{
C_{\text{exposed}}
=
C_{\text{scene}}2^{EV}
}
$$

where increasing EV by 1 doubles brightness:

$$
EV+1
\Rightarrow
2C.
$$

Reducing by one stop:

$$
EV-1
\Rightarrow
\frac12C.
$$

Your Kairo shader currently performs exactly:

```glsl
hdrColor =
    sceneColor *
    exp2(camera.viewportParameters.y);
```

Since:

$$
\operatorname{exp2}(x)=2^x,
$$

that field is effectively an EV exposure control.

---

destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**A texture is a sampled signal**

Suppose there exists an ideal continuous function:

$$
f(u,v).
$$

A digital texture does not store that continuous function.

It stores discrete samples:

$$
f[i,j].
$$

These samples are **texels**.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{texture sampling is a signal-reconstruction problem}
}
$$

not merely “look up a color in an image.”

This viewpoint explains:

- nearest filtering,
- bilinear filtering,
- mipmaps,
- anisotropy,
- aliasing.

parts.title: Texels versus pixels

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Texel versus pixel**

A **texel** belongs to a texture.

A **pixel** belongs to an output image.

They are not necessarily one-to-one.

One texel may cover hundreds of pixels during magnification.

Thousands of texels may map into a single pixel during minification.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{texel density}
\neq
\text{screen pixel density}
}
$$

and texture filtering exists because we must map between those sampling grids.

---

parts.title: UV coordinates

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**UV coordinates**

A texture coordinate commonly uses:

$$
(u,v)\in[0,1]^2.
$$

For width $W$, height $H$, a simple conceptual conversion is:

$$
x=uW,
\qquad
y=vH.
$$

But texels represent cells with centers, so filtering implementations usually account for the half-texel relationship.

A useful conceptual coordinate for bilinear filtering is:

$$
x=uW-\frac12,
$$

$$
y=vH-\frac12.
$$

Then integer texel centers align naturally with the reconstructed samples.

Actual Vulkan normalized-coordinate sampling has precise rules defined in the sampling specification, including coordinate conversion, image dimensions, wrapping and filtering. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/textures.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

parts.title: Texture wrapping modes

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Wrapping modes**

What happens if:

$$
u=1.25?
$$

### Repeat

$$
u'=u-\lfloor u\rfloor.
$$

So:

$$
1.25\rightarrow0.25.
$$

---

### Clamp-to-edge

$$
u'=
\operatorname{clamp}(u,0,1).
$$

So:

$$
1.25\rightarrow1.
$$

---

### Mirrored repeat

Intervals alternate direction:

```text
0→1
1→0
0→1
...
```

This avoids the discontinuity that ordinary repetition produces at every tile boundary for some textures.

Your current `TextureSampler` supports:

```text
Repeat
MirroredRepeat
ClampToEdge
```

for U/V.

---

**Nearest sampling**

Nearest chooses the closest stored sample.

Conceptually:

$$
i=\operatorname{round}(x),
$$

j=\operatorname{round}(y).
$$

Then:

$$
C=T[i,j].
$$

Advantages:

- cheap,
- preserves hard pixel-art edges,
- deterministic sample choice.

Disadvantages:

- blocky magnification,
- severe minification aliasing.

parts.title: Bilinear texture filtering

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Bilinear filtering**

Let texture coordinate map to:

$$
x=i+\alpha,
$$

$$
y=j+\beta
$$

where:

$$
0\le\alpha,\beta<1.
$$

Four texels contribute:

$$
T_{00}=T[i,j],
$$

$$
T_{10}=T[i+1,j],
$$

$$
T_{01}=T[i,j+1],
$$

$$
T_{11}=T[i+1,j+1].
$$

Interpolate horizontally:

$$
A=(1-\alpha)T_{00}+\alpha T_{10},
$$

$$
B=(1-\alpha)T_{01}+\alpha T_{11}.
$$

Then vertically:

$$
\boxed{
C=(1-\beta)A+\beta B.
}
$$

Expanded:

$$
C=
(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)T_{00}
+
\alpha(1-\beta)T_{10}
+
(1-\alpha)\beta T_{01}
+
\alpha\beta T_{11}.
$$

This is a separable triangle filter.

---

parts.title: Trilinear texture filtering

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Trilinear filtering**

Suppose:

$$
\lambda=3.25.
$$

Bilinear sample level 3:

$$
C_3.
$$

Bilinear sample level 4:

$$
C_4.
$$

Then interpolate:

$$
\boxed{
C=
0.75C_3+0.25C_4.
}
$$

This is trilinear filtering:

- bilinear in $u,v$ at first mip,
- bilinear in $u,v$ at second mip,
- linear between mip levels.

Vulkan's `VK_SAMPLER_MIPMAP_MODE_LINEAR` similarly selects neighboring mip levels and interpolates between them. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/09_Generating_Mipmaps.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

parts.title: Texture minification and aliasing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Bilinear does not solve minification**

Suppose a distant surface maps one screen pixel onto a:

$$
64\times64
$$

texel footprint.

That pixel conceptually represents information from:

$$
4096
$$

source texels.

Bilinear filtering samples only four nearby texels.

Four samples cannot represent the average of 4096 high-frequency texels.

This violates sampling theory and causes:

- moiré,
- shimmering,
- temporal crawling,
- unstable fine patterns.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{\text{bilinear filtering is reconstruction, not sufficient prefiltering}}
$$

for heavy minification.

---

**Nyquist intuition**

If the underlying texture contains frequency $f$, the screen sampling rate must be at least:

$$
2f
$$

to represent it without aliasing.

When the texture footprint shrinks on screen, high-frequency components exceed the screen's Nyquist limit.

They must be removed **before sampling**.

This is exactly what mipmaps provide.

---

parts.title: Mipmaps

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Mipmaps**

Mip level 0:

$$
W\times H.
$$

Level 1:

$$
\frac W2\times\frac H2.
$$

Level 2:

$$
\frac W4\times\frac H4.
$$

Eventually:

$$
1\times1.
$$

Example:

```text
1024×1024
512×512
256×256
128×128
64×64
32×32
16×16
8×8
4×4
2×2
1×1
```

Each level is a prefiltered representation suitable for a larger texture footprint.

---

**Total mipmap memory**

For an uncompressed square texture:

$$
1+\frac14+\frac1{16}+\frac1{64}+\cdots
$$

is a geometric series.

Its sum tends toward:

$$
\frac{1}{1-\frac14}
=
\frac43.
$$

Therefore a complete mip chain costs only about:

$$
\boxed{33\%}
$$

more storage than the base image.

This is extraordinarily cheap relative to the quality and cache benefits.

---

parts.title: Mipmap generation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Correct mip generation**

A simplistic color mip takes a 2×2 block:

$$
C_{00},C_{10},C_{01},C_{11}
$$

and averages:

$$
C'=
\frac{
C_{00}+C_{10}+C_{01}+C_{11}
}{4}.
$$

But that average must happen in the **correct domain**.

For color:

```text
sRGB bytes
  ↓ decode
linear RGB
  ↓ average/filter
linear RGB mip
  ↓ encode if stored in sRGB format
sRGB bytes
```

Your KairoAssets implementation does exactly that.

---

**Normal maps cannot be mipmapped like ordinary RGB**

Suppose two normals are:

$$
N_1=(1,0,0),
$$

$$
N_2=(0,1,0).
$$

Their simple average is:

$$
(0.5,0.5,0).
$$

Its length is:

$$
\sqrt{0.5}
\approx0.707.
$$

It is no longer a unit normal.

A basic normal-map mip generator therefore:

1. decodes RGB to vectors,
2. averages vectors,
3. renormalizes,
4. re-encodes.

Your KairoAssets mip builder explicitly does this for normal maps.

That is an excellent example of:

$$
\boxed{
\text{texture semantic determines the correct filtering operation}.
}
$$

---

parts.title: Mipmap level selection

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Mipmap level selection**

Suppose UV changes by:

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},
\quad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial x},
\quad
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y},
\quad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}.
$$

Convert normalized UV derivatives into base-level texel units:

$$
\mathbf d_x=
\left(
W\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},
H\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}
\right),
$$

$$
\mathbf d_y=
\left(
W\frac{\partial u}{\partial y},
H\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}
\right).
$$

A common isotropic footprint estimate is:

$$
\rho=
\max(
\|\mathbf d_x\|,
\|\mathbf d_y\|
).
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
\lambda=\log_2\rho
}
$$

is the desired mip LOD.

Examples:

If:

$$
\rho=1
$$

then:

$$
\lambda=0.
$$

Use base level.

If:

$$
\rho=2
$$

then:

$$
\lambda=1.
$$

If:

$$
\rho=8
$$

then:

$$
\lambda=3.
$$

Vulkan similarly derives implicit LOD from coordinate derivatives, with the exact scale-factor and LOD procedure specified by the API. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/textures.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

**Why logarithm appears**

Every mip level halves resolution.

A scale factor of:

$$
2
$$

means one level down.

A scale of:

$$
4=2^2
$$

means two levels down.

A scale of:

$$
8=2^3
$$

means three levels down.

Therefore:

$$
\lambda=\log_2\rho.
$$

The logarithm is not an arbitrary graphics convention.

It follows directly from the geometric mip pyramid.

---

parts.title: Texture-coordinate derivatives

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Derivatives again**

Last pass we used:

```glsl
dFdx(inTexCoord)
dFdy(inTexCoord)
```

to build a tangent basis.

The texture hardware also needs essentially the same information.

A shader expression:

```glsl
texture(baseColorMap, inTexCoord)
```

normally performs **implicit LOD** lookup in the fragment stage.

The sampler derives how rapidly the UV changes across neighboring fragments and selects an appropriate mip level. Vulkan explicitly states that implicit-LOD image instructions calculate derivatives from neighboring fragment coordinates and use those derivatives for LOD selection. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/textures.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{fragment quads}
\rightarrow
UV derivatives
\rightarrow
texture footprint
\rightarrow
LOD
}
$$

is an actual hardware/dataflow connection.

---

parts.title: Anisotropic filtering

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Texture footprint is not generally square**

Consider a floor stretching into the distance.

Near the camera, one pixel might cover:

$$
2\times2
$$

texels.

Farther away, due to foreshortening, one screen pixel might cover an elongated region:

$$
2\times64
$$

texels.

An isotropic mip level sees essentially the largest dimension:

$$
64,
$$

and picks a low-resolution mip suitable for that scale.

But along the short direction, that mip is far too blurry.

This is why trilinear filtering causes distant ground textures to lose detail.

---

**Anisotropic filtering**

Anisotropic filtering recognizes that the footprint can be elongated.

Instead of approximating it as a square/circle, think of an ellipse.

Let major and minor footprint lengths be:

$$
a,\quad b.
$$

Anisotropy ratio:

$$
\boxed{
A=\frac{a}{b}.
}
$$

For:

$$
A=1
$$

the footprint is isotropic.

For:

$$
A=16
$$

it is highly elongated.

Anisotropic filtering samples more intelligently along the long direction while retaining higher resolution across the short direction.

The exact algorithm is implementation dependent in Vulkan, controlled by sampler anisotropy state and hardware limits. [docs.vulkan.org](https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/textures.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

**Kairo currently has anisotropy effectively disabled**

Your sampler contains:

```cpp
create.maxAnisotropy = 1.0f;
```

but does not enable:

```cpp
create.anisotropyEnable = VK_TRUE;
```

The zero-initialized structure therefore has anisotropy disabled.

So today:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Kairo = trilinear isotropic filtering}
}
$$

not anisotropic filtering.

A production change would need to:

- query sampler-anisotropy feature support,
- enable it,
- clamp requested anisotropy to device limits.

---

parts.title: Texture compression concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Texture compression**

Uncompressed RGBA8 costs:

$$
4\text{ bytes/texel}.
$$

A 4096×4096 texture requires:

$$
4096^2\times4
\approx67.1\text{ MB}
$$

before mipmaps.

With full mip chain:

$$
67.1\times\frac43
\approx89.5\text{ MB}.
$$

Ten such textures approach:

$$
895\text{ MB}.
$$

This is why GPU texture compression matters.

---

**Block compression**

Many GPU formats compress small blocks independently.

For example, BC1 uses 4×4 blocks.

A block represents:

$$
16\text{ texels}
$$

using 8 bytes.

So:

$$
\frac{8\times8\text{ bits}}
{16}
=
4\text{ bits/texel}.
$$

Compared with RGBA8:

$$
32\text{ bits/texel}.
$$

That is an 8× reduction.

Because blocks are independently decodable, the GPU can still perform random texture access without decompressing the entire image.

---

**Compression is semantic too**

Different texture types prefer different formats.

Examples:

```text
base color:
BC7 / ASTC high-quality color

normal XY:
BC5

single-channel masks:
BC4

mobile:
ASTC / ETC families
```

Why BC5 for normals?

Normal mapping can store:

$$
x,y
$$

and reconstruct:

$$
z=
\sqrt{
\max(
0,
1-x^2-y^2
)
}.
$$

So two high-quality signed-ish channels can be better than wasting general RGBA compression on XYZ.

---

**Kairo currently has no GPU block-compressed texture path**

Your current texture enum supports only:

```text
R8
RG8
RGBA8
RGBA16Float
```

No BCn, ASTC or ETC formats are represented yet.

So this portion of M116 is currently a future asset/runtime capability.

A later production texture artifact should probably encode:

```text
pixel/block format
color space
semantic
mip chain
possibly platform transcoding target
```

rather than assuming raw pixels.

---

parts.title: Normal maps

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Normal maps**

A geometric normal approximates surface orientation at mesh resolution.

A normal map stores much higher-frequency orientation information.

Typically RGB encodes a tangent-space vector.

Stored value:

$$
C\in[0,1]^3.
$$

Decode:

$$
\boxed{
N_t=2C-1.
}
$$

For the neutral normal:

$$
N_t=(0,0,1).
$$

Its encoded RGB is:

$$
(0.5,0.5,1).
$$

Which explains the characteristic bluish appearance of normal maps.

The glTF specification likewise defines tangent-space normal textures as linear data, maps sampled RGB with $2C-1$, and requires the normal to be normalized before lighting. [Khronos Registry](https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

parts.title: Tangent-space normal mapping

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Why tangent space**

Suppose the same normal-map texture is used on surfaces facing:

- +X,
- +Y,
- +Z.

If the map stored world-space normals, it could not simply rotate with the object.

Tangent space creates a local surface frame:

$$
T=\text{tangent},
$$

$$
B=\text{bitangent},
$$

$$
N=\text{surface normal}.
$$

A tangent-space map stores perturbations relative to that frame.

Thus the same texture naturally follows:

- object rotation,
- surface orientation,
- UV parameterization.

---

**TBN matrix**

Build:

$$
\boxed{
TBN=
\begin{bmatrix}
T&B&N
\end{bmatrix}
}
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
N_{\text{world}}
=
TBN\,N_{\text{tangent}}.
}
$$

For:

$$
N_t=(0,0,1),
$$

we obtain:

$$
N_w=N.
$$

For:

$$
N_t=(1,0,0),
$$

we obtain:

$$
N_w=T.
$$

So the tangent-space vector's XYZ coordinates mean weights along:

$$
T,B,N.
$$

---

parts.title: Building a tangent basis

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Textures and surface detail
destinations.exact_quote:
**Building tangent and bitangent from geometry + UVs**

Take triangle edges:

$$
E_1=P_1-P_0,
$$

$$
E_2=P_2-P_0.
$$

Texture-coordinate differences:

$$
\Delta UV_1=
(u_1-u_0,v_1-v_0),
$$

$$
\Delta UV_2=
(u_2-u_0,v_2-v_0).
$$

We assume:

$$
E_1=
T\Delta u_1+
B\Delta v_1,
$$

$$
E_2=
T\Delta u_2+
B\Delta v_2.
$$

In matrix form:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
E_1&E_2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
T&B
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta u_1&\Delta u_2\\
\Delta v_1&\Delta v_2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The determinant is:

$$
D=
\Delta u_1\Delta v_2
-
\Delta u_2\Delta v_1.
$$

If:

$$
D=0,
$$

UV mapping is locally singular.

Otherwise:

$$
r=\frac1D.
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
T=
r(
E_1\Delta v_2
-
E_2\Delta v_1
)
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
B=
r(
E_2\Delta u_1
-
E_1\Delta u_2
).
}
$$

---

**Tangent should be orthogonalized**

Interpolated normals and tangents may cease to be exactly orthogonal.

Given normal $N$, Gram-Schmidt tangent correction:

$$
\boxed{
T'=
\operatorname{normalize}
(
T-N(N\cdot T)
)
}
$$

Then bitangent can be reconstructed as:

$$
B=
h(N\times T')
$$

where:

$$
h\in\{-1,+1\}
$$

is handedness.

This avoids storing an entire bitangent vector.

parts.title: Bitangent handedness

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Bitangent handedness
destinations.exact_quote:
**Bitangent handedness**

Mirrored UV islands reverse texture-space orientation.

The determinant:

$$
D=
\Delta u_1\Delta v_2-
\Delta u_2\Delta v_1
$$

changes sign under such mirroring.

Therefore the tangent frame may be right-handed or left-handed.

A common representation stores tangent:

$$
(T_x,T_y,T_z,h)
$$

where:

$$
h=\pm1.
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
B=h(N\times T).
}
$$

If handedness is ignored, normal maps can invert or produce seams on mirrored UV islands.

---

**Canonical tangent construction**

```cpp
struct TangentFrame
{
    Vec3 tangent;
    Vec3 bitangent;
};

parts.title: Height maps

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Height maps
destinations.exact_quote:
**Height maps**

A height map stores:

$$
h(u,v)
$$

rather than a direction.

It describes scalar surface elevation.

A normal can be derived from its gradient.

Locally, if:

$$
z=h(u,v),
$$

then tangent directions are approximately:

$$
P_u=
(1,0,h_u),
$$

$$
P_v=
(0,1,h_v).
$$

Their cross product is:

$$
P_u\times P_v
=
(-h_u,-h_v,1).
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
N
\propto
\left(
-\frac{\partial h}{\partial u},
-\frac{\partial h}{\partial v},
1
\right).
}
$$

This shows the relationship:

$$
\boxed{
\text{height map}
\rightarrow
\text{gradient}
\rightarrow
\text{normal map}.
}
$$

A normal map essentially stores local differential orientation directly.

---

**Height versus normal information**

parts.title: Parallax mapping concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Parallax mapping
destinations.exact_quote:
**Parallax mapping**

Normal mapping changes lighting orientation but does not change where texture features appear as the camera moves.

Parallax mapping uses height to shift UVs according to view direction.

Transform viewing direction into tangent space:

$$
V_t=(V_x,V_y,V_z).
$$

A simple offset model is approximately:

$$
\boxed{
\Delta UV
=
s\,h(u,v)
\frac{(V_x,V_y)}{V_z}
}
$$

where $s$ controls apparent depth.

Then sample using:

$$
UV'=UV-\Delta UV
$$

depending on height convention.

As:

$$
V_z\rightarrow0
$$

at grazing angles, the shift becomes large.

That is where basic parallax approximations break down.

---

**Why parallax mapping is still fake geometry**

Parallax mapping changes texture lookup.

It does **not** move the rasterized surface.

Therefore it cannot correctly change:

- silhouette,
- true occlusion against other objects,
- physical intersection,
- cast-shadow geometry.

A brick wall may appear recessed internally but retain a perfectly flat silhouette.

Steep parallax and parallax occlusion mapping improve self-occlusion and ray-height intersection approximations, but still operate inside the original geometric surface.

---

**Displacement mapping**

parts.title: Displacement mapping concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Displacement mapping
destinations.exact_quote:
Displacement actually changes position:

$$
\boxed{
P'=P+hN.
}
$$

Now the geometry itself moves.

Therefore displacement can affect:

- silhouette,
- depth,
- shadows,
- intersections,
- rasterized coverage.

But if the base mesh is too coarse, displacing only existing vertices cannot represent high-frequency height.

Therefore displacement often requires:

- dense meshes,
- tessellation,
- subdivision,
- mesh shader amplification,
- offline subdivision.

This is why displacement is more expensive but more geometrically correct.

---

**Normal vs parallax vs displacement**

Think of these as increasing levels of geometric commitment:

| Technique | Changes shading normal | Changes texture position | Changes geometry/depth | Changes silhouette |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Normal map | Yes | No | No | No |
| Basic parallax | Usually + normal | Yes | No | No |
| POM / steep parallax | Yes | Yes + approximate self-occlusion | No | Usually no |
| Displacement | Yes indirectly | Geometry moves | Yes | Yes |

The best technique depends on viewing distance and geometric importance.

---

parts.title: Diffuse reflection

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Diffuse reflection is not “light multiplied by color”
destinations.exact_quote:
**Diffuse reflection is not “light multiplied by color”**

Consider light entering a material such as chalk, plastic paint or skin.

Some photons enter the surface, scatter internally, and eventually leave at different locations/directions.

At real-time rendering scales we often approximate that complicated subsurface process as **diffuse reflection at one point**.

The simplest idealization is Lambertian reflection.

Its defining property is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{outgoing radiance is independent of outgoing direction}
}
$$

not that the object “looks equally bright from all directions” in every possible perceptual sense.

The BRDF is constant with direction.

---

parts.title: Lambertian BRDF derivation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Deriving the Lambertian BRDF
destinations.exact_quote:
**Deriving the Lambertian BRDF**

Let diffuse reflectance or albedo be

$$
\rho.
$$

Physically:

$$
0\le\rho\le1.
$$

Suppose incident irradiance is

$$
E.
$$

A perfectly diffuse surface reflects total exitant power fraction

$$
\rho E.
$$

If outgoing radiance is constant over the hemisphere:

$$
L_o=C.
$$

Exitant radiant exitance is obtained by integrating outgoing radiance:

$$
M=
\int_{\Omega^+}
L_o(\omega_o)
(N\cdot\omega_o)
\,d\omega_o.
$$

Since $L_o=C$,

$$
M=
C
\int_{\Omega^+}
\cos\theta\,d\omega.
$$

From Pass 3,

$$
\int_{\Omega^+}
\cos\theta\,d\omega
=
\pi.
$$

Therefore:

$$
M=\pi C.
$$

But the reflected energy must be:

$$
M=\rho E.
$$

So:

$$
\pi C=\rho E
$$

and therefore:

$$
C=\frac{\rho}{\pi}E.
$$

Thus the Lambert BRDF is

$$
\boxed{
f_{\text{Lambert}}
=
\frac{\rho}{\pi}
}
$$

rather than merely $\rho$.

The $1/\pi$ is not an arbitrary “PBR correction.”

It is the normalization required so integrating the constant diffuse lobe over the hemisphere returns reflectance $\rho$.

---

**Why old shaders often omit $1/\pi$**

A historical real-time shader might compute:

$$
C=
\rho\,L_i\,\max(N\cdot L,0).
$$

That can look perfectly usable because light intensities are artistically tuned around the missing constant.

But a physically interpretable BRDF should be:

$$
C=
\frac{\rho}{\pi}
L_i
(N\cdot L).
$$

If your light intensity conventions were authored around the first equation, suddenly introducing $1/\pi$ makes everything about 3.14 times darker.

This is why physically based rendering is not achieved by swapping one shader function.

parts.title: BRDF definition

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: BRDF definition
destinations.exact_quote:
**BRDF definition**

BRDF means:

$$
\text{Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function}.
$$

It answers:

> Given radiance arriving from direction $\omega_i$, how much outgoing radiance is generated toward $\omega_o$?

Formally:

$$
\boxed{
f_r(\omega_i,\omega_o)
=
\frac{dL_o(\omega_o)}
{dE_i(\omega_i)}
}
$$

but

$$
dE_i
=
L_i(\omega_i)
(N\cdot\omega_i)
d\omega_i.
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
f_r(\omega_i,\omega_o)
=
\frac{
dL_o(\omega_o)
}{
L_i(\omega_i)
(N\cdot\omega_i)
d\omega_i
}
}
$$

and consequently:

$$
dL_o
=
f_r
L_i
(N\cdot\omega_i)
d\omega_i.
$$

Integrating all incoming directions gives the reflection part of the rendering equation:

$$
\boxed{
L_o(\omega_o)
=
\int_{\Omega^+}
f_r(\omega_i,\omega_o)
L_i(\omega_i)
(N\cdot\omega_i)
d\omega_i.
}
$$

This equation is the backbone of essentially everything from direct PBR shading to path tracing.

---

**BRDF units**

Radiance units are:

$$
[L]
=
\frac{\mathrm W}
{\mathrm{m^2\,sr}}.
$$

Irradiance units are:

$$
[E]
=
\frac{\mathrm W}{\mathrm{m^2}}.
$$

Therefore:

$$
[f_r]
=
\frac{L}{E}
$$

so:

$$
[f_r]
=
\frac{
\mathrm W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}
}{
\mathrm W\,m^{-2}
}
$$

giving:

$$
\boxed{
[f_r]=\mathrm{sr}^{-1}.
}
$$

That is why a BRDF is not literally a reflectance percentage.

It is a directional density.

---

parts.title: BRDF reciprocity

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: BRDF reciprocity
destinations.exact_quote:
**BRDF reciprocity**

For passive reciprocal materials under ordinary optical assumptions:

$$
\boxed{
f_r(\omega_i,\omega_o)
=
f_r(\omega_o,\omega_i)
}
$$

This is Helmholtz reciprocity.

If light can travel from direction $A$ to direction $B$ through the material's scattering behavior, reversing the path has the same reflectance.

Lambert satisfies this trivially:

$$
\frac{\rho}{\pi}
=
\frac{\rho}{\pi}.
$$

Cook–Torrance microfacet reflection is also constructed to satisfy reciprocity when its terms are symmetric.

This property becomes especially useful in light transport algorithms because camera paths and light paths can sometimes be reversed mathematically.

---

**BRDF energy conservation**

parts.title: BRDF energy conservation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: BRDF energy conservation
destinations.exact_quote:
**BRDF energy conservation**

A surface must not reflect more energy than it receives unless it is actively emitting energy.

For every incoming direction $\omega_i$,

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\Omega^+}
f_r(\omega_i,\omega_o)
(N\cdot\omega_o)
\,d\omega_o
\le1.
}
$$

For Lambert:

$$
f_r=\frac{\rho}{\pi}.
$$

Then:

$$
\int_{\Omega^+}
\frac{\rho}{\pi}
\cos\theta_o
d\omega_o
=
\frac{\rho}{\pi}\pi
=
\rho.
$$

So energy conservation becomes simply:

$$
\rho\le1.
$$

That is why Lambert's normalization works.

---

**Reflectance can be colored**

For RGB:

$$
\rho=
(\rho_r,\rho_g,\rho_b).
$$

Energy conservation applies spectrally; in an RGB approximation we enforce it channel-wise.

For example:

$$
\rho=(0.8,0.2,0.1)
$$

means the material returns much more red-band energy than blue-band energy.

It does not mean the surface creates red light.

It selectively absorbs other wavelengths.

---

parts.title: Specular reflection

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Specular reflection
destinations.exact_quote:
**Specular reflection**

For a perfectly smooth mirror, one incident direction maps into exactly one reflected direction.

Let incoming ray direction $I$ point **toward** the surface and normal $N$ point outward.

Reflection is:

$$
\boxed{
R=
I-2(I\cdot N)N
}
$$

If instead using our PBR convention where $L$ points outward toward the light, the incident travel direction is:

$$
I=-L.
$$

For perfect mirror reflection viewed along $V$,

$$
V=R.
$$

Equivalently, the microfacet normal that reflects $L$ into $V$ must align with the half vector:

$$
\boxed{
H=
\frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}.
}
$$

---

**A perfect mirror BRDF is a delta distribution**

A perfect mirror does not have an ordinary finite-width specular lobe.

All reflected energy goes into one direction.

Mathematically the BRDF contains a Dirac delta.

Informally:

$$
f_{\text{mirror}}
\sim
F\,\delta(\omega_o-R(\omega_i)).
$$

This is why a perfect mirror cannot be correctly represented by “roughness = exactly zero” in a naive finite GGX formula without care.

As roughness approaches zero, the microfacet distribution approaches a delta-like spike.

Kairo therefore clamps real-time roughness to:

$$
0.04
$$

to avoid a numerically singular distribution.

That is a pragmatic real-time choice, not a statement that physically perfect mirrors do not exist.

---

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Fresnel reflection
destinations.exact_quote:
**Fresnel reflection**

When electromagnetic radiation reaches an interface between two media, some energy reflects and some transmits.

The fraction depends on:

$$
\eta_i,\eta_t,
$$

the incoming and transmitted refractive indices, and on incidence angle.

Even perfectly smooth transparent glass reflects some light.

This means:

> “Transparent” does not mean “no reflection.”

At grazing angles, even ordinary glass becomes strongly reflective.

That is Fresnel behavior.

---

**Exact dielectric Fresnel equations**

parts.title: Schlick Fresnel approximation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Schlick Fresnel
destinations.exact_quote:
**Schlick Fresnel**

Schlick's approximation is:

$$
\boxed{
F(\cos\theta)
=
F_0
+
(1-F_0)(1-\cos\theta)^5.
}
$$

In microfacet reflection, use:

$$
\cos\theta=
V\cdot H
$$

or equivalently $L\cdot H$ under ideal reflection geometry.

At normal incidence:

$$
\cos\theta=1
$$

so:

$$
F=F_0.
$$

At grazing incidence:

$$
\cos\theta\rightarrow0
$$

so:

$$
F\rightarrow1.
$$

That reproduces the major physical behavior extremely cheaply.

Kairo currently implements exactly:

```glsl
vec3 FresnelSchlick(float cosTheta, vec3 F0)
{
    return F0 +
           (1.0 - F0) *
           pow(1.0 - cosTheta, 5.0);
}
```

---

parts.title: Refractive index

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Refractive index
destinations.exact_quote:
**Refractive index**

Refractive index is:

$$
\boxed{
\eta=\frac{c}{v}
}
$$

where $c$ is light speed in vacuum and $v$ is phase velocity in the material.

Typical values are roughly:

$$
\eta_{\text{air}}\approx1.0003,
$$

$$
\eta_{\text{water}}\approx1.33,
$$

$$
\eta_{\text{glass}}\approx1.45-1.6,
$$

$$
\eta_{\text{diamond}}\approx2.42.
$$

IOR controls both:

$$
\text{refraction direction}
$$

and

$$
F_0.
$$

So if a material exposes both arbitrary IOR and arbitrary $F_0$, they may become physically inconsistent unless deliberately treated as artistic parameters.

---

parts.title: Conductors versus dielectrics

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Dielectrics versus conductors
destinations.exact_quote:
**Dielectrics versus conductors**

A dielectric such as:

```text
plastic
glass
ceramic
wood coating
water
```

allows electromagnetic fields to penetrate substantially before absorption/scattering.

Its interface specular reflection is usually nearly achromatic in visible RGB for many common materials.

Its visible body color generally comes from transmitted light being absorbed/scattered internally.

Thus for an opaque dielectric:

$$
\boxed{
\text{baseColor mainly controls diffuse/body reflection}
}
$$

while:

$$
\boxed{
F_0\text{ is usually low and near-neutral}.
}
$$

A conductor such as:

```text
gold
copper
silver
aluminium
```

has mobile electrons and strongly absorbs transmitted electromagnetic energy.

Its refractive index is complex:

$$
\boxed{
\tilde{\eta}
=
\eta+i\kappa
}
$$

where:

$$
\eta=\text{ordinary refractive-index term},
$$

$$
\kappa=\text{extinction coefficient}.
$$

This produces wavelength-dependent interface reflection.

Consequently metals often have **colored specular reflections**.

---

parts.title: F0 for dielectrics

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Fresnel at normal incidence
destinations.exact_quote:
At normal incidence:

$$
\theta_i=\theta_t=0.
$$

Therefore:

$$
\cos\theta_i=\cos\theta_t=1.
$$

Both polarization equations collapse to:

$$
\boxed{
F_0=
\left(
\frac{\eta_i-\eta_t}
{\eta_i+\eta_t}
\right)^2.
}
$$

For air:

$$
\eta_i\approx1.
$$

For common glass:

$$
\eta_t\approx1.5.
$$

Then:

$$
F_0=
\left(
\frac{1-1.5}
{1+1.5}
\right)^2
$$

$$
=
\left(
\frac{-0.5}{2.5}
\right)^2
$$

$$
=
0.04.
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{F_0\approx4\%}
$$

for IOR 1.5.

That is the origin of the ubiquitous:

```glsl
vec3 F0 = vec3(0.04);
```

It is not a magic PBR constant.

It corresponds to a dielectric around IOR 1.5.

---

parts.title: Colored specular response of metals

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Colored F0 for metals
destinations.exact_quote:
**Colored $F_0$ for metals**

Instead of:

$$
F_0=(0.04,0.04,0.04),
$$

a metal may have:

$$
F_0=(0.95,0.64,0.54)
$$

or another strongly colored triplet depending on the conductor.

In metallic-roughness rendering, we approximate this through:

$$
\boxed{
F_0=
(1-m)F_{0,\text{dielectric}}
+
mC_{\text{base}}.
}
$$

For:

$$
m=0
$$

we obtain dielectric:

$$
F_0=0.04.
$$

For:

$$
m=1
$$

we obtain:

$$
F_0=C_{\text{base}}.
$$

Current Kairo does exactly:

```glsl
vec3 f0 =
    mix(vec3(0.04),
        baseColor,
        metallic);
```

---

parts.title: Microfacet surface model

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Microfacet theory
destinations.exact_quote:
A rough surface appears macroscopically smooth-ish, but microscopically it consists of many tiny mirror-like facets.

Each microfacet has its own normal:

$$
M.
$$

Every individual microfacet is assumed to reflect specularly.

A visible highlight arises because some subset of those facets happen to have the exact orientation needed to reflect $L$ into $V$.

For perfect reflection that orientation is:

$$
M=H.
$$

Therefore the BRDF asks:

> How many microfacets have normals close to $H$, how much Fresnel reflection do they produce, and how many are visible rather than masked or shadowed?

This gives the three famous microfacet terms:

$$
\boxed{
D\,F\,G.
}
$$

---

**The microfacet normal distribution**

parts.title: Microfacet normals

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: The microfacet normal distribution
destinations.exact_quote:
The NDF:

$$
D(M)
$$

describes the statistical distribution of microfacet orientations.

More precisely, $D(M)$ is an area-density-like function over microfacet normals.

A proper isotropic NDF obeys a projected-area normalization:

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\Omega^+}
D(M)(N\cdot M)
\,d\omega_M
=
1.
}
$$

That cosine matters.

$D$ is not simply a probability density over directions.

If you need an actual microfacet-normal PDF sampled proportional to projected microfacet area, then often:

$$
p(M)=D(M)(N\cdot M).
$$

Later, importance sampling will depend on precisely this distinction.

---

**Roughness controls the NDF**

parts.title: Normal-distribution functions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Roughness controls the NDF
destinations.exact_quote:
**Roughness controls the NDF**

At tiny roughness:

```text
most microfacets ≈ macro normal
```

so:

$$
D(H)
$$

is highly concentrated around:

$$
H=N.
$$

The highlight becomes:

- small,
- sharp,
- intense.

At larger roughness:

```text
microfacet normals distributed broadly
```

so the lobe becomes:

- wider,
- dimmer at the peak,
- visible over more reflection directions.

Energy is being redistributed angularly.

Roughness should not simply “reduce reflection strength.”

---

parts.title: GGX or Trowbridge-Reitz distribution

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: GGX / Trowbridge-Reitz
destinations.exact_quote:
**GGX / Trowbridge-Reitz**

The isotropic GGX NDF can be written:

$$
\boxed{
D_{\mathrm{GGX}}(N,H,\alpha)
=
\frac{
\alpha^2
}{
\pi
\left[
(N\cdot H)^2(\alpha^2-1)+1
\right]^2
}
}
$$

for:

$$
N\cdot H>0.
$$

Equivalent tangent-angle form:

$$
D(\theta_h)
=
\frac{
\alpha^2
}{
\pi
\cos^4\theta_h
(\alpha^2+\tan^2\theta_h)^2
}.
$$

The first form is much nicer for shader implementation.

Current Kairo:

```glsl
float DistributionGGX(
    vec3 N,
    vec3 H,
    float roughness)
{
    float alpha  = roughness * roughness;
    float alpha2 = alpha * alpha;

    float NdotH =
        max(dot(N, H), 0.0);

    float d =
        NdotH * NdotH *
        (alpha2 - 1.0) + 1.0;

    return alpha2 /
        (Pi * d * d);
}
```

That is the standard GGX structure.

---

**Why GGX became so popular**

GGX has a relatively long tail.

That means noticeably tilted microfacets remain more probable than with distributions such as Beckmann.

Visually this creates:

- broader grazing highlights,
- realistic long specular tails,
- pleasing rough surfaces.

Real surfaces often exhibit this kind of long-tail behavior more convincingly than classical Phong-like distributions.

It also has tractable sampling and masking-shadowing formulas.

That combination made GGX an excellent production choice.

---

parts.title: Beckmann distribution concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Beckmann distribution
destinations.exact_quote:
**Beckmann distribution**

A classic isotropic Beckmann NDF is:

$$
\boxed{
D_{\mathrm B}(\theta_h)
=
\frac{
\exp\left(
-\tan^2\theta_h/\alpha^2
\right)
}{
\pi\alpha^2\cos^4\theta_h
}.
}
$$

Its tail falls exponentially.

GGX falls much more slowly.

Therefore, far from the normal:

$$
D_{\mathrm{GGX}}
>
D_{\mathrm{Beckmann}}
$$

for comparable roughness in many regions.

In practical visual language:

```text
Beckmann → shorter/tighter tail
GGX      → heavier/longer specular tail
```

Neither is “universally more physically correct.”

They represent different statistical surface models.

---

parts.title: Roughness parameterization

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Perceptual roughness versus microfacet alpha
destinations.exact_quote:
**Perceptual roughness versus microfacet $\alpha$**

A common production mapping is:

$$
\boxed{
\alpha=r^2
}
$$

where:

$$
r\in[0,1]
$$

is artist-facing roughness.

Why square it?

Because direct use of $\alpha$ tends not to produce a perceptually uniform slider.

Squaring gives artists finer control near the smooth region where small changes strongly alter highlights.

Kairo uses exactly:

```glsl
alpha = roughness * roughness;
```

inside GGX.

Then the formula uses:

$$
\alpha^2.
$$

Therefore shader code may contain:

```glsl
float alpha = roughness * roughness;
float alphaSquared = alpha * alpha;
```

which means:

$$
\alpha^2=r^4.
$$

That is intentional.

Do not “simplify” it because you think roughness was accidentally squared twice.

---

**A roughness naming trap**

Different codebases use names differently.

One engine might call:

```text
roughness = artist parameter r
alpha     = r²
```

another might call:

```text
roughness = alpha
```

and another might pass:

```text
alphaSquared
```

directly.

Therefore seeing:

```cpp
a = roughness * roughness;
a2 = a * a;
```

cannot be judged without knowing parameter semantics.

Many supposed PBR bugs are naming bugs.

---

parts.title: Geometric shadowing and masking

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Microfacet masking and shadowing
destinations.exact_quote:
**Microfacet masking and shadowing**

Imagine a rough surface seen at grazing angle.

Some microfacets oriented toward the camera are blocked by neighboring microfacets.

That is **masking**.

Likewise, some microfacets oriented toward the light cannot receive that light because another microfacet blocks it.

That is **shadowing**.

The NDF $D$ alone counts microfacet orientations regardless of whether those microfacets are actually visible from both directions.

So we need:

$$
\boxed{
G(L,V)
}
$$

with:

$$
0\le G\le1.
$$

---

parts.title: Smith masking-shadowing model

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Smith masking-shadowing
destinations.exact_quote:
**Smith masking-shadowing**

Smith theory builds the two-direction geometry function from one-direction visibility terms:

$$
\boxed{
G(L,V)
=
G_1(L)\,G_1(V)
}
$$

for a common separable approximation.

A GGX-compatible exact-ish isotropic $G_1$ can be written:

$$
\boxed{
G_1(V)
=
\frac{
2(N\cdot V)
}{
(N\cdot V)
+
\sqrt{
\alpha^2+
(1-\alpha^2)(N\cdot V)^2
}
}
}
$$

for positive $N\cdot V$.

Equivalent Smith lambda formulations are also common.

The geometric interpretation remains:

$$
G_1(V)
=
\text{fraction of relevant microfacets visible from }V.
$$

---

**Schlick-GGX approximation**

parts.title: Geometry term approximations

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Schlick-GGX approximation
destinations.exact_quote:
**Schlick-GGX approximation**

A cheaper approximation is:

$$
\boxed{
G_{\text{Schlick}}(x)
=
\frac{x}
{x(1-k)+k}
}
$$

where:

$$
x=N\cdot V
$$

or:

$$
N\cdot L.
$$

Then:

$$
G=
G_{\text{Schlick}}(N\cdot L)
G_{\text{Schlick}}(N\cdot V).
$$

A common direct-lighting remap is:

$$
\boxed{
k=\frac{(r+1)^2}{8}.
}
$$

That is exactly what current Kairo uses:

```glsl
float k =
    ((roughness + 1.0) *
     (roughness + 1.0)) / 8.0;
```

This is an approximation to Smith GGX, not the NDF itself.

---

parts.title: Cook-Torrance microfacet BRDF

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Cook–Torrance microfacet BRDF
destinations.exact_quote:
**Cook–Torrance microfacet BRDF**

We now combine:

$$
D=\text{microfacet orientation density},
$$

$$
F=\text{Fresnel reflection},
$$

$$
G=\text{masking-shadowing}.
$$

The specular microfacet BRDF is:

$$
\boxed{
f_s(L,V)
=
\frac{
D(H)F(V,H)G(L,V)
}{
4(N\cdot L)(N\cdot V)
}
}
$$

for valid directions in the upper hemisphere.

That is the Cook–Torrance-style microfacet reflection model.

Every term has a geometric or electromagnetic meaning.

---

**Why the denominator exists at all**
