parts.title: Deriving the denominator 4(NdotL)(NdotV)

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Why the denominator exists at all
destinations.exact_quote:
This denominator is one of the most memorized and least understood parts of PBR.

It is not:

> “a normalization number somebody discovered experimentally.”

The microfacet model counts surface area in one geometric domain and predicts radiance in another.

Several coordinate/projection conversions are required.

The key ingredients are:

$$
\boxed{
\text{macro-surface projected area}
}
$$

versus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{microfacet projected area}
}
$$

and the transformation between:

$$
\boxed{
\text{half-vector solid angle}
}
$$

and:

$$
\boxed{
\text{reflected outgoing-direction solid angle}.
}
$$

For perfect specular reflection:

$$
H=
\frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}.
$$

The reflection mapping has the Jacobian:

$$
\boxed{
d\omega_H
=
\frac{
d\omega_V
}{
4|V\cdot H|
}.
}
$$

That factor $4$ is one crucial part of the final denominator.

The remaining projected-area conversions produce the $N\cdot L$ and $N\cdot V$ terms.

After converting microfacet area distribution into reflected outgoing radiance per macroscopic projected area and outgoing solid angle, the factors reduce to:

$$
\boxed{
4(N\cdot L)(N\cdot V)
}.
$$

The half-vector dot factors arising during the intermediate microfacet projection/Jacobian transformation cancel for ideal reflection because:

$$
L\cdot H=V\cdot H.
$$

The result is therefore exactly:

$$
f_s=
\frac{DFG}
{4(N\cdot L)(N\cdot V)}.
$$

The important conceptual memory is:

$$
\boxed{
4N_LN_V
=
\text{geometry/Jacobian normalization required to express microscopic mirror area as a macroscopic BRDF}.
}
$$

---

**Why the denominator becomes numerically dangerous**

At grazing angles:

$$
N\cdot L\rightarrow0
$$

or

$$
N\cdot V\rightarrow0.
$$

The denominator approaches zero.

A naive implementation can produce:

$$
\infty
$$

or:

$$
NaN.
$$

Production code therefore typically checks:

$$
N\cdot L>0,
\qquad
N\cdot V>0
$$

and clamps the denominator:

```glsl
max(
    4.0 * NdotL * NdotV,
    1e-5);
```

Kairo does exactly this.

This epsilon is numerical protection, not part of the physical BRDF.

---

destinations.heading: Material workflow: metallic-roughness
destinations.exact_quote:
**Material workflow: metallic-roughness**

The metallic-roughness workflow attempts to encode a wide range of opaque materials using relatively intuitive artist parameters:

$$
C_{\text{base}},
\qquad
m,
\qquad
r.
$$

Where:

$$
m=\text{metallic},
\qquad
r=\text{roughness}.
$$

This is the workflow used by glTF's core PBR model and many engines.

Its genius is not that nature literally contains a “metallic slider.”

It is that the slider efficiently selects between two major material classes:

$$
\text{dielectric}
\leftrightarrow
\text{conductor}.
$$

---

parts.title: Base color in metallic-roughness PBR

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Base-color semantics change with metallic
destinations.exact_quote:
**Base-color semantics change with metallic**

For dielectric:

$$
m=0.
$$

Base color represents approximate diffuse/body reflectance:

$$
C_d=C_{\text{base}}.
$$

Specular normal-incidence reflectance remains near:

$$
F_0\approx0.04.
$$

For metal:

$$
m=1.
$$

Diffuse becomes approximately zero.

Base color becomes specular normal-incidence color:

$$
F_0=C_{\text{base}}.
$$

Thus the same input field changes physical role depending on material class.

---

parts.title: Roughness parameter semantics

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Roughness semantics
destinations.exact_quote:
**Roughness semantics**

Roughness controls microfacet orientation spread.

It does **not** fundamentally control how much total specular energy exists.

At lower roughness:

```text
narrow + intense highlight
```

At higher roughness:

```text
broad + weaker peak
```

The lobe redistributes energy over angle.

In practical single-scattering microfacet models, some energy can be lost due to unresolved multiple scattering between facets, especially at high roughness, but the intended semantic remains angular spread.

---

parts.title: Ambient occlusion material input

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Ambient occlusion input
destinations.exact_quote:
**Ambient occlusion input**

Material AO is often interpreted approximately as:

$$
A\in[0,1]
$$

representing reduced accessibility of indirect environmental illumination.

The most important practical rule is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{AO generally should not simply darken direct lights}.
}
$$

A cavity can be strongly occluded from broad environment lighting but still receive a direct flashlight beam.

Kairo currently applies AO around its ambient/environment expression:

```glsl
ambient =
    (... ambient/environment ...)
    * ambientOcclusion;
```

while direct light remains outside that multiplication.

That is the right broad conceptual placement.

---

parts.title: Specular-glossiness workflow

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Specular-glossiness workflow
destinations.exact_quote:
**Specular-glossiness workflow**

Another PBR parameterization uses:

$$
C_{\text{diffuse}},
$$

$$
C_{\text{specular}},
$$

$$
g=\text{glossiness}.
$$

Glossiness is roughly inverse roughness:

$$
r\approx1-g
$$

though exact conversions depend on the model.

This workflow provides direct artistic control over specular color.

But it makes it easier to author physically inconsistent combinations such as:

```text
bright diffuse
+
very bright specular
```

whose summed reflected energy exceeds one.

Metallic-roughness reduces some of this freedom in exchange for stronger physical plausibility.

---

parts.title: Energy split between diffuse and specular

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: The diffuse/specular energy split
destinations.exact_quote:
**The diffuse/specular energy split**

Fresnel tells us fraction:

$$
F
$$

of incident interface energy that reflects specularly.

For an opaque dielectric, the remaining fraction available to enter the material is approximately:

$$
1-F.
$$

Some of that later returns as diffuse/body scattering.

Therefore a common real-time energy split is:

$$
\boxed{
k_s=F
}
$$

and:

$$
\boxed{
k_d=(1-F)(1-m).
}
$$

Then:

$$
f=
k_d\frac{C_{\text{base}}}{\pi}
+
f_s.
$$

The metallic factor ensures:

$$
m=1
\Rightarrow
k_d=0.
$$

---

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Diffuse normalization again
destinations.exact_quote:
**Diffuse normalization again**

If an artist chooses base-color reflectance:

$$
C=(0.8,0.2,0.1),
$$

the BRDF is not:

$$
f_d=C.
$$

It is:

$$
\boxed{
f_d=\frac{C}{\pi}.
}
$$

Why?

Because integrating the lobe must recover:

$$
C.
$$

This is the fundamental interpretation:

$$
\boxed{
\text{base color}
\approx
\text{hemispherical diffuse reflectance}
}
$$

not the BRDF magnitude itself.

---

parts.title: Clearcoat lobe concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Clearcoat
destinations.exact_quote:
**Clearcoat**

Clearcoat models a thin, smooth dielectric layer above a base material.

Think:

- car paint,
- varnished wood,
- lacquer,
- coated carbon fiber.

The clearcoat lobe generally has:

- low dielectric $F_0$,
- independent roughness/gloss,
- relatively narrow specular behavior,
- reduced underlying-layer energy because some light is reflected by the coat first.

Conceptually:

$$
L=
L_{\text{coat}}
+
(1-F_{\text{coat,in}})
(1-F_{\text{coat,out}})
L_{\text{base}}
$$

in a more careful layered treatment.

Simple real-time models approximate this.

---

**GTR1 clearcoat concept**

Disney clearcoat is commonly represented with a GTR1-like distribution rather than the ordinary GGX/GTR2 distribution.

A common GTR1 NDF is:

$$
D_{\mathrm{GTR1}}
=
\frac{
\alpha^2-1
}{
\pi
\ln(\alpha^2)
\left[
1+(\alpha^2-1)(N\cdot H)^2
\right]
}
$$

for $\alpha\neq1$.

You do not need to memorize this equation for M118.

The important architectural concept is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{one material may contain multiple physically meaningful reflection lobes with different roughness distributions}.
}
$$

Current Kairo's real-time material does not yet expose clearcoat.

---

parts.title: Sheen lobe concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: Sheen
destinations.exact_quote:
**Sheen**

Sheen models soft grazing reflection seen in materials such as cloth and fabrics.

Examples:

- velvet,
- satin-like surfaces,
- fibres.

Unlike clearcoat, it is not simply another glossy varnish.

It approximates scattering caused by microfibres and grazing-oriented structures.

A simple Disney-style sheen contribution is related to:

$$
(1-L\cdot H)^5
$$

multiplied by a sheen color/tint.

Thus it tends to appear primarily at grazing configurations.

Current Kairo does not yet expose a sheen lobe.

---

**Why just “adding lobes” can violate energy conservation**

destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
A triangle renderer represents a surface through connectivity.

A triangle gives three vertices:

$$
v_0,v_1,v_2
$$

and the rasterizer determines which pixels are covered by the projected triangle.

The triangle is fundamentally a **piecewise planar surface primitive**.

parts.next_action: Require the learner to predict which representation carries connectivity and which supplies a continuous footprint before proceeding to covariance.
parts.scope: An actual matched first-use passage was reviewed; this is not full chapter, source-exhaustion or final pedagogical signoff.

worker_assessment.required_skill: Distinguish triangle coverage, which depends on projected connectivity, from Gaussian support, which weights pixels by distance from a center.
worker_assessment.definitions_evidence: The opening contrasts a triangle as a piecewise-planar surface primitive with a Gaussian record containing center, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color.
worker_assessment.derivation_or_algorithm_evidence: No derivation is required for the representation contrast; the section motivates the different pixel-coverage question answered by a spatial basis function.
worker_assessment.worked_example_evidence: The text contrasts an explicitly connected wall mesh with overlapping kernels whose appearance suggests a wall without defining a watertight surface. This is conceptual, not a numeric trace.
worker_assessment.exercise_solution_evidence: No explicit learner exercise with a worked answer tied to this contrast was found in the reviewed first-use span.
worker_assessment.verification_evidence: No dedicated executable comparison of triangle and Gaussian coverage was verified for this part.
worker_assessment.limits: The example explains representation meaning, not equivalence between captured appearance and physical geometry.

parts.title: Gaussian functions in one dimension

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
Start with:

$$
g(x)
=
\exp
\left(
-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}
{2\sigma^2}
\right).
$$

This is the shape-only Gaussian.

If we want a normalized probability density:

$$
\boxed{
p(x)
=
\frac{1}
{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
\exp
\left(
-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}
{2\sigma^2}
\right)
}
$$

where:

$$
\mu=\text{mean},
$$

$$
\sigma=\text{standard deviation},
$$

parts.next_action: Have the learner compute g(μ+2σ) by hand and explain why the rasterizer need not include the probability normalization factor.
parts.scope: An actual matched first-use passage was reviewed; this is not full chapter, source-exhaustion or final pedagogical signoff.

worker_assessment.required_skill: Evaluate a one-dimensional Gaussian weight from mean and variance and interpret its falloff in standard-deviation units.
worker_assessment.definitions_evidence: Defines shape-only g(x), normalized probability density p(x), mean μ, standard deviation σ, and variance σ²; distinguishes normalized density from the unnormalized splat weight.
worker_assessment.derivation_or_algorithm_evidence: The exponent is dimensionless and scales squared displacement by 2σ²; the text connects x=μ+σ to exponent −1/2 and the one-sigma weight.
worker_assessment.worked_example_evidence: At 1σ, 2σ, and 3σ the unnormalized weights are e^(−1/2)≈0.6065, e^(−2)≈0.1353, and e^(−4.5)≈0.0111; this motivates a practical 3σ truncation.
worker_assessment.exercise_solution_evidence: The three-sigma comparison is worked in prose, but no separately posed exercise/solution is identified in this passage.
worker_assessment.verification_evidence: No dedicated standalone 1D Gaussian executable test was verified; the later renderer tests cover projected kernels instead.
worker_assessment.limits: A 3σ cutoff is an implementation approximation to infinite support, not an exact Gaussian boundary.

parts.title: Gaussian functions in multiple dimensions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
For:

$$
\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d
$$

the normalized Gaussian is:

$$
\boxed{
p(\mathbf x)
=
\frac{
1
}{
(2\pi)^{d/2}
|\Sigma|^{1/2}
}
\exp
\left[
-\frac12
(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^T
\Sigma^{-1}
(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)
\right]
}
$$

where:

$$
\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^d
$$

and:

$$
\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}.
$$

The central expression is:

$$
\boxed{
q(\mathbf x)
=
(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^T
\Sigma^{-1}
(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)
}
$$

called the squared Mahalanobis distance.

Gaussian weight:

$$
w=e^{-q/2}.
$$

parts.title: Covariance matrix of a multivariate Gaussian

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
For a random vector:

$$
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
X_1\\
X_2\\
X_3
\end{bmatrix},
$$

covariance is:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma
=
E[
(X-\mu)
(X-\mu)^T
].
}
$$

In 3D:

$$
\Sigma=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_x^2 & \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_{xz}\\
\sigma_{xy} & \sigma_y^2 & \sigma_{yz}\\
\sigma_{xz} & \sigma_{yz} & \sigma_z^2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Because covariance is symmetric:

$$
\Sigma^T=\Sigma.
$$

So a general symmetric 3×3 covariance has six independent values.

parts.title: Covariance as directional spread

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
This is one of the most useful interpretations.

Take unit direction:

$$
\mathbf u.
$$

Project random displacement onto that direction:

$$
Y=
\mathbf u^T(X-\mu).
$$

Then:

$$
Var(Y)
=
E[
(\mathbf u^T(X-\mu))^2
].
$$

Rewrite:

$$
=
E[
\mathbf u^T
(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T
\mathbf u
].
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
Var_{\mathbf u}
=
\mathbf u^T
\Sigma
\mathbf u.
}
$$

This equation tells you the variance of the Gaussian along **any direction**.

parts.title: Positive-definite covariance matrices

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
For a valid nondegenerate Gaussian covariance we want:

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf x^T
\Sigma
\mathbf x
>
0
\quad
\forall\mathbf x\ne0.
}
$$

That means:

$$
\Sigma\succ0.
$$

Equivalent for symmetric $\Sigma$:

$$
\lambda_i>0
\quad
\forall i.
$$

Then:

$$
det(\Sigma)>0
$$

and:

$$
\Sigma^{-1}
$$

exists.

---

**Positive semidefinite versus definite**

If one axis scale becomes zero:

$$
\lambda_3=0,
$$

then:

$$
\Sigma\succeq0
$$

but not:

$$
\Sigma\succ0.
$$

It represents a collapsed distribution, perhaps an exact mathematical disc.

But:

$$
\Sigma^{-1}
$$

does not exist.

Rasterization eventually needs an inverse screen covariance, so numerical implementations avoid exact degeneracy.

This is one reason positive scale parameterizations are valuable.

parts.title: Parameterizing a 3D Gaussian by scale and rotation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
Storing arbitrary six covariance values directly has problems.

Optimization could produce:

$$
\Sigma
$$

that is not positive semidefinite.

Instead define:

$$
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_x&0&0\\
0&s_y&0\\
0&0&s_z
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and rotation:

$$
R\in SO(3).
$$

Construct:

$$
M=RS.
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma
=
MM^T
=
RS^2R^T.
}
$$

Because:

$$
S^2=
diag(
s_x^2,
s_y^2,
s_z^2
),
$$

all positive scales imply positive eigenvalues.

parts.title: Log-scale storage and exponential decoding

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
Maveb's canonical Gaussian does not store:

$$
s_x,s_y,s_z.
$$

It stores:

```cpp
logScale
```

so:

$$
\boxed{
s_i=e^{\ell_i}.
}
$$

where:

$$
\ell_i
$$

is the learned/stored log scale.

---

**Why log scale is useful**

First:

$$
e^\ell>0
$$

for all finite $\ell$.

Thus negative physical scale cannot occur.

Second, additive log changes correspond to multiplicative physical changes:

$$
e^{\ell+\Delta}
=
e^\ell e^\Delta.
$$

For small $\Delta$:

$$
e^\Delta
\approx
1+\Delta.
$$

So optimization naturally makes relative scale changes.

Third:

$$
\frac{ds}{d\ell}
=
e^\ell
=
s.
$$

Gradient magnitude scales with physical size.

parts.title: Quaternion storage for Gaussian orientation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
Maveb stores quaternion:

$$
q=(w,x,y,z).
$$

Current canonical structure:

```cpp
std::array<float, 4>
rotation
{
    1,0,0,0
};
```

Its PLY documentation explicitly preserves GraphDECO's:

$$
(w,x,y,z)
$$

property order.

---

**Normalize the quaternion**

Rotation quaternion should satisfy:

$$
\|q\|=1.
$$

So:

$$
q'
=
\frac{q}{\|q\|}.
$$

Maveb's loader rejects a near-zero quaternion:

$$
\|q\|^2<10^{-16}
$$

and normalizes every accepted Gaussian.

The Metal kernel normalizes again before matrix construction:

```metal
normalize(
    gaussian.rotation)
```

which is a useful defensive measure.

A Gaussian needs a base opacity:

$$
\alpha_0.
$$

At screen offset $\Delta p$, final local alpha will later resemble:

$$
\alpha(\Delta p)
=
\alpha_0
\exp
\left(
-\frac12
\Delta p^T
\Sigma_{2D}^{-1}
\Delta p
\right).
$$

At its center:

$$
\Delta p=0
$$

so:

$$
\alpha(0)=\alpha_0.
$$

Thus $\alpha_0$ is maximum primitive opacity before any additional clamps.

parts.title: Opacity logits and sigmoid decoding

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: THE 3D GAUSSIAN AS A GEOMETRIC PRIMITIVE
destinations.exact_quote:
Just as scale is stored in an unconstrained domain, opacity is stored as a logit:

$$
o\in\mathbb R.
$$

Decode:

$$
\boxed{
\alpha_0
=
\sigma(o)
=
\frac1{1+e^{-o}}.
}
$$

Therefore:

$$
0<\alpha_0<1.
$$

---

**Why logits help optimization**

Directly optimizing:

$$
\alpha\in[0,1]
$$

would require explicit constraints.

Logit is unconstrained.

The sigmoid maps it naturally.

Derivative:

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d\alpha}{do}
=
\alpha(1-\alpha).
}
$$

Maximum derivative occurs around:

$$
\alpha=0.5.
$$

Near 0 or 1 gradients saturate.

That is the standard tradeoff.

destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
If each Gaussian stored only:

$$
RGB
$$

then appearance would be view independent.

But real scenes contain:

- specularities,

\mathbf d

color becomes approximately:

$$
\boxed{
C(\mathbf d)
=
\sum_i
c_iY_i(\mathbf d).
}
$$

Each:

$$
Y_i
$$

is a spherical harmonic basis function.

Each:

$$
c_i
$$

is learned.

parts.title: Spherical-coordinate direction representation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
A normalized Cartesian direction:

$$
\mathbf d=
(x,y,z),
\quad
x^2+y^2+z^2=1
$$

can be written using angles.

Under one common convention:

$$
x=\sin\theta\cos\phi,
$$

$$
y=\sin\theta\sin\phi,
$$

$$
z=\cos\theta.
$$

Where:

$$
\theta
$$

is polar angle and:

$$
\phi
$$

is azimuth.

However, you do **not** need to compute:

$$
\theta,\phi
$$

to evaluate low-order real SH.

Polynomial expressions in:

$$
x,y,z
$$

are cheaper.

Maveb does exactly that.

---

parts.title: Spherical harmonics as angular basis functions

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
You could store an arbitrary function:

$$
C:S^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^3.
$$

But storing an entire function for every Gaussian is impossible.

Instead approximate it with a finite basis:

$$
C(\mathbf d)
\approx
\sum_{l=0}^{L}
\sum_{m=-l}^{l}
c_{lm}
Y_l^m(\mathbf d).
$$

This is analogous to Fourier series.

Fourier basis decomposes periodic 1D signals.

Spherical harmonics decompose functions on the sphere.

---

parts.title: SH degree and number of coefficients

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
SH functions are indexed by:

$$
l\ge0
$$

and:

$$
-l\le m\le l.
$$

For each degree $l$, number of functions is:

$$
2l+1.
$$

Total coefficients through degree $L$:

$$
N(L)
=
\sum_{l=0}^{L}
(2l+1).
$$

Use:

$$
\sum_{l=0}^{L}(2l+1)
=
(L+1)^2.
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
N(L)=(L+1)^2.
}
$$

---


| Degree $L$ | Basis coefficients per color | Total RGB coefficients | `f_rest_*` count |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 3 | 0 |
| 1 | 4 | 12 | 9 |
| 2 | 9 | 27 | 24 |
| 3 | 16 | 48 | 45 |

Why does degree 3 have:

$$
45
$$

rest values?

There are:

$$
16
$$

coefficients per color.

The DC term is already stored separately:

$$
1.
$$

Remaining:

$$
15
$$

per color.

Three colors:

$$
3\times15
=
45.
$$

Exactly Maveb's representation.

parts.title: Real spherical-harmonic basis functions concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
Maveb follows the standard real SH convention used by the GraphDECO renderer.

Degree zero:

$$
Y_0=
C_0
$$

with:

$$
C_0=
0.28209479177387814.
$$

Degree one:

$$
Y_1=-C_1y,
$$

$$
Y_2=C_1z,
$$

$$
Y_3=-C_1x,
$$

where:

$$
C_1=
0.4886025119029199.
$$

---

**Degree-two functions**

Maveb evaluates:

$$
Y_4=
1.0925484305920792xy,
$$

$$
Y_5=
-1.0925484305920792yz,
$$

$$
Y_6=
0.31539156525252005
(2z^2-x^2-y^2),
$$

$$
Y_7=
-1.0925484305920792xz,
$$

$$
Y_8=
0.5462742152960396
(x^2-y^2).
$$

These are real SH polynomial basis functions after normalization constants are folded in.

---

**Degree-three functions**

Maveb/GraphDECO degree-three terms are:

$$
Y_9=
-0.5900435899266435
y(3x^2-y^2),
$$

$$
Y_{10}
=
2.890611442640554xyz,
$$

$$
Y_{11}
=
-0.4570457994644658
y(4z^2-x^2-y^2),
$$

$$
Y_{12}
=
0.3731763325901154
z(2z^2-3x^2-3y^2),
$$

$$
Y_{13}
=
-0.4570457994644658
x(4z^2-x^2-y^2),
$$

$$
Y_{14}
=
1.445305721320277
z(x^2-y^2),
$$

$$
Y_{15}
=
-0.5900435899266435
x(x^2-3y^2).
$$

Current Maveb CPU and Metal implementations use these same constants.

The canonical GraphDECO CUDA implementation uses the same polynomial basis and adds a 0.5 color offset after SH evaluation. [GitHub](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization/blob/main/cuda_rasterizer/forward.cu?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

parts.title: PLY property declarations

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
PLY allows properties:

```text id="68k852"
property float x
property double opacity
property uint some_id
```

Maveb supports common signed/unsigned 8/16/32-bit integers and float32/float64 scalar fields.

For Gaussian vertices it rejects:

```text id="gkre1f"
property list ...
```

because a 3DGS Gaussian record is expected to be a flat scalar structure.

---

**Parse by name, not fixed column index**

This is important.

Do not assume:

$$
column_0=x,
column_1=y,...
$$

unless schema guarantees it.

Maveb parses property declarations, then assigns each scalar based on its name.

Therefore property order can vary while meaning remains intact.

This is robust.

---

parts.title: Binary little-endian PLY Gaussian parsing

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
Binary payload is:

```text id="j6pgmr"
vertex0 property0 bytes
vertex0 property1 bytes
...
vertex1 property0 bytes
...
```

Stride:

$$
S=
\sum_i
sizeof(property_i).
$$

Expected payload:

$$
PayloadBytes
=
VertexCount\times S.
$$

Maveb checks this exactly.

That prevents truncated/oversized malformed payloads.

---

**Manual little-endian reconstruction**

For unsigned integer bytes:

$$
b_0,b_1,\dots
$$

little-endian value:

$$
v=
\sum_i
b_i2^{8i}.
$$

Maveb explicitly reconstructs values from bytes.

That keeps file endianness semantics independent of host assumptions.

Float bit patterns can then be interpreted through the corresponding scalar handling.

---

parts.title: Stable Gaussian identifiers versus vector indices

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: SPHERICAL HARMONICS, PLY AND IDENTITY
destinations.exact_quote:
Suppose Gaussian vector is:

```text id="e6vf6b"
index 0 → A
index 1 → B
index 2 → C
```

Sort by depth:

```text id="riprkz"
index 0 → C
index 1 → A
index 2 → B
```

If identity means:

$$
index,
$$

then Gaussian A changed identity from:

$$
0\rightarrow1.
$$

That is unacceptable for:

- editor selection,
- physics correspondence,
- persistent edits,
- local repair,
- provenance.

---

**Stable identity**

Instead:

```text id="juc7yl"
A → stable ID 1001
B → stable ID 1002
C → stable ID 1003
```

Sorting changes storage indices, not identity.

You maintain:

$$
ID\rightarrow currentIndex
$$

as a transient lookup.

---

parts.title: Camera intrinsics fx and fy in Gaussian projection

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
Intrinsics matrix:

$$
\boxed{
K=
\begin{bmatrix}
f_x&0&c_x\\
0&f_y&c_y\\
0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}.
}
$$

$f_x,f_y$ are in **pixel units**.

If vertical field of view is:

$$
FOV_y
$$

and image height:

$$
H,
$$

then:

$$
\tan(FOV_y/2)
=
\frac{H/2}{f_y}.
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
f_y=
\frac{H}
{2\tan(FOV_y/2)}.
}
$$

For square pixels:

$$
f_x
$$

can be derived consistently from horizontal FOV or aspect.

If:

$$
FOV_x
=
2\arctan(
aspect\tan(FOV_y/2)
),
$$

then:

$$
f_x=
\frac{W}
{2\tan(FOV_x/2)}.
$$

Under square-pixel/aspect-consistent construction this yields the expected equivalent focal scale.

---

**Principal point**

Usually:

$$
c_x\approx W/2,
$$

$$
c_y\approx H/2.
$$

But calibrated cameras need not have centered principal point.

Maveb's reference camera stores both explicitly:

```text id="30s5gu"
focalX
focalY
centerX
centerY
```

which is the more general model.

parts.title: Why a projected 3D Gaussian becomes a 2D ellipse

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
Under a purely linear transformation:

$$
Y=AX+b,
$$

a Gaussian remains Gaussian:

$$
X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)
$$

implies:

$$
Y
\sim
\mathcal N(
A\mu+b,
A\Sigma A^T
).
$$

Perspective projection is not linear because of:

$$
X/Z,\quad Y/Z.
$$

So it does not globally transform a Gaussian into a mathematically exact Gaussian.

Instead we linearize projection around its center.

Locally:

$$
projection
\approx
affine.
$$

Affine transform of Gaussian is Gaussian.

Therefore the projected footprint is approximated by a 2D Gaussian.

Its constant-density contours are ellipses.

This local affine approximation is the same fundamental machinery used by EWA splatting. [vcg.seas.harvard.edu](https://vcg.seas.harvard.edu/content/3-publications/20010101-surface-splatting/p371-zwicker.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

parts.title: Local linearization of perspective projection

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
Let projection:

$$
\mathbf f:
\mathbb R^3
\rightarrow
\mathbb R^2.
$$

For point near mean:

$$
\mathbf x=
\mu+\delta.
$$

Taylor expansion:

$$
\mathbf f(\mu+\delta)
=
\mathbf f(\mu)
+
J_{\mathbf f}(\mu)\delta
+
O(\|\delta\|^2).
$$

Drop higher-order terms:

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf f(\mu+\delta)
\approx
\mathbf f(\mu)
+
J\delta.
}
$$

So local perturbations transform by:

$$
\delta_{screen}
\approx
J\delta_{camera}.
$$

Then covariance follows directly.

parts.title: Projection Jacobian derivation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
Projection:

$$
u(X,Y,Z)
=
f_x\frac XZ+c_x.
$$

Compute derivatives:

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial X}
=
\frac{f_x}{Z}.
$$

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial Y}
=
0.
$$

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial Z}
=
-f_x\frac{X}{Z^2}.
$$

Similarly:

$$
v=
f_y\frac YZ+c_y.
$$

So:

$$
\frac{\partial v}{\partial X}=0,
$$

$$
\frac{\partial v}{\partial Y}
=
\frac{f_y}{Z},
$$

$$
\frac{\partial v}{\partial Z}
=
-f_y\frac{Y}{Z^2}.
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
J=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{f_x}{Z}
&
0
&
-\frac{f_xX}{Z^2}
\\
0
&
\frac{f_y}{Z}
&
-\frac{f_yY}{Z^2}
\end{bmatrix}.
}
$$

This equation must become instinctive.

---

parts.title: Adding screen-space low-pass variance for stability concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
c\leftarrow c+0.3.
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma_s'
=
\Sigma_s
+
0.3I.
}
$$

The canonical GraphDECO rasterizer uses the same constant and explicitly describes it as a low-pass stabilization ensuring Gaussians retain a minimum screen footprint. [GitHub](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization/blob/main/cuda_rasterizer/forward.cu?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

**Why adding $\lambda I$ helps**

Eigenvalues of:

$$
\Sigma
$$

are:

$$
\lambda_i.
$$

Eigenvalues of:

$$
\Sigma+\epsilon I
$$

become:

$$
\lambda_i+\epsilon.
$$

So the smallest eigenvalue can no longer collapse below $\epsilon$, ignoring numerical roundoff.

That improves:

- invertibility,
- minimum pixel footprint,
- stability,
- anti-aliasing behavior.

---

**What $0.3$ means**

Variance:

$$
0.3\text{ pixels}^2.
$$

Corresponding standard deviation:

$$
\sqrt{0.3}
\approx0.548\text{ pixels}.
$$

A 3σ radius from that term alone is:

$$
3\sqrt{0.3}
\approx1.64\text{ pixels}.
$$

So even an extremely tiny projected splat retains a nonzero footprint.

---

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md

We now have:

\boxed{
\Sigma_{2D}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a&b\\
b&c
\end{bmatrix}.
}
$$

Interpretation:

$$
a=\sigma_x^2,
$$

$$
c=\sigma_y^2,
$$

while:

$$
b
$$

describes correlation/rotation.

If:

$$
b=0,
$$

ellipse axes align with screen axes.

If:

$$
b\ne0,
$$

ellipse is rotated.

---

**Example**

Suppose:

$$
\Sigma=
\begin{bmatrix}
9&0\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Standard deviations:

$$
3,\ 1.
$$

So one-sigma ellipse has radii:

$$
3,\ 1.
$$

Three-sigma:

$$
9,\ 3.
$$

If we rotate covariance 45°, diagonal entries/off-diagonal terms change, while eigenvalues remain:

$$
9,\ 1.
$$

Same ellipse shape.

Different screen orientation.

a&b\\
b&c

determinant:

$$
\boxed{
D=ac-b^2.

For SPD 2×2 covariance we need:

and:

Geometrically, determinant relates to ellipse area.

Product of eigenvalues:

$$
\lambda_1\lambda_2=D.

One-sigma ellipse area:

$$
A=
\pi
\sqrt{\lambda_1}
\sqrt{\lambda_2}
=
\boxed{
\pi\sqrt{D}.
}
$$

So determinant approaching zero means the ellipse collapses toward a line.

parts.title: Eigenvalues of a 2D covariance matrix

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
Solve:

$$
det(
\Sigma-\lambda I
)
=0.
$$

For:

$$
\Sigma=
\begin{bmatrix}
a&b\\
b&c
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$$
(a-\lambda)
(c-\lambda)
-b^2=0.
$$

Expand:

$$
\lambda^2
-
(a+c)\lambda
+
(ac-b^2)
=0.
$$

Quadratic formula:

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_{\pm}
=
\frac{
(a+c)
\pm
\sqrt{
(a-c)^2+4b^2
}
}{2}.
}
$$

Maveb computes:

```cpp
discriminant =
    sqrt(
      max(
        0,
        (a-c)^2 +
        4b^2));

maximumEigenvalue =
    0.5 *
    (a+c+discriminant);
```

Exactly:

$$
\lambda_{max}.
$$

---

**Eigenvector orientation**

For debugging or tight oriented geometry, ellipse angle can be obtained from:

$$
\boxed{
\theta=
\frac12
atan2(
2b,
a-c
).
}
$$

A major-axis unit vector:

$$
\mathbf e_{max}
=
(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)
$$

with sign/order adjusted according to which eigenvalue it corresponds to.

Maveb's simple CPU oracle does not need this because it uses an isotropic square bound based on $\lambda_{max}$.

Vulkax's projected representation does preserve major/minor oriented axes for raster geometry, so eigenvector interpretation becomes operational there.

parts.title: Bounding a projected Gaussian on screen

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
Maveb uses square:

$$
[x_c-r,x_c+r]
\times
[y_c-r,y_c+r].
$$

This contains the entire 3σ ellipse because every directional variance is bounded by:

$$
\lambda_{max}.
$$

Formally for unit $\mathbf u$:

$$
\mathbf u^T
\Sigma
\mathbf u
\le
\lambda_{max}.
$$

Hence no ellipse direction extends beyond:

$$
3\sqrt{\lambda_{max}}.
$$

---

**A tighter axis-aligned bound is possible**

For ellipse:

$$
\Delta^T
\Sigma^{-1}
\Delta
\le k^2,
$$

maximum x coordinate displacement is:

$$
\boxed{
|dx|_{max}
=
k\sqrt{a}.
}
$$

Maximum y:

$$
\boxed{
|dy|_{max}
=
k\sqrt{c}.
}
$$

So tighter AABB can use:

$$
r_x=3\sqrt a,
$$

$$
r_y=3\sqrt c.
$$

The $\lambda_{max}$ square is simpler and always conservative but can cause extra raster/tile work for very elongated Gaussians.

That performance distinction becomes important in Pass 16.

---

**Why conservative bounds are required**

A false positive bound:

> rasterize some pixels where Gaussian ultimately has negligible/no support

costs performance.

A false negative bound:

> fail to rasterize a pixel with valid contribution

changes the rendered image.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{bounding must err outward, never inward}.
}
$$

---

Maveb's reference renderer uses:

$$
Z<nearPlane
$$

or:

$$
Z>farPlane
$$

to reject.

Because reference camera looks along:

$$
+Z.
$$

This means:

$$
Z\le0
$$

is behind or at camera.

Near plane additionally prevents unstable:

$$
1/Z
$$

and:

$$
1/Z^2.

There is a subtle approximation.

A Gaussian center might satisfy:

$$
Z<near
$$

while its covariance volume extends into visible space.

Center culling would remove the whole primitive.

This is not a mathematically exact clipping of the Gaussian volume.

Most real 3DGS rasterizers rely on point-center/frustum-style visibility approximations because splats are generally sufficiently localized.

If you use gigantic Gaussians near the camera, this becomes a potential artifact.

That is a good stress test for Maveb.

destinations.exact_quote:
After low-pass regularization:

$$
D=
ac-b^2.
$$

Maveb checks:

$$
D\le10^{-12}
$$

or non-finite.

If so, reject.

Why?

Because conic needs:

$$
1/D.
$$

A tiny determinant produces huge coefficients and numerical instability.

---

**Determinant threshold alone is not a complete condition-number test**

Suppose:

$$
\lambda_1=10^{12},
$$

$$
\lambda_2=10^{-6}.
$$

Then:

$$
det=
10^6,
$$

which looks large.

But condition number:

$$
\kappa=
\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}
=
10^{18}.
$$

The matrix is terribly ill-conditioned.

For hostile inputs, a stronger test considers:

$$
\lambda_{min},
$$

or a scale-relative criterion such as:

$$
\boxed{
det
>
\epsilon
(trace(\Sigma))^2.
}
$$

The $+0.3I$ regularization already greatly limits this problem for ordinary 3DGS data.

**Radius sanity**

Maveb CPU oracle additionally rejects:

$$
r>10^6
$$

as unsafe.

This protects the reference implementation from a pathological Gaussian causing effectively unbounded raster work.

The inspected Metal projection kernel checks:

$$
isfinite(r)
$$

and:

$$
r>0
$$

plus screen overlap, but does not contain that same explicit $10^6$ upper bound.

That means hostile/extreme covariance cases can have slightly different failure behavior between CPU and GPU paths.

For ordinary learned assets this probably does not matter, but a correctness oracle should have an explicit stress case for it.

---


At every screen point:

$$
0<w\le1.
$$

Thus:

$$
\alpha(p)
=
\alpha_0w(p)
\le
\alpha_0.

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
This gives a very useful proof.

If:

$$
\alpha_0<\alpha_{threshold},
$$

then:

$$
\alpha(p)
<
\alpha_{threshold}
$$

for **every pixel**.

Therefore the Gaussian can be culled before projection/raster scheduling with no effect under that thresholding policy.

---

**Maveb's current behavior**

Maveb CPU reference does not currently projection-cull based solely on base opacity.

It projects the Gaussian, then during per-pixel evaluation computes:

$$
\alpha
=
\min(
0.99,
\alpha_0
e^{-q/2}
)
$$

and skips if:

$$
\boxed{
\alpha<
1/255.
}
$$

Because:

$$
w\le1,
$$

a Gaussian with:

$$
\alpha_0<1/255
$$

will necessarily contribute nothing anywhere.

So moving that check into projection would be a mathematically safe optimization relative to the existing per-pixel threshold.

---

**Vulkax already models opacity as a projection cull reason**

Its native projection result accounting explicitly distinguishes:

```text id="qdflga"
Visible
Opacity
BehindCamera
OutsideImage
```

and validates:

$$
InputSplats
=
Visible
+
CulledOpacity
+
CulledBehind
+
CulledOutside.
$$

That is a useful diagnostic model.

Maveb could expose the same category counters in its projection pipeline if detailed visibility telemetry becomes useful.

parts.title: Screen tiling for Gaussian rasterization

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
#### First-use completion — schedule the projected ellipse into actual tile work

We already know the screen-space center, conic, bounding radius, depth, color and source identity. A projected Gaussian is now a *bounded screen-space workload*. The remaining questions are concrete: which pixels might it affect, how do GPU threads find the Gaussians relevant to their tile without testing every Gaussian in the scene, and how do those contributors reach the pixel in an order suitable for transmittance compositing? We can answer them here, without deferring tiling and sorting to another numbered pass.

Let a render target have width $W$, height $H$, and square tile width $T$ pixels. Give tiles integer coordinates $(t_x,t_y)$, with $0\le t_x<\lceil W/T\rceil$ and $0\le t_y<\lceil H/T\rceil$. The conservative circular bound derived from the screen covariance is a circle of radius $r=3\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}$ around projected center $(u,v)$. The actual Gaussian ellipse may cover much less area; the circle is useful because it allows cheap rejection without missing the entire three-sigma ellipse. Clip its screen rectangle to the viewport. If the rectangle is empty, the Gaussian contributes no tile references.

For a nonempty clipped rectangle, conservatively map the minimum and maximum screen coordinates to tile indices by dividing by $T$ and taking the floor, clamped to valid tile coordinates. The exact upper-bound formula depends on whether the rectangle uses inclusive or exclusive pixel bounds. Never mix conventions: using an exclusive upper bound with an inclusive floor can either generate an unnecessary extra tile or, worse, omit a boundary sample after a mismatched clamp. Conservative overcount only wastes work; undercount removes contributions.

For example, let $W=H=64$, $T=16$, the center be $(20,20)$ and radius be $10$ pixels. Its bound runs from coordinate $10$ through $30$ on each axis, so it intersects tile columns 0 and 1 and tile rows 0 and 1. It emits four references, one each for tiles $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$. Those references do *not* copy the full Gaussian record: they name the Gaussian (by a stable index or validated handle) and the tile that may need it.

A scalable implementation is a count–scan–scatter pipeline. In the **count** stage each visible Gaussian reports how many tile references it requires. Suppose three Gaussians request counts $[2,0,1]$. An **exclusive scan** constructs offsets $[0,2,2,3]$. The first Gaussian owns output slots 0 and 1, the second owns an empty range beginning and ending at 2, and the third owns slot 2. The last offset is the required capacity $K=3$. This is a memory-allocation proof: before scattering, the producer knows how many references exist and which nonoverlapping range belongs to each Gaussian. A parallel GPU scan must establish that these offsets are ready before the scatter dispatch reads them. A workgroup barrier alone does not complete a cross-workgroup scan.

```text
# Read-only projected records, already validated and viewport-clipped.
for each gaussian i:
    tile_rectangle[i] = conservative_tile_range(center[i], radius[i])
    count[i] = number_of_tiles(tile_rectangle[i])

offset[0] = 0
for i in [0, gaussian_count):
    offset[i+1] = checked_add(offset[i], count[i])

This pseudocode makes each intermediate state explicit. **Count** is one integer per input Gaussian. **Scan** owns a prefix array of $N+1$ entries. **Scatter** writes exactly $K=\sum_i count_i$ references. **Sort** groups those references by tile and establishes the compositing order. **Raster** evaluates the actual conic at individual pixel samples, eliminating false positives left by the conservative tile bound. The tile list is therefore an acceleration structure for contributors, not a final visibility answer.

destinations.exact_quote:
Finally, the dependency graph is executable, not decorative: projected records must be ready before count; scan must finish before scatter; references must be complete and sorted before raster; and output attachments must survive until the final consumer. The source Gaussian buffer must remain allocated while references still contain its indices. A resize invalidates tile geometry and may require reallocation. An edit that changes Gaussian count, covariance, opacity or camera pose requires rebuilding the affected candidate ranges; reusing old ranges without a proof of conservativeness can silently remove pixels.

The immediate reconstruction test is now possible: for the 64-by-64 target, independently enumerate the four tile coordinates of the $(20,20)$ radius-10 Gaussian, verify the count–scan–scatter ranges on $[2,0,1]$, and compare the final two-Gaussian pixel against the earlier front-to-back CPU oracle. This proves separate facts about indexing, memory safety, order and color rather than accepting one plausible-looking screenshot as evidence for every stage.

parts.title: Filling flattened tile-reference arrays

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: FROM A 3D ELLIPSOID TO A SCREEN-SPACE CONIC
destinations.exact_quote:
transmittance *= (1-alpha)
            if transmittance < cutoff_T: break
        C += transmittance * linear_background
```

This pseudocode makes each intermediate state explicit. **Count** is one integer per input Gaussian. **Scan** owns a prefix array of $N+1$ entries. **Scatter** writes exactly $K=\sum_i count_i$ references. **Sort** groups those references by tile and establishes the compositing order. **Raster** evaluates the actual conic at individual pixel samples, eliminating false positives left by the conservative tile bound. The tile list is therefore an acceleration structure for contributors, not a final visibility answer.

A naive renderer considers all $N$ splats for each of the $M$ tiles, producing $O(NM)$ potential pair tests. A tiled pipeline instead emits $K$ actual overlap references and sorts or bins them. A small compact Gaussian can touch very few tiles; a giant close-up Gaussian can touch nearly all of them. This changes both the asymptotic work and the memory budget. Use a counter width that can represent the total $K$, check multiplication/addition overflow, and set a deliberate policy for unreasonably large footprints. Prefix-sum and sorting are not free, so on small workloads the simplest CPU or GPU path may still be faster. Measure count, scan, scatter, sort and raster time separately.

**Depth ordering is not implied by the GPU's stored depth convention.** Choose a monotone near-to-far key in the declared camera space, then encode or compare it consistently. A reversed-Z depth buffer, a positive-Z computer-vision camera and a negative-Z graphics camera may all represent the same physical scene with different numeric depth order. At equal depths use a deterministic tie policy if reproducibility matters, while recognizing that per-Gaussian center-depth sorting is only an approximation when spatially extended kernels intersect.

Finally, the dependency graph is executable, not decorative: projected records must be ready before count; scan must finish before scatter; references must be complete and sorted before raster; and output attachments must survive until the final consumer. The source Gaussian buffer must remain allocated while references still contain its indices. A resize invalidates tile geometry and may require reallocation. An edit that changes Gaussian count, covariance, opacity or camera pose requires rebuilding the affected candidate ranges; reusing old ranges without a proof of conservativeness can silently remove pixels.

The immediate reconstruction test is now possible: for the 64-by-64 target, independently enumerate the four tile coordinates of the $(20,20)$ radius-10 Gaussian, verify the count–scan–scatter ranges on $[2,0,1]$, and compare the final two-Gaussian pixel against the earlier front-to-back CPU oracle. This proves separate facts about indexing, memory safety, order and color rather than accepting one plausible-looking screenshot as evidence for every stage.

---

parts.title: Global versus per-tile Gaussian sorting

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: TILING, REFERENCE EXPANSION, SORTING AND COMPOSITING
destinations.exact_quote:
Sorting is not optional.

---


One option:

Sort every visible Gaussian globally by depth:

$$
G_{near}\rightarrow G_{far}.
$$

Then each tile can reference Gaussians in that order.

This is conceptually simple.

But if we duplicate a Gaussian across tiles anyway, sorting expanded references can directly produce per-tile contiguous ranges.

Maveb sorts:

$$
(tile,depth)
$$

references.

That simultaneously groups by tile and orders by depth.

---

**Why per-tile ordering is enough**

A pixel only receives Gaussians whose footprints overlap its tile.

Therefore relative ordering of:

$$
G_A
$$

in tile 12 and:

$$
G_B
$$

in tile 98 is irrelevant.

They can never affect the same pixel.

So a global total ordering contains unnecessary ordering constraints.

The true requirement is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{all splats that may affect the same pixel must be correctly ordered}.
}
$$

Tile-local sort is a conservative way to ensure that.

---


Suppose two splats have equal depth:

$$
z_A=z_B.
$$

Their alpha blend order still potentially changes output.

If GPU sorting arbitrarily permutes equal keys each frame, you can get:

- flickering,
- nondeterministic captures,
- CPU/GPU mismatch,
- difficult debugging.

So sort should be stable.

**Maveb's stability**

References are generated deterministically:

Gaussian index ascending.

Within each Gaussian, tile Y then tile X ascending.

The radix scatter uses prefix ranks preserving input order within each bucket.

Thus equal sort keys preserve initial relative order.

That gives deterministic tie behavior.

This matters much more than it first appears.

Comparison sort costs roughly:

$$
O(M\log M).
$$

Keys are fixed-width integers.

Radix sort can achieve:

$$
O(kM)
$$

where $k$ is number of digit passes.

parts.title: GPU radix sorting for Gaussian keys concept

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: TILING, REFERENCE EXPANSION, SORTING AND COMPOSITING
destinations.exact_quote:
**LSD radix sort**

Least-significant-digit radix sort processes low-order digit first.

For a multi-component composite key:

$$
(tile,depth),
$$

if stable sorting is used, sort **secondary** key first, then primary key.

We want tile primary, depth secondary.

So:

$$
\boxed{
\text{sort depth first}
\rightarrow
\text{sort tile second}.
}
$$

Because tile sort is stable, depth order inside each tile is preserved.

That is exactly Maveb's pass ordering.

---

**Maveb parallel radix**

Each `uint2` has:

$$
64\text{ bits total}.
$$

Default optimized path uses:

$$
4\text{-bit digits}.
$$

Each 32-bit component therefore needs:

$$
32/4=8
$$

passes.

Depth:

$$
8
$$

passes.

Tile:

$$
8
$$

passes.

Total:

$$
\boxed{16\text{ radix passes}.}
$$

The shader:

```metal
component =
    pass < 8
        ? key.x
        : key.y;
```

is therefore deliberate.

---

**One radix pass**

For one digit with:

$$
16
$$

possible buckets, Maveb performs:

```text id="asjrz1"
Histogram
↓
Global/group prefix offsets
↓
Stable scatter
```

Histogram determines how many elements belong to each bucket.

Prefix determines output starting address.

Stable scatter places each key/value at destination.

This is again:

$$
\boxed{
\text{count}
\rightarrow
\text{scan}
\rightarrow
\text{scatter}.
}
$$

The exact same GPU pattern appears again.

---

**SIMD-group acceleration**

Maveb's histogram uses:

```metal
simd_sum()
```

for bucket counts.

Scatter uses:

```metal
simd_prefix_exclusive_sum()
```

for rank inside the SIMD group.

For one element belonging to bucket $b$, local destination is:

$$
base_{group,b}
+
rank_{withinWorkgroup,b}.
$$

This avoids one atomic per sorted element.

---

**Why ping-pong buffers**

Sorting cannot safely scatter arbitrary elements in-place.

So Maveb owns:

```text id="t35rr1"
Keys A
Keys B

Values A
Values B.
```

Each pass:

$$
A\rightarrow B
$$

then:

$$
B\rightarrow A.
$$

After an even number of passes:

$$
16,
$$

result returns to A.

That is why range construction later reads:

```cpp
keysA_
```

and composite reads:

```cpp
valuesA_.
```

---

**Serial radix fallback**

Fallback uses:

$$
8\text{-bit digits}.
$$

Each 32-bit component:

$$
4
$$

passes.

Two components:

$$
8
$$

passes.

It is intentionally serial and deterministic.

Again:

$$
\text{fallback exists for correctness},
$$

not performance claims.

---

parts.title: Transmittance accumulation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: TILING, REFERENCE EXPANSION, SORTING AND COMPOSITING
destinations.exact_quote:
**Accumulated opacity formulation**

Instead of storing $T$, Maveb stores accumulated opacity:

$$
A=1-T.
$$

Then:

$$
T=1-A.
$$

Contribution:

$$
\boxed{
w_i=
(1-A_i)\alpha_i.
}
$$

Update:

$$
A_{i+1}
=
A_i+w_i.
$$

Maveb code:

```metal
contribution =
    (1.0f - opacity)
    * alpha;

color +=
    contribution
    * gaussian.color;

opacity +=
    contribution;
```

Exactly equivalent.

---

**Prove opacity recurrence**

Suppose:

$$
A_i=1-T_i.
$$

Then:

$$
A_{i+1}
=
A_i
+
(1-A_i)\alpha_i.
$$

Substitute:

$$
1-T_i
+
T_i\alpha_i
$$

$$
=
1-T_i(1-\alpha_i).
$$

Thus:

$$
T_{i+1}
=
T_i(1-\alpha_i).
$$

Correct.

---


After $n$ splats:

$$
\boxed{
T_n
=
\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}
(1-\alpha_i).
}
$$

Therefore accumulated opacity:

$$
\boxed{
A_n
=
1-
\prod_i(1-\alpha_i).
}
$$

Contribution of splat $i$:

$$
\boxed{
w_i
=
\alpha_i
\prod_{j<i}
(1-\alpha_j).
}
$$

This formula is worth memorizing.

It says:

> A Gaussian contributes its own alpha multiplied by how much light remains visible through everything in front of it.

Maveb terminates when:

$$
A>0.999.
$$

Equivalent:

$$
\boxed{
T<0.001.
}
$$

Remaining maximum contribution from bounded color $C_{max}$:

$$
\le
0.001C_{max}.
$$

That gives an actual error interpretation.

---

**Early termination saves exactly the expensive tail**

Dense scenes often have many splats behind already-opaque foreground.

Without early out:

```text id="ss9s8z"
evaluate
exp
blend
evaluate
exp
blend
...
```

for potentially hundreds/thousands of hidden splats.

With front-to-back compositing, once $T$ is tiny:

$$
\boxed{\text{stop}.}
$$

This is one reason front-to-back ordering is operationally valuable.

Maveb counts:

```text id="7ar1nv"
earlyTerminations
```

in GPU statistics.

That is useful performance evidence.

---


Traditional “over” can also be evaluated back-to-front.

Start with background:

$$
C=C_{bg}.
$$

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md

destinations.exact_quote:
---


Define premultiplied sample color:

$$
\tilde C_i
=
\alpha_i c_i.
$$

Then front-to-back:

$$
C
\leftarrow
C+
T\tilde C_i.
$$

and:

$$
T
\leftarrow
T(1-\alpha_i).
$$

Premultiplication cleanly separates:

$$
\text{color energy}
$$

from:

$$
\text{remaining transparency}.
$$

Maveb effectively computes premultiplied contribution on the fly:

```metal
contribution *
gaussian.color
```

where:

$$
contribution=T\alpha.
$$

---

**Why straight-color interpolation causes edge problems**

If transparent colors are stored as straight RGB, fully transparent pixels can carry arbitrary RGB.

Filtering/interpolation may pull those hidden colors into visible borders.

Premultiplied representation satisfies:

$$
\alpha=0
\Rightarrow
\tilde C=0.
$$

This generally behaves better under filtering/compositing.

---


Naively:

$$
e^{-q/2}
$$

can underflow for huge:

$$
q.
$$

parts.title: Avoiding numerical underflow in Gaussian evaluation

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: TILING, REFERENCE EXPANSION, SORTING AND COMPOSITING
destinations.exact_quote:
For float32, sufficiently negative exponents become subnormal then zero.

But Maveb does something better:

```metal
if (distance > 9)
    continue;

alpha =
    opacity *
    exp(-0.5 * distance);
```

Therefore exponent argument always lies:

$$
[-4.5,0]
$$

for evaluated samples.

No meaningful exponential underflow can occur.

This is a perfect example of:

$$
\boxed{
\text{algorithmic culling improves numerical robustness as well as performance}.
}
$$

---

**Transmittance underflow**

Another issue is:

$$
T=
\prod_i(1-\alpha_i).
$$

After many splats, $T$ may become extremely small.

But Maveb stops at:

$$
T<10^{-3}.
$$

So it never multiplies through thousands of values toward true floating-point underflow.

Again:

$$
\boxed{
\text{early termination prevents both wasted work and pathological numerics}.
}
$$

---

parts.title: CPU reference Gaussian rasterizer loop ordering

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: CPU ORACLE, METAL EXECUTION AND QUANTITATIVE AGREEMENT
destinations.exact_quote:
Maveb's CPU oracle first projects all valid Gaussians.

Then:

```cpp
std::ranges::stable_sort(
    projected,
    {},
    &Projected::depth);
```

Since reference camera uses:

$$
+Z
$$

forward and smaller positive $Z$ is closer:

$$
\boxed{
\text{ascending depth}
=
\text{front-to-back}.
}
$$

Stable sort preserves source order for equal depth.

This is deliberately compatible with deterministic GPU ordering.

---

**Why a CPU oracle should be simple**

The CPU reference implementation should optimize primarily for:

$$
\boxed{
\text{clarity + determinism + correctness}.
}
$$

Not maximum performance.

If CPU and GPU share the same clever algorithm and same bug, comparison proves nothing.

A useful oracle should be independent enough that implementation mistakes are unlikely to correlate.

Maveb's CPU rasterizer does not run the GPU's radix pipeline.

It globally stable-sorts projected records, then rasterizes them.

Good.

---

**Yet CPU still avoids pathological $P\times N$**

Maveb partitions the image into horizontal:

$$
16\text{-row bands}.
$$

For each projected Gaussian it computes pixel AABB and inserts a `BandEntry` into every intersected horizontal band.

Then each band processes only relevant Gaussians.

This is not the exact same 16×16 tile algorithm as GPU.

That difference is useful.

---

**Why deterministic threading survives**

Global projected list is already sorted.

Band lists receive Gaussians in that sorted order.

Every band owns disjoint rows.

So threads never concurrently update the same pixel.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{thread scheduling does not affect pixel accumulation order}.
}
$$

This gives deterministic multi-threaded CPU output.

That is an excellent oracle design.

---

(R_{DC},G_{DC},B_{DC},padding).

This is a GPU-friendly fixed-size record.

Projection:

1\ GPU\ thread
\leftrightarrow
1\ Gaussian.
}

Kernel receives:

[[thread_position_in_grid]]

and exits if:

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md

destinations.exact_quote:
Current projected record:

```cpp id="2lb4al"
struct AetherProjectedGaussian
{
    float4 centerDepthRadius;
    float4 conicOpacity;
    float4 color;

    uint4 tileBounds;
    uint4 sourceCountValid;
};
```

Size:

$$
\boxed{80\text{ bytes}.}
$$

---

**Field semantics**

$$
centerDepthRadius
=
(c_x,c_y,z,r).
$$

$$
conicOpacity
=
(A,B,C,\alpha_0).
$$

$$
color
=
(R,G,B,1).
$$

`tileBounds` contains:

$$
(minX,minY,maxX,maxY)
$$

in tile coordinates.

`sourceCountValid` currently stores:

$$
(sourceIndex,\ overlapCount,\ valid,\ SHdegree).
$$

This is a well-designed projection product because composite kernel no longer needs:

- world-space covariance,
- quaternion,
- log scale,
- SH coefficients,
- camera projection math.

All that expensive work was amortized once per Gaussian.

---

**Projection is a representation-lowering stage**

This resembles compiler lowering.

Rich representation:

```text id="jyhwui"
3D mean
quaternion
scale
SH coefficients
opacity logit
```

becomes:

```text id="z54oi2"
2D center
depth
conic
opacity
color
tile bounds
```

The second form is exactly what rasterization needs.

This is why GPU pipelines benefit from explicit intermediate representations.

---


There are at least two broad ways to splat.

Raster approach:

Create one quad per projected Gaussian.

Rasterize quad.

Fragment shader evaluates Gaussian.

Use blending.

Compute approach:

Tile/bin Gaussians.

Dispatch one thread per pixel.

Explicitly loop ordered splats and perform compositing.

parts.title: Metal raster or compute compositing strategies

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: CPU ORACLE, METAL EXECUTION AND QUANTITATIVE AGREEMENT
destinations.exact_quote:
Maveb currently chooses compute.

---

**Raster splat advantages**

Hardware rasterization gives:

- coverage generation,
- primitive setup,
- blend units,
- easy quad projection.

A simple Gaussian renderer can be built quickly this way.

Vulkax even contains projected-raster paths using generated quad geometry.

---

**Raster disadvantages**

Correct ordering for millions of translucent splats remains difficult.

Blend hardware cannot magically solve arbitrary per-pixel ordering.

A global splat order may work approximately but has problems with overlapping anisotropic geometry and per-tile ordering.

You may also pay:

- huge quad overdraw,
- fragment invocation outside true ellipse,
- per-splat draw/instance management.

---

**Compute advantages**

Compute lets renderer explicitly control:

$$
\text{tile list}
$$

$$
\text{ordering}
$$

$$
\text{early termination}
$$

$$
\text{debug IDs/depth}
$$

$$
\text{overflow handling}.
$$

This makes it an excellent fit for serious 3DGS rasterization.

---

**Compute disadvantage**

You implement much more yourself:

- scan,
- sort,
- ranges,
- pixel loops,
- synchronization.

Which is precisely why Maveb has 13 compute pipelines for this subsystem.

---


Dependencies:

```text id="sd09sx"
Projection writes:
    projected
    counts

Scan reads counts
writes offsets

Key generation reads:
    projected
    offsets
writes:
    keys
    values

Radix reads/writes:
    keys
    values

Range construction reads keys
writes ranges

Composite reads:
    projected
    sorted values
    ranges

Composite writes:
    color/depth/ID textures
```

These are real RAW dependencies.

---

parts.title: Synchronization between projection, sort/bin, and composite stages

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: CPU ORACLE, METAL EXECUTION AND QUANTITATIVE AGREEMENT
destinations.exact_quote:
**Current Metal synchronization strategy**

Maveb ends the compute encoder after each stage.

Then creates the next encoder on the **same command buffer**.

The relevant buffers use normal tracked Metal hazard semantics; the pipeline is not using an explicit untracked-memory scheme here.

Thus Metal orders and tracks producer→consumer dependencies across encoders.

There is no long sequence of Vulkan-style manual barriers in `GaussianPipeline::encode()`.

That does **not** mean synchronization is absent.

It means:

$$
\boxed{
\text{dependency is expressed through ordered encoders + Metal resource hazard tracking}.
}
$$

Exactly the Metal-vs-Vulkan distinction from Pass 13.

---

**Why separate encoders are convenient here**

Each stage has a clear boundary:

```text id="9acmg5"
Projection encoder ends
↓
Scan encoder starts
```

so Metal can understand that a producer phase precedes consumer phase.

Within one compute encoder, if dispatches read data written by previous dispatch without sufficient implicit scope, memory-barrier semantics may be needed.

Maveb's design avoids ambiguity by giving major stages separate encoders.

---

parts.title: CPU-versus-GPU Gaussian image comparison

destinations.file: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography.md
destinations.heading: CPU ORACLE, METAL EXECUTION AND QUANTITATIVE AGREEMENT
destinations.exact_quote:
A serious GPU renderer needs an oracle.

Test conditions should use identical:

$$
\text{Gaussian asset},
$$

$$
\text{camera intrinsics/extrinsics},
$$

$$
\text{viewport},
$$

$$
\text{background},
$$

$$
\text{SH convention},
$$

$$
\text{alpha thresholds}.
$$

Then render:

$$
I_{CPU}
$$

and:

$$
I_{GPU}.
$$

Compare in:

$$
\boxed{\text{linear color space}.}
$$

Do not compare after arbitrary tone mapping if testing the Gaussian integrator itself.

---

**Maveb's current correctness philosophy**

The repository's accepted Metal Gaussian ADR says the standard renderer includes:

- projection,
- anisotropic covariance,
- culling,
- overlap counts,
- exclusive offsets,
- key generation,
- stable ordering,
- tile ranges,
- front-to-back composition,
- depth,
- IDs,
- early termination,
- bounded overflow.

It also specifies a Metal test spanning more than one scan/radix block with shuffled depths and varying colors, compared against the CPU oracle.

That is exactly the kind of test needed.

I did **not** find a current repository implementation named specifically around all four curriculum metrics—RMSE, PSNR, maximum error and changed-pixel fraction—in the inspected Gaussian test paths, so the formulas below are the validation methodology required by the curriculum rather than a claim that Maveb already exposes each metric as a production API.

---


For two images with:

$$
N
$$

scalar channel samples:

$$
e_i=
G_i-R_i.
$$

MSE:

$$
\boxed{
MSE=
\frac1N
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
e_i^2.
}
$$

RMSE:

$$
\boxed{
RMSE=
\sqrt{
\frac1N
\sum_i
(G_i-R_i)^2
}.
}
$$

Units are same as image values.

If image is linear normalized RGB, RMSE of:

$$
10^{-3}
$$

means average magnitude of numerical difference is small.

But exact acceptable threshold depends on scene, precision and expected backend differences.

Do not invent universal threshold.

destinations.exact_quote:
For backend numerical validation, RMSE plus max error is often less ambiguous.

---


Define:

$$
\boxed{
E_{\max}
=
\max_{p,c}
|G_{p,c}-R_{p,c}|.
}
$$

RMSE can hide one catastrophic pixel.

Example:

One pixel error:

$$
1
$$

among a million perfect pixels gives small RMSE.

But max error reveals:

$$
1.
$$

So both matter.

---

**Location of max error**

Do not store only scalar max.

Store:

```cpp id="vgsyyh"
struct MaxError
{
    float Error;
    uint32_t X;
    uint32_t Y;
    uint32_t Channel;
};
```

Then debugger can inspect:

- Gaussian ID,
- depth,
- tile,
- sort rank,
- conic.

That turns a metric into a diagnostic.

---


Choose threshold:

$$
\epsilon.
$$

Define changed indicator:

$$
I_p=
\begin{cases}
1,&
\max_c|\Delta_{p,c}|>\epsilon\\
0,&
\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
F_{changed}
=
\frac1P
\sum_p I_p.
}
$$

This distinguishes:

> tiny errors everywhere

from:

> large/localized errors in one region.

---

destinations.exact_quote:
**Why RMSE + max + changed fraction is much more informative**

Case A:

Every pixel differs by:

$$
10^{-4}.
$$

Low RMSE.

Low max.

Changed fraction maybe 100% for tiny epsilon.

Likely systematic floating-point variation.

Case B:

Only 1% pixels wrong by:

$$
0.5.
$$

RMSE might still look moderate.

Max huge.

Changed fraction 1%.

Likely culling/boundary/sorting issue.

Metrics together reveal error structure.

---

**Validate semantic buffers separately**

Maveb already produces:

$$
color,
depth,
ID.
$$

Its debug modes expose:

```text id="zp6hzo"
appearance
logarithmic depth
source ID
tile occupancy
accumulated opacity
SH bands
sort rank
```

That is excellent for fault isolation.

Color mismatch with matching depth/ID suggests:

$$
SH/alpha.
$$

ID mismatch suggests:

$$
ordering/culling.
$$

Tile occupancy mismatch suggests:

$$
projection/bounds/scheduler.
$$

Sort-rank mismatch suggests:

$$
key/radix/ranges.
$$

---

**ID validation**

Away from equal-depth/raster-boundary ambiguities, dominant source ID should often match exactly:

$$
\boxed{
ID_{CPU}(p)=ID_{GPU}(p).
}
$$

A color tolerance cannot excuse a completely different dominant Gaussian unless there is a documented near-tie.

This is an extremely strong validation signal.

---

**Depth validation**

Maveb stores depth of first accepted contributing splat:

CPU:

```cpp
if depth == infinity:
    depth =
        gaussian.depth;
```

GPU:

```metal
if (!isfinite(depth))
    depth =
        gaussian.centerDepthRadius.z;
```

So CPU/GPU should agree closely if sort and alpha thresholds agree.

If they do not:

$$
\boxed{
\text{suspect order before shading}.
}
$$

---

# From an anisotropic kernel to an editable captured world

A 3D Gaussian renderer begins with a compact description of each primitive and ends with a collection of pixel contributions. An editable captured world adds another requirement: when a chair, curtain, or wall changes, the system must still know which records represent it, which physical variables can move them, and how to prove that unrelated image regions remained stable. The useful teaching chain is therefore

$$
\text{trained parameters}
\to \text{3D covariance}
\to \text{screen conic}
\to \text{tile references}
\to \text{ordered compositing}
\to \text{verified semantic edit}.
$$

The first five arrows belong mainly to graphics. The last arrow needs engine identity, storage, physics, and publication contracts. The boundary matters: a fast picture can be an excellent view synthesizer without being a reliable mesh, collider, or editable world. The existing graphics chapter already introduces explicit Gaussian splats and first-order screen covariance; the existing engine material already treats identity, lifetime, renderer boundaries, and frame resources. This bridge connects those ideas without replacing them .

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Stored mean, scale, rotation, opacity, SH] --> B[3D covariance and appearance]
    B --> C[Camera projection and 2D conic]
    C --> D[Tile counts, scan, and references]
    D --> E[Stable tile-depth order]
    E --> F[Per-pixel transmittance and color]
    F --> G[Persistent Gaussian and entity IDs]
    G --> H[Physical support and deformation]
    H --> I[Published revised render state]
```

destinations.exact_quote:
## A primitive with shape and appearance

A triangle stores three corners plus connectivity to adjacent triangles. Its coverage is bounded by straight projected edges, and a collection of triangles explicitly describes a piecewise planar surface. A Gaussian splat starts from a mean $\mu\in\mathbb R^3$ and a covariance matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$. The mean locates the primitive. The covariance describes how its support stretches and tilts in space. Opacity and a directional color model describe how much light it contributes and how that appearance depends on the viewing direction. The 2023 3D Gaussian Splatting paper represents scenes using anisotropic Gaussians initialized from sparse reconstruction points, optimizes their position, covariance, opacity, and spherical-harmonic appearance, and renders visible elements through a tile-based splatting pipeline. Those are properties of that method and its benchmarks, not universal speed or quality guarantees ([Kerbl et al., paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079)).

For displacement $x-\mu$, the unnormalized spatial weight is

$$
w(x)=\exp\left[-\frac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right].
$$

The quadratic $q=(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$ is the squared Mahalanobis distance: it measures distance after scaling and rotating coordinates by the Gaussian shape. A Gaussian’s constant-weight sets are ellipsoids. This formula is not, by itself, a normalized probability density; the normalizing factor involving $|\Sigma|^{-1/2}$ is omitted in common rendering kernels because the primitive’s learned opacity supplies amplitude. That distinction prevents a common category error: rendered opacity is not a probability mass or a physical density.

Covariance is symmetric. If $u$ is a unit direction, its variance along that direction is $u^T\Sigma u$. A convenient representation constructs covariance from a rotation $R$ and positive axis scales $s=(s_x,s_y,s_z)$:

$$
\Sigma=R\operatorname{diag}(s_x^2,s_y^2,s_z^2)R^T.
$$

The squares appear because scale is a standard-deviation-like length while covariance stores variance. With identity rotation and $s=(2,1,0.25)$, the covariance is $\operatorname{diag}(4,1,0.0625)$. The one-standard-deviation ellipsoid has semiaxes $(2,1,0.25)$; a three-sigma support approximation has semiaxes $(6,3,0.75)$. This is a concrete way to distinguish scale from covariance before involving a camera.

The factorization also explains positivity. Let $M=R\operatorname{diag}(s)$. Then $\Sigma=MM^T$. For any vector $x$,

$$
x^T\Sigma x=x^TMM^Tx=\|M^Tx\|^2\ge 0.
$$

Thus $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite. To invert it, it must be positive definite: no axis may collapse and $M$ must be nonsingular. A quaternion used to construct $R$ must also be normalized; otherwise its matrix formula may not describe an orthonormal rotation. In an implementation, finite inputs and sensible numeric ranges still need checks because exponentiating an extreme log scale can overflow or underflow. A mathematical positivity argument does not protect a parser from hostile values.

Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting also stores view-dependent color. Spherical harmonics (SH) are a finite basis of smooth functions over viewing directions. A color channel is approximated as $C(d)=\sum_k c_kY_k(d)$, with coefficients $c_k$ and basis functions $Y_k$. Degree $L$ contains $(L+1)^2$ terms per channel: degree three has sixteen terms per color, and if the degree-zero coefficient is stored separately, fifteen remaining terms per channel, or forty-five higher-order values total. The direction convention is part of the data contract. Reversing the view direction changes the sign of odd-degree terms, so a model can have plausible geometry and still show wrong view-dependent color. Test degree zero first—it should not vary with camera direction—then activate one degree-one coefficient at a time.

A PLY file is a container of named scalar properties, not a universal 3DGS schema. A loader must define property names, accepted scalar types, byte order, record size, optional coefficient counts, and malformed-input behavior. Parsing by declared property name is safer than assuming that position occupies the first three columns. The distinction between stored and decoded values matters: log-scales and opacity logits are optimizer-friendly encodings; decoding them belongs at a clearly defined boundary. Likewise, a source array index is stable only while the array’s order stays fixed. It is not a persistent primitive identity when compaction or filtering reorders records.

**Translation affects the mean, not covariance**

If:

$$
X'=AX+b,

then:

$$
E[X']
=
A\mu+b.

$$
Cov(X')
=
A\Sigma A^T.

Translation disappears because:

$$
(X'+-\mu')
=
A(X-\mu).
$$

So center transformation uses:

$$
R\mu+t.
$$

Covariance uses only:

$$
R\Sigma R^T.
$$

destinations.heading: From an anisotropic kernel to an editable captured world
destinations.exact_quote:
For 3DGS, a surface often emerges from many overlapping anisotropic kernels.

You can have:

$$
G_1+G_2+\cdots+G_N
$$

forming the appearance of a wall even though no triangle says:

> these three samples define a wall.

This is why Gaussian scenes are powerful representations of captured appearance but are not automatically equivalent to watertight physical geometry.

That distinction will become central in M150.

destinations.exact_quote:
### THE COMPLETE PASS-15 TRANSFORMATION

You should now be able to start from one PLY row and reach the screen-space ellipse without hand-waving.

Stored Gaussian:

$$
\boxed{
G=
(
\mu,
\ell,
q,
o,
SH
).
}
$$

Decode scales:

$$
\boxed{
s=e^\ell.
}
$$

Normalize quaternion:

$$
\boxed{
q\leftarrow
q/\|q\|.
}
$$

Construct rotation:

$$
R=R(q).
$$

Construct 3D covariance:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma_w
=
R
diag(s_x^2,s_y^2,s_z^2)
R^T.
}
$$

Decode opacity:

$$
\boxed{
\alpha_0=
sigmoid(o).
}
$$

Evaluate view-dependent SH color:

$$
\boxed{
C(\mathbf d)
=
\max
\left(
0,
0.5+
\sum_i
c_iY_i(\mathbf d)
\right).
}
$$

Transform center:

$$
\boxed{
\mu_c=
R_c\mu_w+t_c
=
(X,Y,Z).
}
$$

Cull invalid depth.

Project center:

$$
\boxed{
u=
f_xX/Z+c_x,
\qquad
v=
f_yY/Z+c_y.
}
$$

Transform covariance:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma_c=
R_c\Sigma_wR_c^T.
}
$$

Construct Jacobian:

$$
\boxed{
J=
\begin{bmatrix}
f_x/Z&0&-f_xX/Z^2\\
0&f_y/Z&-f_yY/Z^2
\end{bmatrix}.
}
$$

Project covariance:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma_{2D}
=
J\Sigma_cJ^T.
}
$$

Regularize:

$$
\boxed{
\Sigma'_{2D}
=
\Sigma_{2D}
+
0.3I.
}
$$

Write:

$$
\Sigma'=
\begin{bmatrix}
a&b\\
b&c
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Check:

$$
\boxed{
D=ac-b^2>0.
}
$$

Invert:

$$
\boxed{
C=
\frac1D
\begin{bmatrix}
c&-b\\
-b&a
\end{bmatrix}.
}
$$

Largest eigenvalue:

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_{max}
=
\frac{
a+c+
\sqrt{(a-c)^2+4b^2}
}{
2
}.
}
$$

Three-sigma conservative radius:

$$
\boxed{
r=
3\sqrt{\lambda_{max}}.
}
$$

Cull if screen rectangle does not intersect viewport.

What survives is a projected splat containing approximately:

**Validate semantic buffers separately**

Maveb already produces:

$$
color,
depth,
ID.
$$

Its debug modes expose:

```text id="zp6hzo"
appearance
logarithmic depth
source ID
tile occupancy
accumulated opacity
SH bands
sort rank
```

That is excellent for fault isolation.

Color mismatch with matching depth/ID suggests:

$$
SH/alpha.
$$

ID mismatch suggests:

$$
ordering/culling.
$$

Tile occupancy mismatch suggests:

$$
projection/bounds/scheduler.
$$

Sort-rank mismatch suggests:

$$
key/radix/ranges.
$$

---

**ID validation**

Away from equal-depth/raster-boundary ambiguities, dominant source ID should often match exactly:

$$
\boxed{
ID_{CPU}(p)=ID_{GPU}(p).
}
$$

A color tolerance cannot excuse a completely different dominant Gaussian unless there is a documented near-tie.

This is an extremely strong validation signal.

---
